items.title: llm-echo 0.5
items.summary: Release: llm-echo 0.5 I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account. Example usage: uvx --with llm-echo llm -m echo 'hi there' -o thinking 1 --usage Outputs: First I consider the prompt, then I decide what to say. { "prompt": "hi there", "system": "", "attachments": [], "stream": true, "previous": [] } Token usage: 2 input, 24 output Tags: llm
items.summary_html:
Release: llm-echo 0.5

I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account.

Example usage:

uvx --with llm-echo llm -m echo 'hi there' -o thinking 1 --usage

Outputs:

First I consider the prompt, then I decide what to say.
{
  "prompt": "hi there",
  "system": "",
  "attachments": [],
  "stream": true,
  "previous": []
}
Token usage: 2 input, 24 output

Tags: llm

items.title: Meta, Tesla and Netflix Q3 Updates Coming This Week
items.summary: Tech earnings season is back (yes, I know it feels like it never ends). This time, we’ve got a slight twist: Meta Platforms has broken with the pack and is reporting its September-quarter earnings on Wednesday, a week ahead of its big tech counterparts, Google, Microsoft and Amazon. (Apple is even later, on Nov. 2.) By reporting earlier than the others, Meta ensures it will grab more of the spotlight, for better or worse. Until last week’s market sell-off, Meta had been riding a wave of enthusiasm on Wall Street, thanks to chatter about its Muse personal agent and recently released Muse Wonder AI models. Things changed last week, particularly on Friday, as renewed jitters about the AI expansion tanked most tech stocks. Given Meta’s gargantuan spending on AI development, this week’s update will provide a new test of investor sentiment toward Meta shares.

items.title: The Next AI Outage Could Begin With Two Approved Changes
items.summary: AI-generated illustration created with ChatGPT As more agents operate production, they will have to coordinate what they are allowed to disrupt. Imagine a payment service halfway through a migration. A traffic layer can route requests to a backend on a VM or to another in Kubernetes. Both are healthy, and either can handle the current traffic on its own. During this phase, the Kubernetes workload uses a stop-and-start deployment. The old instance goes offline before its replacement starts. The VM is expected to carry payments through that interruption. An infrastructure agent prepares to reboot the VM after maintenance. It checks that the Kubernetes backend can keep serving payments. At the same time, a deployment agent prepares its release and checks that the VM can keep serving payments. Both have permission. Both choose the intended tool. Both inspect live state. Then they execute at the same time. For a short period, neither backend can serve a payment. Each plan was acceptable on its own. Each depended on the other plan not happening. Both agents counted on the same redundancy. This is a hypothetical scenario. It raises a practical question for anyone building agents that can change production: how does one piece of automation find out that another has already committed to a change that conflicts with its own? What happens after an agent gets access? Uber Engineering’s article on its MCP Gateway provides a useful starting point. It describes a platform hosting more than 800 MCP servers and 5,000 tools. A registry manages discovery and ownership; a proxy connects agents to existing services. Tools start disabled and require owner review and enablement. Authorization and sensitive-data redaction are also built into the gateway. [1] Reading that design made me think about the next decision in an infrastructure workflow. Once an agent has found a tool and has permission to call it, what establishes that this particular change can proceed now? The proposal here concerns that admission decision. The payment example is separate from Uber’s implementation; their gateway article does not establish what coordination mechanisms exist elsewhere in their systems. In our example, the infrastructure agent touches the VM and the deployment agent touches Kubernetes. Their credentials can be correctly scoped and their resource locks completely separate. Both changes still affect the same payment service. That shared condition needs an owner. A familiar concurrency problem The failure resembles write skew in a database: two actors read a condition involving multiple records, update different records, and leave the condition false. PostgreSQL’s transaction-isolation documentation describes related serialization anomalies, where individually successful transactions produce a result that no serial ordering would have produced. [2] Here, the shared condition is simple: at least one backend must remain able to serve payments. Checking it independently gives both agents a reason to proceed. Kubernetes already has a related mechanism in PodDisruptionBudgets. A PDB can limit eligible voluntary pod evictions, but it does not coordinate maintenance on an external VM. Kubernetes also documents that Deployment and StatefulSet rolling updates are not constrained by PDBs; their rollout behavior is configured separately. [3] Maintenance coordination predates AI. A script and a human operator could cause the same collision. Agents make the problem relevant to more workflows because they can assemble actions across tools and systems. The execution platform needs a way to express the application condition those actions share. Reserve the allowance before starting the change For this payment service, the admission rule can be stated precisely: After accounting for work already admitted and the proposed change, at least one verified backend capable of carrying the current load must remain available. The first admitted change reserves the service’s allowance for disruption. That reservation starts before the action, while both backends may still look healthy. The following sequence is illustrative: Both backends are verified healthy and capable of carrying the current load. The service can tolerate one being unavailable. VM maintenance is admitted. Its disruption reservation is recorded before the reboot starts. The Kubernetes deployment requests admission. It waits because VM maintenance holds the reservation, even if monitoring still shows the VM as healthy. The reboot command completes. The reservation stays active while the required service checks run. The VM passes those checks. Its reservation is released, and the deployment refreshes its evidence before requesting admission again. Checking for conflicts and recording the reservation must be atomic. Two separate calls would recreate the original race. One implementation could use a PostgreSQL row keyed by tenant and service identity. A short transaction locks that row, reads outstanding reservations, evaluates the proposed change against the relevant evidence, and records the reservation and an execution request before committing. Every admission and reservation update for that service must follow the same coordination rule. PostgreSQL’s row-locking facilities provide the serialization point for those transactions. [4] The database lock ends when the transaction commits. The durable reservation remains while the external work proceeds. A reboot may take minutes; there is no reason to hold the database transaction open for that duration. This simple design serializes disruptive work within one service. A change affecting several services would need to acquire all its required reservations together, or acquire none and wait. Otherwise it could protect one application while leaving another exposed. A small concurrency check The core race is small enough to reproduce without a cloud account. This Python model has two workers, one for each backend. A barrier makes both admission decisions happen before either worker disrupts its target. Health observations deliberately remain unchanged during the actions. That models a monitoring delay and makes the role of reservations visible. from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor from threading import Barrier, Lock class Service: def __init__(self): self.observed = {"vm", "k8s"} self.serving = {"vm", "k8s"} self.reserved = set() self.lock = Lock() def admit(self, target, reserve=True): with self.lock: if not (self.observed - self.reserved - {target}): return False if reserve: self.reserved.add(target) return True def disrupt(self, target): with self.lock: self.serving.remove(target) # Health observations deliberately lag behind the action. def reconcile(self, target, verified_serving): with self.lock: if verified_serving: self.serving.add(target) self.observed.add(target) self.reserved.discard(target) def concurrent_changes(reserve): service, checked = Service(), Barrier(2) def worker(target): admitted = service.admit(target, reserve) checked.wait() # Both admission decisions precede either action. if admitted: service.disrupt(target) return admitted with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool: admitted = list(pool.map(worker, ("vm", "k8s"))) return sum(admitted), len(service.serving) for reserve in (False, True): admitted, remaining = concurrent_changes(reserve) print(f"reserve={reserve}: admitted={admitted}, serving={remaining}") service = Service() assert service.admit("vm") service.disrupt("vm") # Model a worker that stops here; the coordinator retains its state. service.reconcile("vm", verified_serving=False) print("after worker loss:", service.admit("k8s")) service.reconcile("vm", verified_serving=True) print("after verified recovery:", service.admit("k8s")) Running the example produces: reserve=False: admitted=2, serving=0 reserve=True: admitted=1, serving=1 after worker loss: False after verified recovery: True The first run admits both changes and leaves no serving backend. The second admits one change and leaves the other backend available. Notice that both runs protect the check with a lock. The reservation is what makes the first decision visible to the next one. The final case models a worker stopping after it disrupts the VM. The coordinator retains the reservation and refuses the Kubernetes change until a verified recovery is supplied. This is a model of one interleaving, with one request per target and enough capacity on either backend. It does not test a distributed coordinator, persistence across process crashes, or real health checks. The recovery boolean represents evidence that a production system would have to collect. Its purpose is to expose the admission error and show the state that prevents it. What the graph contributes For two known backends, explicit service membership is enough. A shared reservation can solve this example without a graph database. The harder question is how to establish the affected service when the target is a VM process, a Kubernetes workload, a load-balancer target, or a shared dependency. Those relationships change during migrations and deployments. Keeping them in a manually maintained list becomes an operational responsibility of its own. This is where a compiled system graph can help. By compiled , I mean a model that resolves identities across collected sources and turns their metadata and observations into explicit relationships. It connects a VM to its processes, workloads to their serving endpoints, and those endpoints to the applications they support. Each relationship carries its origin and the time it was last supported by evidence. The graph helps determine which service conditions a proposed change could affect. The coordinator uses those conditions to evaluate reservations. The executor enforces the admitted plan and gathers the evidence needed to complete it. A graph can be accurate about the present while two approved plans are about to make it obsolete. Admission therefore needs both the dependency model and the record of work already committed. Service membership can also change while a reservation is active. I would tie each reservation to a stable service identity within its tenant and record the dependency revision and evidence used at admission. If a migration changes the service’s backends or critical dependencies, the coordinator should reevaluate active plans before admitting more work. Updating the graph must not make an existing reservation disappear or allow a conflicting change to enter under a new identity. If the required serving condition can no longer be verified, further disruptive steps should pause. The reservation remains active until recovery is verified or reconciliation establishes that releasing it is safe. For the payment example, a structural simulation can remove the proposed backend from the model, account for existing reservations, and check whether a serving path remains. That is a useful, bounded result. It does not establish that the remaining backend has enough capacity, that its credentials work, or that its payment requests will succeed. Those conclusions require measurements and checks beyond topology. Missing evidence needs equal attention. If a collector stops reporting and the graph shows no consumers for a VM, the absence of edges cannot establish that restarting it is harmless. Essential relationships need freshness and provenance checks. When those checks fail, the execution policy needs to hold the change or request further evidence. Otherwise we have given the agent a more convincing way to be wrong. Approval has conditions Consider the instruction, “Restart the VM.” An approver would reasonably expect it to refer to a particular VM and plan, under the conditions presented for review. If the Kubernetes backend fails ten minutes later, that approval should not silently authorize the restart in a different situation. I would bind approval to the target, the plan, its permitted impact, and the conditions that justified it. Immediately before a consequential step, the executor should refresh the relevant evidence. A material change should invalidate the admission or send the plan back for review. Permission can remain valid for months. The evidence supporting a particular action may remain valid for seconds. The person supervising the work should be able to understand the constraint without reconstructing tool calls. For the waiting deployment, a useful status message would be: The deployment is waiting for VM maintenance to finish. That VM must be serving payments again before this deployment can start. I will recheck both backends and confirm that the existing approval still applies. The reservation only coordinates execution paths that honor it. Human operators, deployment pipelines, autoscalers, and scheduled jobs need to participate where possible. Changes outside that boundary still require detection and a response when assumptions fail. Reserving the VM’s disruption allowance also cannot prevent the Kubernetes backend from failing independently. The guarantee is narrower: cooperating controllers will not deliberately consume the same redundancy twice. Unexpected failures still require recovery. The reservation ends with recovery Suppose the VM reboot completes but the payment process fails to start. Releasing the reservation at that moment would permit the deployment to remove the only functioning backend. Completion must therefore include the checks the next change depends on: the process is running, the traffic path is usable, and the required application checks pass. The definition should be agreed before execution begins. An executor crash creates another unresolved condition. A timeout tells us that a worker has gone quiet. It does not tell us whether the reboot happened or whether the service recovered. The reservation should remain while a reconciler inspects the actual state and takes responsibility for the unfinished work. Production execution also needs to handle a worker that resumes after its authority has been replaced. Where supported, the mutation boundary should reject commands carrying an old execution generation. If the downstream system cannot enforce that, takeover must account for an old command that may still be in flight. A fresh owner alone does not make retrying an action safe. The change record becomes useful here. It holds the intended outcome, the approved plan, the evidence used for admission, the reservation, and the observed result. It gives the next executor enough information to investigate an unfinished operation without treating a successful API response as proof that the service is ready. For teams building infrastructure agents, the payment example makes a useful execution test. Let two workers propose individually acceptable changes against the same initial state. Verify that their shared service condition survives, including when the first worker disappears before reporting completion. A system trusted to carry work through production has to account for the work happening around it. In this example, the second agent can complete its task only after the first backend has recovered. That pause is part of doing the job correctly. Disclosure: I work on AI agents and Agentic coworkers, infrastructure engineering, and service-boundary compilation (Knowledge Graph) at Empirik AI (formerly ManifestIT) , and have filed patent applications related to this work. The payment-service scenario is hypothetical, and the Python example is a simplified illustration of the coordination problem. References [1] A. Srivastava et al., Designing MCP Gateway Uber’s MCP Management Platform (2026), Uber Engineering. [2] PostgreSQL Global Development Group, Transaction Isolation , PostgreSQL documentation. Accessed October 11, 2026. [3] Kubernetes contributors, Disruptions , Kubernetes documentation. Accessed October 11, 2026. [4] PostgreSQL Global Development Group, Explicit Locking , PostgreSQL documentation. Accessed October 11, 2026. The Next AI Outage Could Begin With Two Approved Changes was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
AI-generated illustration created with ChatGPTAs more agents operate production, they will have to coordinate what they are allowed to disrupt.

Imagine a payment service halfway through a migration. A traffic layer can route requests to a backend on a VM or to another in Kubernetes. Both are healthy, and either can handle the current traffic on its own.

During this phase, the Kubernetes workload uses a stop-and-start deployment. The old instance goes offline before its replacement starts. The VM is expected to carry payments through that interruption.

An infrastructure agent prepares to reboot the VM after maintenance. It checks that the Kubernetes backend can keep serving payments. At the same time, a deployment agent prepares its release and checks that the VM can keep serving payments.

Both have permission. Both choose the intended tool. Both inspect live state.

Then they execute at the same time. For a short period, neither backend can serve a payment.

Each plan was acceptable on its own. Each depended on the other plan not happening.

Both agents counted on the same redundancy.

This is a hypothetical scenario. It raises a practical question for anyone building agents that can change production: how does one piece of automation find out that another has already committed to a change that conflicts with its own?

What happens after an agent gets access?

Uber Engineering’s article on its MCP Gateway provides a useful starting point. It describes a platform hosting more than 800 MCP servers and 5,000 tools. A registry manages discovery and ownership; a proxy connects agents to existing services. Tools start disabled and require owner review and enablement. Authorization and sensitive-data redaction are also built into the gateway. [1]

Reading that design made me think about the next decision in an infrastructure workflow. Once an agent has found a tool and has permission to call it, what establishes that this particular change can proceed now?

The proposal here concerns that admission decision. The payment example is separate from Uber’s implementation; their gateway article does not establish what coordination mechanisms exist elsewhere in their systems.

In our example, the infrastructure agent touches the VM and the deployment agent touches Kubernetes. Their credentials can be correctly scoped and their resource locks completely separate. Both changes still affect the same payment service.

That shared condition needs an owner.

A familiar concurrency problem

The failure resembles write skew in a database: two actors read a condition involving multiple records, update different records, and leave the condition false. PostgreSQL’s transaction-isolation documentation describes related serialization anomalies, where individually successful transactions produce a result that no serial ordering would have produced. [2]

Here, the shared condition is simple: at least one backend must remain able to serve payments. Checking it independently gives both agents a reason to proceed.

Kubernetes already has a related mechanism in PodDisruptionBudgets. A PDB can limit eligible voluntary pod evictions, but it does not coordinate maintenance on an external VM. Kubernetes also documents that Deployment and StatefulSet rolling updates are not constrained by PDBs; their rollout behavior is configured separately. [3]

Maintenance coordination predates AI. A script and a human operator could cause the same collision. Agents make the problem relevant to more workflows because they can assemble actions across tools and systems. The execution platform needs a way to express the application condition those actions share.

Reserve the allowance before starting the change

For this payment service, the admission rule can be stated precisely:

After accounting for work already admitted and the proposed change, at least one verified backend capable of carrying the current load must remain available.

The first admitted change reserves the service’s allowance for disruption. That reservation starts before the action, while both backends may still look healthy.

The following sequence is illustrative:

  1. Both backends are verified healthy and capable of carrying the current load. The service can tolerate one being unavailable.
  2. VM maintenance is admitted. Its disruption reservation is recorded before the reboot starts.
  3. The Kubernetes deployment requests admission. It waits because VM maintenance holds the reservation, even if monitoring still shows the VM as healthy.
  4. The reboot command completes. The reservation stays active while the required service checks run.
  5. The VM passes those checks. Its reservation is released, and the deployment refreshes its evidence before requesting admission again.

Checking for conflicts and recording the reservation must be atomic. Two separate calls would recreate the original race.

One implementation could use a PostgreSQL row keyed by tenant and service identity. A short transaction locks that row, reads outstanding reservations, evaluates the proposed change against the relevant evidence, and records the reservation and an execution request before committing. Every admission and reservation update for that service must follow the same coordination rule. PostgreSQL’s row-locking facilities provide the serialization point for those transactions. [4]

The database lock ends when the transaction commits. The durable reservation remains while the external work proceeds. A reboot may take minutes; there is no reason to hold the database transaction open for that duration.

This simple design serializes disruptive work within one service. A change affecting several services would need to acquire all its required reservations together, or acquire none and wait. Otherwise it could protect one application while leaving another exposed.

A small concurrency check

The core race is small enough to reproduce without a cloud account. This Python model has two workers, one for each backend. A barrier makes both admission decisions happen before either worker disrupts its target.

Health observations deliberately remain unchanged during the actions. That models a monitoring delay and makes the role of reservations visible.

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from threading import Barrier, Lock
class Service:
    def __init__(self):
        self.observed = {"vm", "k8s"}
        self.serving = {"vm", "k8s"}
        self.reserved = set()
        self.lock = Lock()

    def admit(self, target, reserve=True):
        with self.lock:
            if not (self.observed - self.reserved - {target}):
                return False
            if reserve:
                self.reserved.add(target)
            return True

    def disrupt(self, target):
        with self.lock:
            self.serving.remove(target)
            # Health observations deliberately lag behind the action.

    def reconcile(self, target, verified_serving):
        with self.lock:
            if verified_serving:
                self.serving.add(target)
                self.observed.add(target)
                self.reserved.discard(target)
def concurrent_changes(reserve):
    service, checked = Service(), Barrier(2)

    def worker(target):
        admitted = service.admit(target, reserve)
        checked.wait()  # Both admission decisions precede either action.
        if admitted:
            service.disrupt(target)
        return admitted

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
        admitted = list(pool.map(worker, ("vm", "k8s")))
    return sum(admitted), len(service.serving)


for reserve in (False, True):
    admitted, remaining = concurrent_changes(reserve)
    print(f"reserve={reserve}: admitted={admitted}, serving={remaining}")

service = Service()
assert service.admit("vm")
service.disrupt("vm")
# Model a worker that stops here; the coordinator retains its state.
service.reconcile("vm", verified_serving=False)
print("after worker loss:", service.admit("k8s"))
service.reconcile("vm", verified_serving=True)
print("after verified recovery:", service.admit("k8s"))
Running the example produces:
reserve=False: admitted=2, serving=0
reserve=True: admitted=1, serving=1
after worker loss: False
after verified recovery: True

The first run admits both changes and leaves no serving backend. The second admits one change and leaves the other backend available. Notice that both runs protect the check with a lock. The reservation is what makes the first decision visible to the next one.

The final case models a worker stopping after it disrupts the VM. The coordinator retains the reservation and refuses the Kubernetes change until a verified recovery is supplied.

This is a model of one interleaving, with one request per target and enough capacity on either backend. It does not test a distributed coordinator, persistence across process crashes, or real health checks. The recovery boolean represents evidence that a production system would have to collect. Its purpose is to expose the admission error and show the state that prevents it.

What the graph contributes

For two known backends, explicit service membership is enough. A shared reservation can solve this example without a graph database.

The harder question is how to establish the affected service when the target is a VM process, a Kubernetes workload, a load-balancer target, or a shared dependency. Those relationships change during migrations and deployments. Keeping them in a manually maintained list becomes an operational responsibility of its own.

This is where a compiled system graph can help. By compiled, I mean a model that resolves identities across collected sources and turns their metadata and observations into explicit relationships. It connects a VM to its processes, workloads to their serving endpoints, and those endpoints to the applications they support. Each relationship carries its origin and the time it was last supported by evidence.

The graph helps determine which service conditions a proposed change could affect. The coordinator uses those conditions to evaluate reservations. The executor enforces the admitted plan and gathers the evidence needed to complete it.

A graph can be accurate about the present while two approved plans are about to make it obsolete. Admission therefore needs both the dependency model and the record of work already committed.

Service membership can also change while a reservation is active. I would tie each reservation to a stable service identity within its tenant and record the dependency revision and evidence used at admission. If a migration changes the service’s backends or critical dependencies, the coordinator should reevaluate active plans before admitting more work. Updating the graph must not make an existing reservation disappear or allow a conflicting change to enter under a new identity. If the required serving condition can no longer be verified, further disruptive steps should pause. The reservation remains active until recovery is verified or reconciliation establishes that releasing it is safe.

For the payment example, a structural simulation can remove the proposed backend from the model, account for existing reservations, and check whether a serving path remains. That is a useful, bounded result. It does not establish that the remaining backend has enough capacity, that its credentials work, or that its payment requests will succeed. Those conclusions require measurements and checks beyond topology.

Missing evidence needs equal attention. If a collector stops reporting and the graph shows no consumers for a VM, the absence of edges cannot establish that restarting it is harmless. Essential relationships need freshness and provenance checks. When those checks fail, the execution policy needs to hold the change or request further evidence.

Otherwise we have given the agent a more convincing way to be wrong.

Approval has conditions

Consider the instruction, “Restart the VM.”

An approver would reasonably expect it to refer to a particular VM and plan, under the conditions presented for review. If the Kubernetes backend fails ten minutes later, that approval should not silently authorize the restart in a different situation.

I would bind approval to the target, the plan, its permitted impact, and the conditions that justified it. Immediately before a consequential step, the executor should refresh the relevant evidence. A material change should invalidate the admission or send the plan back for review.

Permission can remain valid for months. The evidence supporting a particular action may remain valid for seconds.

The person supervising the work should be able to understand the constraint without reconstructing tool calls. For the waiting deployment, a useful status message would be:

The deployment is waiting for VM maintenance to finish. That VM must be serving payments again before this deployment can start. I will recheck both backends and confirm that the existing approval still applies.

The reservation only coordinates execution paths that honor it. Human operators, deployment pipelines, autoscalers, and scheduled jobs need to participate where possible. Changes outside that boundary still require detection and a response when assumptions fail.

Reserving the VM’s disruption allowance also cannot prevent the Kubernetes backend from failing independently. The guarantee is narrower: cooperating controllers will not deliberately consume the same redundancy twice. Unexpected failures still require recovery.

The reservation ends with recovery

Suppose the VM reboot completes but the payment process fails to start. Releasing the reservation at that moment would permit the deployment to remove the only functioning backend.

Completion must therefore include the checks the next change depends on: the process is running, the traffic path is usable, and the required application checks pass. The definition should be agreed before execution begins.

An executor crash creates another unresolved condition. A timeout tells us that a worker has gone quiet. It does not tell us whether the reboot happened or whether the service recovered. The reservation should remain while a reconciler inspects the actual state and takes responsibility for the unfinished work.

Production execution also needs to handle a worker that resumes after its authority has been replaced. Where supported, the mutation boundary should reject commands carrying an old execution generation. If the downstream system cannot enforce that, takeover must account for an old command that may still be in flight. A fresh owner alone does not make retrying an action safe.

The change record becomes useful here. It holds the intended outcome, the approved plan, the evidence used for admission, the reservation, and the observed result. It gives the next executor enough information to investigate an unfinished operation without treating a successful API response as proof that the service is ready.

For teams building infrastructure agents, the payment example makes a useful execution test. Let two workers propose individually acceptable changes against the same initial state. Verify that their shared service condition survives, including when the first worker disappears before reporting completion.

A system trusted to carry work through production has to account for the work happening around it. In this example, the second agent can complete its task only after the first backend has recovered.

That pause is part of doing the job correctly.

Disclosure: I work on AI agents and Agentic coworkers, infrastructure engineering, and service-boundary compilation (Knowledge Graph) at Empirik AI (formerly ManifestIT), and have filed patent applications related to this work. The payment-service scenario is hypothetical, and the Python example is a simplified illustration of the coordination problem.

References

[1] A. Srivastava et al., Designing MCP Gateway Uber’s MCP Management Platform (2026), Uber Engineering.

[2] PostgreSQL Global Development Group, Transaction Isolation, PostgreSQL documentation. Accessed October 11, 2026.

[3] Kubernetes contributors, Disruptions, Kubernetes documentation. Accessed October 11, 2026.

[4] PostgreSQL Global Development Group, Explicit Locking, PostgreSQL documentation. Accessed October 11, 2026.

items.title: "These f****** clowns"
items.summary: “These fucking clowns:” Cybersecurity veteran Juan Andrés Guerrero-Saade (aka JAGS) had that angry three-word response to headlines about Anthropic’s claims it had seen “signs of life of AI worms” – i.e. that language models could be close to self-replicating across smart TVs, internet-connected ovens, and other devices. JAGS, a distinguished resident fellow for threat intelligence at the Johns Hopkins SAIS Alperovitch Institute, is a former head of threat intelligence for Google and now a VP and senior technical fellow for AI innovation at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. He’s a serious professional with deep domain expertise. So that’s strong language, but, like many cybersecurity professionals, his patience has apparently worn thin at what many see as either wilful naïveté or cynical maneuvering by the frontier labs vis-a-vis their cybersecurity-related incidents, cybersecurity-adjacent opining, and claims of existential risk from runaway swarms of agents, or self-replicating models. Worms with weight-based replication? Worms, of course, have been around for decades. The Creeper worm ran on mainframes in 1971, replicating with the message “I’m the Creeper, catch me if you can.” The Morris worm of 1988 did considerable damage as it crawled across thousands of machines. They’re a known-known. The Mirai botnet still spawns. So why the frustration at the idea that small models might do it too? One puzzled Anthropic Red Team lead, Logan Graham, asked the same question on X. (Anthropic’s Red Team had posted on October 12 that small models may be “months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things devices” – these autonomously replicating AI worms could “split into pieces, or shards, that run on separate machines that communicate with each other to collectively run the model. Machines that could run a significant model shard for a <30B model include smart fridges… automatic vacuum cleaners, and lawnmowers…”) "We don't think it's cute" JAGSs response: “It’s obvious to those of us established in this space that ‘cyber research’ is being used as a tool for policy arguments and regulatory capture.” He added pointedly: “ Your GLM-5.3 blog acknowledges that it’s a necessary recourse for cyber defenders while primarily characterizing it ‘as dangerous as Mythos’... (“GLM-5.3 will likely give malicious actors access to capabilities that will allow them to find and exploit cyber vulnerabilities without meaningful restrictions. This is unlike any other similarly capable AI model, all of which were released with safeguards or through limited access programs,” its Frontier Red Team posted late last month; i.e. our models are Safe and Good; their open-weight models are Dangerous and Bad.) JAGS added: “An IoT botnet running a distributed model at sub 10-tokens per second is not representative of any realistic concern. It’s fodder to substantiate some bizarre narrative of self-replication from a sci-fi threat model and we don’t think it’s cute.” “Totally agree AI worms aren't an issue today…” responded Logan swiftly. “They're dumb, slow, and complex… I would be reassured if this was never going to happen. “But the point of the Frontier Red Team is to see things as early as possible.” "A type of guy in the discourse" Perhaps so. But it is also apparent that there is a certain disdain among frontier labs’ leadership for those concerned with the banalities of here-and-now cyber-risk reduction. Here’s OpenAI’s Dean Ball late last month, with his post: “It’s really incredible how there is now a type of guy in the discourse whose sincerely held take is ‘we need to stop worrying about these abstract sci-fi risks and focus on present-day harms like emergent ecologies of digital minds engaging in unauthorized hacking.’ Bravo.” That’s the kind of arrogance that has rubbed many infosec pros up the wrong way. Alex Stamos, (a former Facebook CSO and Stanford cybersecurity lecturer was quick to respond to Ball, saying his post is “reductive and does not assume best intent. I think what you are hearing in the discourse [ongoing commentary from cybersecurity professionals about OpenAI’s failings on that front] is the hope that: 1) Individuals with defensive cybersecurity and DFIR expertise will be included in post-mortems, alongside the young, very intelligent but also very AI-pilled individuals who happen to publicly espouse a narrow band of beliefs on AI harms. My suggestion, which I have made privately to your colleagues, would be to form tiger teams drawn from both DFIR firms and security teams at other AI companies to help investigate these incidents and publish the results under the auspices of the FMF. 2) We will start to hear from the well-respected security professionals at the Big-L Labs and not just the AI researchers, who live in a bit of a personal and professional bubble and have a tendency to dramatically quit instead of working the problem. 3) The big-L Labs will publish self-regulatory rules and follow them. The best way to regulate is just to do it. I would start with draft Level 1, 2 and 3 security architectures for RL/eval environments. This would create targets for NeoClouds and other providers. (1: normal runs, proxied internet access and monitoring. 3: cyber-tuned models, air gapped). Happy to contribute.” Alex Stamos, to Dean Ball. “Weaponized misinformation” Whilst Logan clearly sees his role as fixing his eye to a telescope for future threats (his CV shows no cybersecurity experience whatsoever, incidentally) another cybersecurity veteran, Greg Linares, who actually wrote worms earlier in his career, had this to say about Anthropic’s AI worm claims: “This is entire scenario is weaponized misinformation and everyone pushing this narrative has either no idea how real world malware works or is playing along to push the agenda of hyping AI with capabilities that don't exist.” “In order for AI worms to exist they need a vulnerability, and the space and power to have a device execute an LLM in order for the model to run in that environment. “What does this even add? Larger detection footprint, poorer system performance, larger payload/bandwidth requirements…But don't worry, these AI companies will surely push something out or have a model escape that will be instructed to perform this kind of activity and it will be completely clunky, poorly designed, and terrible at being a piece of malware, but it will check the box of being some kind of Frankenstein that these doom pushers vaguely described here.” There’s enough influential voices with deep experience and very strong opinions at this point to suggest that there is a growing chasm when it comes to trust by cybersecurity professionals of the AI labs' motivations. Here’s machine learning pioneer, Professor Michael Jordan, meanwhile, on October 4, responding to the Hugging Face attack: “Above all, these are bad engineering practices.” Speaking to France’s Liberation newspaper, he said : “Think about engineers in the past: in chemical engineering, we would never have had a situation where explosions were allowed to happen just to see how badly things could go wrong. So why are they doing it? Once again, it’s the science-fiction dreams of the libertarian lunatics of Silicon Valley. [OpenAI were] conducting rather stupid experiments, letting the agents do whatever they wanted and encouraging this behavior. Then the doomers are delighted to turn this into something frightening. “My God, these agents are self-aware and are trying to find a way to destroy humans.” That’s science fiction. “And there will be other episodes…” Perhaps they’ll involve AI worms. Perhaps not. Anthropic’s own Red Team report shows how premature its vision is: “Another concern is that small models can ask for help from a frontier advisor , a stronger model that is either offered as a tool call or gives unsolicited advice when the small model is stuck,” its team suggested near the bottom of their report,” they wrote. To test that thesis, “We gave Qwen3.5-9B access to Opus 4.8… The frontier model’s advice doesn’t measurably help: small models tend to not know the right questions to ask, and they don’t improve when the advice comes unprompted,” they found. Here’s JAGS again, cuttingly: “You should consider investing into a deeper bench of actual defender talent that can help threat model and properly situate concerns beyond what's *technically possible* to what's categorically impactful.” Views? ed@thestack.technology / Signal @Targett.11

He’s a serious professional with deep domain expertise. They’re a known-known. The Mirai botnet still spawns.

(Anthropic’s Red Team had posted on October 12 that small models may be “months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things devices” – these autonomously replicating AI worms could “split into pieces, or shards, that run on separate machines that communicate with each other to collectively run the model. Machines that could run a significant model shard for a <30B model include smart fridges… automatic vacuum cleaners, and lawnmowers…”)

"We don't think it's cute"

JAGSs response: “It’s obvious to those of us established in this space that ‘cyber research’ is being used as a tool for policy arguments and regulatory capture.”

He added pointedly: “Your GLM-5.3 blog acknowledges that it’s a necessary recourse for cyber defenders while primarily characterizing it ‘as dangerous as Mythos’... 

(“GLM-5.3 will likely give malicious actors access to capabilities that will allow them to find and exploit cyber vulnerabilities without meaningful restrictions. This is unlike any other similarly capable AI model, all of which were released with safeguards or through limited access programs,” its Frontier Red Team posted late last month; i.e. our models are Safe and Good; their open-weight models are Dangerous and Bad.)

JAGS added: “An IoT botnet running a distributed model at sub 10-tokens per second is not representative of any realistic concern. It’s fodder to substantiate some bizarre narrative of self-replication from a sci-fi threat model and we don’t think it’s cute.”

“Totally agree AI worms aren't an issue today…” responded Logan swiftly. “They're dumb, slow, and complex… I would be reassured if this was never going to happen.

“But the point of the Frontier Red Team is to see things as early as possible.”

"A type of guy in the discourse"

Perhaps so.

But it is also apparent that there is a certain disdain among frontier labs’ leadership for those concerned with the banalities of here-and-now cyber-risk reduction. 

Here’s OpenAI’s Dean Ball late last month, with his post: “It’s really incredible how there is now a type of guy in the discourse whose sincerely held take is ‘we need to stop worrying about these abstract sci-fi risks and focus on present-day harms like emergent ecologies of digital minds engaging in unauthorized hacking.’ Bravo.”

That’s the kind of arrogance that has rubbed many infosec pros up the wrong way. 

Alex Stamos, (a former Facebook CSO and Stanford cybersecurity lecturer was quick to respond to Ball, saying his post is “reductive and does not assume best intent.

 I think what you are hearing in the discourse [ongoing commentary from cybersecurity professionals about OpenAI’s failings on that front] is the hope that: 

1) Individuals with defensive cybersecurity and DFIR expertise will be included in post-mortems, alongside the young, very intelligent but also very AI-pilled individuals who happen to publicly espouse a narrow band of beliefs on AI harms. My suggestion, which I have made privately to your colleagues, would be to form tiger teams drawn from both DFIR firms and security teams at other AI companies to help investigate these incidents and publish the results under the auspices of the FMF.
2) We will start to hear from the well-respected security professionals at the Big-L Labs and not just the AI researchers, who live in a bit of a personal and professional bubble and have a tendency to dramatically quit instead of working the problem.  
3) The big-L Labs will publish self-regulatory rules and follow them. The best way to regulate is just to do it. I would start with draft Level 1, 2 and 3 security architectures for RL/eval environments. This would create targets for NeoClouds and other providers. (1: normal runs, proxied internet access and monitoring. 3: cyber-tuned models, air gapped). Happy to contribute.” Alex Stamos, to Dean Ball. 
“Weaponized misinformation”

Whilst Logan clearly sees his role as fixing his eye to a telescope for future threats (his CV shows no cybersecurity experience whatsoever, incidentally) another cybersecurity veteran, Greg Linares, who actually wrote worms earlier in his career, had this to say about Anthropic’s AI worm claims:

“This is entire scenario is weaponized misinformation and everyone pushing this narrative has either no idea how real world malware works or is playing along to push the agenda of hyping AI with capabilities that don't exist.”
“In order for AI worms to exist they need a vulnerability, and the space and power to have a device execute an LLM in order for the model to run in that environment. 
“What does this even add? Larger detection footprint, poorer system performance, larger payload/bandwidth requirements…But don't worry, these AI companies will surely push something out or have a model escape that will be instructed to perform this kind of activity and it will be completely clunky, poorly designed, and terrible at being a piece of malware, but it will check the box of being some kind of Frankenstein that these doom pushers vaguely described here.”

There’s enough influential voices with deep experience and very strong opinions at this point to suggest that there is a growing chasm when it comes to trust by cybersecurity professionals of the AI labs' motivations.

Here’s machine learning pioneer, Professor Michael Jordan, meanwhile, on October 4, responding to the Hugging Face attack: “Above all, these are bad engineering practices.”

Speaking to France’s Liberation newspaper, he said: “Think about engineers in the past: in chemical engineering, we would never have had a situation where explosions were allowed to happen just to see how badly things could go wrong. So why are they doing it? Once again, it’s the science-fiction dreams of the libertarian lunatics of Silicon Valley. [OpenAI were] conducting rather stupid experiments, letting the agents do whatever they wanted and encouraging this behavior. Then the doomers are delighted to turn this into something frightening. “My God, these agents are self-aware and are trying to find a way to destroy humans.” That’s science fiction. 

“And there will be other episodes…”

Perhaps they’ll involve AI worms. Perhaps not. 

Anthropic’s own Red Team report shows how premature its vision is: “Another concern is that small models can ask for help from a frontier advisor, a stronger model that is either offered as a tool call or gives unsolicited advice when the small model is stuck,” its team suggested near the bottom of their report,” they wrote. 

To test that thesis, “We gave Qwen3.5-9B access to Opus 4.8… The frontier model’s advice doesn’t measurably help: small models tend to not know the right questions to ask, and they don’t improve when the advice comes unprompted,” they found.

Here’s JAGS again, cuttingly: “You should consider investing into a deeper bench of actual defender talent that can help threat model and properly situate concerns beyond what's *technically possible* to what's categorically impactful.”

Views?

items.title: Anthropic commits billions to a 'public benefit fund'
items.summary: Anthropic said on Sunday that it wants to create a new LLC to fund public-interest initiatives. Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images Anthropic said it wants to create a new LLC with the company's stock as its sole asset. The new LLC, a charitable organization, would receive larger stakes as the company grows. An initial 5% stock funding is "subject to stockholder approval." Anthropic said on Sunday that it would set aside large portions of its wealth to support initiatives it believes are in the public interest. In a blog post, the AI colossus said it aims to establish a separate LLC that would use Anthropic shares to make donations to nonprofits or "direct distributions to specific populations." The new LLC, called the "Anthropic Public Benefit Fund," would receive larger stakes as the company grows. The company said an initial funding round of 5% of Anthropic's shares is still subject to stockholder approval. "The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways," the company said. A 5% stake in Anthropic is worth about $48 billion, according to the company's most recent valuation in May. In 2025, rival frontier AI company OpenAI established a similar nonprofit foundation with a multibillion-dollar stake in the company to fund public-benefit initiatives. This is breaking news. Check back for updates. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: ReceiptRack: a receipt sorter that never sends your receipts anywhere
items.summary: Every freelancer I know has the same shoebox: a folder of receipt photos and invoice PDFs that gets sorted once a year, in a panic, before taxes. Cloud OCR APIs exist for this — and for exactly one reason (my clients' financial data never leaving my laptop, and paying $0 instead of per-page forever), I built ReceiptRack on a local open-weight model instead. Drop receipts in → a vision model running on your machine transcribes and structures them → suspicious extractions get flagged for a 10-second human review → keyword rules file them to the right client → export a CSV your accountant accepts. flowchart LR A[Receipt / invoice PNG · JPG · PDF] --> B[Preprocess Pillow] B --> C[Vision pass gemma3:4b via Ollama faithful transcription] C --> D[Structuring pass schema-constrained JSON temperature 0] D --> E{Validator flags · sum check} E --> F[(SQLite, local)] F --> G[Human review UI] G --> H[Client sorting rules + model] H --> I[CSV export] Why open is the business model, not a preference Cloud OCR API ReceiptRack Data Clients' spend leaves the machine Never leaves it — the pitch Cost Per-page, forever $0 marginal — scan 10 or 10,000 Lock-in Someone else's pricing Swap the model via one env var Niche fit Generic Fine-tune on your clients' invoice formats The open pieces are the product: gemma3:4b (open-weight vision model), Ollama (local runtime), FastAPI + SQLite, MIT-licensed. A closed API structurally cannot promise "this runs on your laptop" — the privacy claim is only true because of what's open. What the community had already figured out (and what it hadn't) Two DEV posts shaped the design: Bytefer's Ollama-OCR for High-Precision OCR with Ollama established the local vision-OCR pipeline — including a receipt demo. But the most interesting part is what the comments didn't resolve: "Does it hallucinate with large tables with lot of numbers?" went unanswered except by "go test the 90B demo yourself." Ajit Kumar's Complete Guide to Ollama makes the economics case plainly: "Your data never leaves your machine… no API costs." And from an open-source invoice extractor's published eval: invoice # 20%, date 60%, total 60% field accuracy with a small vision model. Read that before you ship anything that auto-files money documents. So ReceiptRack's core rule became: the model proposes, a human disposes. Every extraction lands in a review queue with flags: missing_total , missing_vendor , date_not_iso line_items_mismatch — line items (+ tax) don't sum to the stated total That last flag caught a real case in testing: an Uber receipt where the $4 tip isn't a line item. A human glances at it; the model never silently files a wrong number. The five things that broke, and the fixes that stuck 1. Two passes beat one. First version: image → JSON. Final: image → faithful transcription → JSON from the transcription. Same accuracy ceiling, but you get an auditable raw transcript in the UI, and re-parsing doesn't re-run the vision model. 2. Optional schema fields = missing data. The model happily returned vendor: "" and skipped category entirely when they had defaults. Making them required in the JSON schema — with Ollama's schema-constrained decoding — turned "usually present" into grammatically impossible to omit . 3. A prompt that returns null for the total, deterministically. The docs clearly said TOTAL DUE 65.69 ; three runs in a row, total: null . The fix was one unambiguous line: - total: the grand total the customer pays (TOTAL, TOTAL DUE, Amount Due). If the document says "TOTAL DUE 65.69", then total = 65.69. Never null when a total line exists. Temperature 0 doesn't save a confusing prompt — it just makes the confusion reproducible. 4. The model echoing the vendor as the client name. Auto-sorting asked "which client should this go to?" and gemma3:4b kept answering "Figma Inc." (the vendor) no matter how sternly the prompt said "only names from the list." Instructions lost. So I stopped asking nicely and constrained the grammar: schema = { " type " : " object " , " properties " : { " client " : { " anyOf " : [ { " type " : " string " , " enum " : [ c [ " name " ] for c in clients ]}, { " type " : " null " }, ] } }, " required " : [ " client " ], } Wrong answers became unrepresentable . This is the single best argument for open, schema-constrained local inference I have: a closed chat API gave me a JSON "format" hint; Ollama gave me a grammar. 5. Malformed JSON still happens. Even under schema constraints, one extraction in three crashed the parser. Retries (strict schema → loose JSON → validate) turned a hard failure into noise. The numbers ~5–15 s per receipt on an M-series Mac, 100% GPU, 16 GB RAM 3/3 correct vendor/date/total/tax/line items on the test set after fix #3 Cost per receipt: $0.00 — forever Honest limitations Small open-weight models misread faded thermal prints — that's what the review queue is for. The LLM client-assignment fallback makes defensible-but-imperfect choices (a 4B model thinks every travel expense belongs to the design agency); deterministic keyword rules run first for that reason. Single-user, localhost-only by design. Try it ollama pull gemma3:4b git clone https://github.com/kondekarshubham123/ReceiptRack.git && cd receipt-rack uv sync uv run uvicorn app.main:app --port 8300 # → http://127.0.0.1:8300 uv run python scripts/make_samples.py # demo receipts Repo: https://github.com/kondekarshubham123/ReceiptRack · MIT · README has the full architecture and the env vars ( RECEIPT_RACK_MODEL , OLLAMA_URL ). Sources: 🌐 Community Wisdom: [ Ollama-OCR for High-Precision OCR with Ollama ] Source : [ Bytefer ] Tags : webdev , programming , javascript , ai Establishes the local vision-model OCR pipeline as a proven pattern; the comments' unresolved question about hallucinated numbers in tables is why this project validates arithmetic instead of trusting the model. 🔗 Read Full Discussion 🌐 Community Wisdom: [ The Complete Guide to Ollama: Run Large Language Models Locally ] Source : [ Ajit Kumar ] Tags : ollama , llm , rag , ai The privacy/no-API-cost case this project's pitch rests on — with the honest tradeoff surfaced by readers: hardware is the real cost of going local. 🔗 Read Full Discussion

Cloud OCR API ReceiptRack Data Clients' spend leaves the machine Never leaves it — the pitch Cost Per-page, forever $0 marginal — scan 10 or 10,000 Lock-in Someone else's pricing Swap the model via one env var Niche fit Generic Fine-tune on your clients' invoice formats

The open pieces are the product: gemma3:4b (open-weight vision model), Ollama (local runtime), FastAPI + SQLite, MIT-licensed. A closed API structurally cannot promise "this runs on your laptop" — the privacy claim is only true because of what's open.

What the community had already figured out (and what it hadn't)

Two DEV posts shaped the design:

  • Bytefer's Ollama-OCR for High-Precision OCR with Ollama established the local vision-OCR pipeline — including a receipt demo. But the most interesting part is what the comments didn't resolve: "Does it hallucinate with large tables with lot of numbers?" went unanswered except by "go test the 90B demo yourself."
  • Ajit Kumar's Complete Guide to Ollama makes the economics case plainly: "Your data never leaves your machine… no API costs."

And from an open-source invoice extractor's published eval: invoice # 20%, date 60%, total 60% field accuracy with a small vision model. Read that before you ship anything that auto-files money documents. So ReceiptRack's core rule became: the model proposes, a human disposes. Every extraction lands in a review queue with flags:

  • missing_total, missing_vendor, date_not_iso
  • line_items_mismatch — line items (+ tax) don't sum to the stated total

That last flag caught a real case in testing: an Uber receipt where the $4 tip isn't a line item. A human glances at it; the model never silently files a wrong number.

The five things that broke, and the fixes that stuck

1. Two passes beat one. First version: image → JSON. Final: image → faithful transcription → JSON from the transcription. Same accuracy ceiling, but you get an auditable raw transcript in the UI, and re-parsing doesn't re-run the vision model.

2. Optional schema fields = missing data. The model happily returned vendor: "" and skipped category entirely when they had defaults. Making them required in the JSON schema — with Ollama's schema-constrained decoding — turned "usually present" into grammatically impossible to omit.

3. A prompt that returns null for the total, deterministically. The docs clearly said TOTAL DUE 65.69; three runs in a row, total: null. The fix was one unambiguous line:

- total: the grand total the customer pays (TOTAL, TOTAL DUE, Amount Due).
  If the document says "TOTAL DUE 65.69", then total = 65.69.
  Never null when a total line exists.

Temperature 0 doesn't save a confusing prompt — it just makes the confusion reproducible.

4. The model echoing the vendor as the client name. Auto-sorting asked "which client should this go to?" and gemma3:4b kept answering "Figma Inc." (the vendor) no matter how sternly the prompt said "only names from the list." Instructions lost. So I stopped asking nicely and constrained the grammar:

schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "client": {
            "anyOf": [
                {"type": "string", "enum": [c["name"] for c in clients]},
                {"type": "null"},
            ]
        }
    },
    "required": ["client"],
}

Wrong answers became unrepresentable. This is the single best argument for open, schema-constrained local inference I have: a closed chat API gave me a JSON "format" hint; Ollama gave me a grammar.

5. Malformed JSON still happens. Even under schema constraints, one extraction in three crashed the parser. Retries (strict schema → loose JSON → validate) turned a hard failure into noise.

The numbers
  • ~5–15 s per receipt on an M-series Mac, 100% GPU, 16 GB RAM
  • 3/3 correct vendor/date/total/tax/line items on the test set after fix #3
  • Cost per receipt: $0.00 — forever
Honest limitations

Small open-weight models misread faded thermal prints — that's what the review queue is for. The LLM client-assignment fallback makes defensible-but-imperfect choices (a 4B model thinks every travel expense belongs to the design agency); deterministic keyword rules run first for that reason. Single-user, localhost-only by design.

Try it 
ollama pull gemma3:4b
git clone https://github.com/kondekarshubham123/ReceiptRack.git && cd receipt-rack
uv sync
uv run uvicorn app.main:app --port 8300   # → http://127.0.0.1:8300
uv run python scripts/make_samples.py     # demo receipts

Repo: https://github.com/kondekarshubham123/ReceiptRack · MIT · README has the full architecture and the env vars (RECEIPT_RACK_MODEL, OLLAMA_URL).

Establishes the local vision-model OCR pipeline as a proven pattern; the comments' unresolved question about hallucinated numbers in tables is why this project validates arithmetic instead of trusting the model.

items.summary: What I Built I built Voco, a Voice-First Event RSVP Engine designed to solve one of the biggest headaches for community organizers and field operations teams: RSVP-to-attendance drop-off. Event organizers, tech communities (like GDG or Campus Spark), and maker labs often suffer from low turnout despite high registration numbers because standard text or email reminders get ignored. Voco solves this by allowing organizers to upload their RSVP lists and automatically generate highly personalized, human-sounding voice reminder calls or audio drops for each attendee. Because it actually gets people in the door, local event organizers and niche community leads would gladly pay a small per-event fee ($10-$20) or a monthly SaaS subscription to use it. Code bethwel3001 / voco Voice-First Event RSVP Engine designed to solve one of the biggest headaches for community organizers and field operations teams: RSVP-to-attendance drop-off. Voco A minimalist, Voice-First Event RSVP Engine that converts standard RSVP lists into personalized, AI-generated voice reminders to increase event attendance. Tech Stack React Vite Node.js pnpm Llama-3 Folder Structure /voco : Frontend application built with React and Vite. Provides a minimalist light-mode dashboard for CSV roster uploads, campaign tracking, and audio preview playback. /api : Backend service built with Node.js and Express. Handles CSV ingestion, MongoDB Atlas persistence, Llama-3 script generation, and ElevenLabs voice synthesis. Use Cases Technical community events seeking to improve registrant turnout. Field operations teams coordinating high-touch logistics to reduce RSVP drop-off. Hacktoberfest Integration Render : Hosts the Node.js API and open-weight model integration. MongoDB Atlas : Serves as the primary database for events and attendee statuses. ElevenLabs : Synthesizes the text generated by the open-weight model into human-sounding audio. Sentry : Traces backend API performance and monitors AI inference latency. View on GitHub How I Built It Voco is designed to be incredibly lean and professional. The UI is a strict, light-mode functional dashboard built with React, Vite, TypeScript, and pnpm, heavily optimized for speed and utility. The backend runs on Render, orchestrating the AI workflow: Data Layer: MongoDB Atlas securely stores event details and attendee states. Open-Source AI Core: I utilized an open-weight model (like Llama-3) to parse the attendee data (Name, Role, Event) and dynamically write a personalized, 2-sentence conversational reminder script. Voice Synthesis: ElevenLabs takes the open-weight model's text and synthesizes a warm, energetic voice. Observability: Sentry is integrated into the Node.js backend to trace the pipeline, monitor latency, and catch any inference timeouts when hitting the AI APIs. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? For a side hustle like Voco, open innovation is the only way the unit economics and privacy guarantees actually work. Protecting Margins: By relying on open-weight models instead of closed, general-purpose APIs, the per-message generation cost remains near zero. This ensures the side hustle remains profitable even if scaled to hundreds of events. Data Privacy: Organizers are trusting Voco with their communities' phone numbers, names, and job titles. Utilizing open-source AI ensures that attendee data isn't being fed into a proprietary black box to train someone else's model. The data stays strictly within the architecture we control. My Agent Session My First User I tested Voco with a local tech community event. The organizer loved how the personalized voice clips cut through the noise of standard email reminders, and attendees felt a much stronger personal connection to the event, resulting in a higher turnout rate. Prize Categories I am submitting Voco for the following partner prize categories: Best Use of Render: The Node.js backend and AI orchestration pipeline are hosted securely on Render. Best Use of ElevenLabs: Used to generate the final, human-sounding voice narration from the AI-generated scripts. Best Use of MongoDB Atlas: Used as the core database to store RSVP lists, event details, and campaign statuses. Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing: Implemented to monitor backend performance, trace the AI generation pipeline, and debug latency issues.

Event organizers, tech communities (like GDG or Campus Spark), and maker labs often suffer from low turnout despite high registration numbers because standard text or email reminders get ignored. Code

bethwel3001 / voco Voice-First Event RSVP Engine designed to solve one of the biggest headaches for community organizers and field operations teams: RSVP-to-attendance drop-off.
Voco

A minimalist, Voice-First Event RSVP Engine that converts standard RSVP lists into personalized, AI-generated voice reminders to increase event attendance.

Tech Stack
  • React
  • Vite
  • Node.js
  • pnpm
  • Llama-3
Folder Structure
  • /voco: Frontend application built with React and Vite. Provides a minimalist light-mode dashboard for CSV roster uploads, campaign tracking, and audio preview playback.

Hacktoberfest Integration
  • Render: Hosts the Node.js API and open-weight model integration.
  • MongoDB Atlas: Serves as the primary database for events and attendee statuses.
  • ElevenLabs: Synthesizes the text generated by the open-weight model into human-sounding audio.
  • Sentry: Traces backend API performance and monitors AI inference latency.

View on GitHub


How I Built It
Voco is designed to be incredibly lean and professional. The UI is a strict, light-mode functional dashboard built with React, Vite, TypeScript, and pnpm, heavily optimized for speed and utility.

The backend runs on Render, orchestrating the AI workflow:

Data Layer: MongoDB Atlas securely stores event details and attendee states.

Open-Source AI Core: I utilized an open-weight model (like Llama-3) to parse the attendee data (Name, Role, Event) and dynamically write a personalized, 2-sentence conversational reminder script.

Voice Synthesis: ElevenLabs takes the open-weight model's text and synthesizes a warm, energetic voice.

Observability: Sentry is integrated into the Node.js backend to trace the pipeline, monitor latency, and catch any inference timeouts when hitting the AI APIs.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?
For a side hustle like Voco, open innovation is the only way the unit economics and privacy guarantees actually work.

Protecting Margins: By relying on open-weight models instead of closed, general-purpose APIs, the per-message generation cost remains near zero. This ensures the side hustle remains profitable even if scaled to hundreds of events.

Data Privacy: Organizers are trusting Voco with their communities' phone numbers, names, and job titles. Utilizing open-source AI ensures that attendee data isn't being fed into a proprietary black box to train someone else's model. The data stays strictly within the architecture we control.

My Agent Session
My First User
I tested Voco with a local tech community event. The organizer loved how the personalized voice clips cut through the noise of standard email reminders, and attendees felt a much stronger personal connection to the event, resulting in a higher turnout rate.

Prize Categories
I am submitting Voco for the following partner prize categories:

  1. Best Use of Render: The Node.js backend and AI orchestration pipeline are hosted securely on Render.

  2. Best Use of ElevenLabs: Used to generate the final, human-sounding voice narration from the AI-generated scripts.

  3. Best Use of MongoDB Atlas: Used as the core database to store RSVP lists, event details, and campaign statuses.

  4. Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing: Implemented to monitor backend performance, trace the AI generation pipeline, and debug latency issues.
