items.title: FinZ: a first-paycheck desk that runs Gemma on the laptop
items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built FinZ is a money desk for a first real paycheck. You write the note the way you would text a friend. $14 matcha after a bad standup, felt like a treat. Gemma, running on your computer through Ollama, turns that into an amount, a direction, a short label, and a feeling. You can change any of those before it is saved. The note hits the desk only when you say so. The desk is one pay period. Cash in, cash out, what's left. In the sample below, take-home is $2,800 every other week. The matcha landed at $16, the paycheck got dropped in, and $2,784 was left. The feeling mix is one survival note and one treat. Leftover cash fills dreams smallest first, so an $800 fridge is full and "Japan with my sister" sits at $1,984 of $4,000. Her reason for the trip is on the card: she turns 30, and the point is to be in the room. Open the dream and FinZ will do two more jobs. A money mood is a short read of the notes already on the desk, held up against that dream. A starter split is three buckets for money she might set aside later: an emergency buffer, cash, and a broad index fund. The page says "not financial advice" before the button and again on the sketch. There are no tickers, and nobody places a trade. The person who would pay for this is in their first year of getting paid, and wants that note read on their own machine. The job is small on purpose. Read a messy line, show the period, move leftover cash toward a named dream, and sketch a boring split when they ask. After ollama pull gemma3:4b , those model calls cost nothing, so the thing for sale is the desk. A metered API on every note would eat a product this small before anyone paid for it. Demo The screenshots are FinZ and Gemma on the same laptop. That is the path where the Mastra agent, the weights, and the ledger share a machine. The public desk is finz-omega.vercel.app . The page is hosted. Gemma runs on the visitor's computer. The guide at finz-omega.vercel.app/guide is the setup: install Ollama, pull gemma3:4b , then start Ollama so the browser is allowed to reach localhost ( OLLAMA_ORIGINS ). A note can then be read on that machine, and the ledger for the demo stays in the browser. The money mood and the starter split are the Mastra agent. They run when you start FinZ yourself, next to Ollama: ollama pull gemma3:4b npm install npm run dev Open http://localhost:47291 . The repo README has the same steps, including the smaller gemma3:1b switch if the laptop is tight on memory. Cash in $2,800, cash out $16. Surplus fills the smaller dream first. Gemma's read was titled "Sister's Trip Still Calling." It names the $2,800 paycheck, then the trip, and it signs off "FinZ, on this laptop." Emergency plus cash is 75%. The index is 25%. A dream happening this year has to come out that way. Code sudeepsarmah / FinZ A local-first personal finance website for Gen Z people who just entered the workforce. FinZ Live site: https://finz-omega.vercel.app A local-first money desk for the first real paycheck. Dreams and feelings up front, a spreadsheet nowhere. Gemma reads a messy note on your laptop. Mastra is the agent harness. Income, expenses, and dreams stay in a SQLite file on the machine. Run on your laptop You need Node.js 22 or newer (FinZ uses the built-in node:sqlite ) and Ollama . Pull the model FinZ runs here: ollama pull gemma3:4b If Ollama did not start a background service (common when systemd is not running), start it in another terminal: ollama serve Then: npm install npm run dev Open http://localhost:47291 . The dev server binds 0.0.0.0:47291 . The first page explains the desk. Start Gemma is a plain-language setup guide at /guide . Onboarding includes a currency (USD, INR, EUR, or GBP). gemma3:1b was the first try. It parsed a matcha note, then invented a purchase when… View on GitHub github.com/sudeepsarmah/FinZ The agent is one Mastra Agent in lib/agent.ts . The model is whatever OLLAMA_MODEL says. The default is gemma3:4b . export const finzAgent = new Agent ({ id : " finz " , name : " FinZ " , instructions : `You are FinZ, the money friend on someone's laptop. They just got a first real paycheck. Be warm, specific, and a little irreverent. Short sentences. No shame. No corporate tone. No hashtags. No bullet lectures. Never invent amounts, entries, or dreams that are not in the prompt. You are not a financial advisor. Allocation sketches only use three buckets: an emergency buffer, cash, and a broad index fund. Never name a ticker, fund company, coin, or individual stock. When asked for JSON, reply with one JSON object and no markdown.` , model : ollama . chat ( MODEL_ID , { think : false }), }); Instructions are not a guarantee. A small model will still invent a purchase, so a finished reflection has to mention the dream, mention a real entry label, and only use dollar amounts that were actually logged. The sketch has its own rule for a dream happening this year: const safe = allocation . emergencyPercent + allocation . cashPercent ; if ( dreams . some (( dream ) => dream . timeline === " this year " ) && allocation . indexPercent >= safe ) { return " A this-year dream needs emergency plus cash to be greater than the index percent. " ; } Fail the check and FinZ asks Gemma once more, with the reason in the prompt. Fail again and the request errors. The bad sketch is not saved. How I Built It The open-weight model is Google's Gemma 3, tag gemma3:4b , served by Ollama at 127.0.0.1:11434 . The agent harness is Mastra ( @mastra/core ), connected with ollama-ai-provider-v2 . I did not fine-tune anything. The model is stock. The behavior comes from the prompt, a loose JSON schema, and the checks above. Three calls: Parse a note into amount, direction, label, emotion, and one sentence. Feelings are a fixed set: survival, treat, glow-up, ick, soft-launch, chaos. Temperature stays low. Rent and a paycheck come out as survival. "Felt like a treat" comes out as treat. Write a money mood. Two sentences. The first names a real entry. The second names the dream. If the desk is empty, the first sentence has to say so, and it is not allowed to invent a purchase. Sketch the three buckets as integers that sum to 100. If risk is set to steady, the index cannot be the biggest bucket. If risk is set high, the emergency buffer still stays at least 15%. I tried gemma3:1b first. It parsed the matcha note correctly, then invented a purchase when I asked for a mood. gemma3:4b stayed on the entries that were actually there. That is the bar. The smaller tag is still a switch, OLLAMA_MODEL=gemma3:1b , for a laptop that cannot hold the 4B weights. The harness stays put. Around the model, the app is Next.js 16, TypeScript, and Tailwind. Amounts are integer cents. Onboarding asks for a name, a currency (USD, INR, EUR, or GBP), take-home, how often it lands, how much movement you can stand, and one to three dreams. The note box will finish the word under the cursor from a local list, so spe can become spent . That completion is the word list. Run it yourself and Node 22's built-in node:sqlite stores the profile, the dreams, and the notes in data/finz.db . The hosted demo cannot keep that file, so its copy of the ledger lives in the browser, and a note that the server cannot read falls back to a direct call from the page to local Ollama. The Mastra path, the one with the repair step, is the app and Ollama on the same computer. A 4B model on a laptop is allowed to be slow: each call can take up to 150 seconds a step. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? This desk is pointless if the note leaves the laptop. The dream in the screenshot is a sister turning 30, and the wish is to be in the room rather than the group chat. That sentence, next to a paycheck, is a bad thing to drop into a request log someone else owns. A closed API can publish a retention policy. Ollama on localhost is a stronger promise: the weights are already on the machine, and the call is to 127.0.0.1 . A side hustle this small also dies if every note has a meter on it. Reading a line, writing two sentences, and sketching three numbers will not support a token bill. One ollama pull and the marginal cost of a mood is electricity. I can charge for the desk, or wait until someone asks to pay, and a vendor's price change does not decide whether the project still runs. I needed to be able to throw the model out. gemma3:1b lied about a purchase. I pointed the same Mastra agent at gemma3:4b and kept the checks. A closed default model would have left me waiting on someone else's changelog, or paying up a SKU, to fix a failure I could already see. The check that rejects an invented dollar amount is there because an open model will wander, and I get to decide what counts as a finished answer. Nothing in that loop needs an account, a key, or a network I trust. Pull the weights once. On a plane, on cafe wifi, or on a laptop that has never held an API key, FinZ still reads the note. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma. Parsing, the money mood, and the starter split are calls to gemma3:4b through Ollama. The 4B tag replaced 1B because the smaller one invented a purchase. Best Use of Mastra. One Mastra agent, id: "finz" , is the harness over that local model. It asks for JSON, and it gets one repair step when a reflection or a split fails the check.

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

FinZ is a money desk for a first real paycheck. You write the note the way you would text a friend.

$14 matcha after a bad standup, felt like a treat.

Gemma, running on your computer through Ollama, turns that into an amount, a direction, a short label, and a feeling. You can change any of those before it is saved. The note hits the desk only when you say so.

The desk is one pay period. Cash in, cash out, what's left. In the sample below, take-home is $2,800 every other week. The matcha landed at $16, the paycheck got dropped in, and $2,784 was left. The feeling mix is one survival note and one treat. Leftover cash fills dreams smallest first, so an $800 fridge is full and "Japan with my sister" sits at $1,984 of $4,000. Her reason for the trip is on the card: she turns 30, and the point is to be in the room.

Open the dream and FinZ will do two more jobs. A money mood is a short read of the notes already on the desk, held up against that dream. A starter split is three buckets for money she might set aside later: an emergency buffer, cash, and a broad index fund. The page says "not financial advice" before the button and again on the sketch. There are no tickers, and nobody places a trade.

The person who would pay for this is in their first year of getting paid, and wants that note read on their own machine. The job is small on purpose. Read a messy line, show the period, move leftover cash toward a named dream, and sketch a boring split when they ask. After ollama pull gemma3:4b, those model calls cost nothing, so the thing for sale is the desk. A metered API on every note would eat a product this small before anyone paid for it.

Demo

The screenshots are FinZ and Gemma on the same laptop. That is the path where the Mastra agent, the weights, and the ledger share a machine.

The public desk is finz-omega.vercel.app. The page is hosted. Gemma runs on the visitor's computer. The guide at finz-omega.vercel.app/guide is the setup: install Ollama, pull gemma3:4b, then start Ollama so the browser is allowed to reach localhost (OLLAMA_ORIGINS). A note can then be read on that machine, and the ledger for the demo stays in the browser.

The money mood and the starter split are the Mastra agent. They run when you start FinZ yourself, next to Ollama:

ollama pull gemma3:4b
npm install
npm run dev

Open http://localhost:47291. The repo README has the same steps, including the smaller gemma3:1b switch if the laptop is tight on memory.

Cash in $2,800, cash out $16. Surplus fills the smaller dream first.

Gemma's read was titled "Sister's Trip Still Calling." It names the $2,800 paycheck, then the trip, and it signs off "FinZ, on this laptop."

Emergency plus cash is 75%. The index is 25%. A dream happening this year has to come out that way.

Code
sudeepsarmah / FinZ A local-first personal finance website for Gen Z people who just entered the workforce.
FinZ

Live site: https://finz-omega.vercel.app

A local-first money desk for the first real paycheck. Dreams and feelings up front, a spreadsheet nowhere. Gemma reads a messy note on your laptop. Mastra is the agent harness. Income, expenses, and dreams stay in a SQLite file on the machine.

Run on your laptop

You need Node.js 22 or newer (FinZ uses the built-in node:sqlite) and Ollama.

Pull the model FinZ runs here:

ollama pull gemma3:4b

If Ollama did not start a background service (common when systemd is not running), start it in another terminal:

ollama serve

Then:

npm install
npm run dev

Open http://localhost:47291. The dev server binds 0.0.0.0:47291. The first page explains the desk. Start Gemma is a plain-language setup guide at /guide. Onboarding includes a currency (USD, INR, EUR, or GBP).

gemma3:1b was the first try. It parsed a matcha note, then invented a purchase when…

View on GitHub

github.com/sudeepsarmah/FinZ

The agent is one Mastra Agent in lib/agent.ts. The model is whatever OLLAMA_MODEL says. The default is gemma3:4b.

export const finzAgent = new Agent({
  id: "finz",
  name: "FinZ",
  instructions: `You are FinZ, the money friend on someone's laptop. They just got a first real paycheck.
Be warm, specific, and a little irreverent. Short sentences. No shame. No corporate tone. No hashtags. No bullet lectures.
Never invent amounts, entries, or dreams that are not in the prompt.
You are not a financial advisor. Allocation sketches only use three buckets: an emergency buffer, cash, and a broad index fund. Never name a ticker, fund company, coin, or individual stock.
When asked for JSON, reply with one JSON object and no markdown.`,
  model: ollama.chat(MODEL_ID, { think: false }),
});

Instructions are not a guarantee. A small model will still invent a purchase, so a finished reflection has to mention the dream, mention a real entry label, and only use dollar amounts that were actually logged. The sketch has its own rule for a dream happening this year:

const safe = allocation.emergencyPercent + allocation.cashPercent;
if (
  dreams.some((dream) => dream.timeline === "this year") &&
  allocation.indexPercent >= safe
) {
  return "A this-year dream needs emergency plus cash to be greater than the index percent.";
}

Fail the check and FinZ asks Gemma once more, with the reason in the prompt. Fail again and the request errors. The bad sketch is not saved.

How I Built It

The open-weight model is Google's Gemma 3, tag gemma3:4b, served by Ollama at 127.0.0.1:11434. The agent harness is Mastra (@mastra/core), connected with ollama-ai-provider-v2. I did not fine-tune anything. The model is stock. The behavior comes from the prompt, a loose JSON schema, and the checks above.

Three calls:

  1. Parse a note into amount, direction, label, emotion, and one sentence. Feelings are a fixed set: survival, treat, glow-up, ick, soft-launch, chaos. Temperature stays low. Rent and a paycheck come out as survival. "Felt like a treat" comes out as treat.
  2. Write a money mood. Two sentences. The first names a real entry. The second names the dream. If the desk is empty, the first sentence has to say so, and it is not allowed to invent a purchase.
  3. Sketch the three buckets as integers that sum to 100. If risk is set to steady, the index cannot be the biggest bucket. If risk is set high, the emergency buffer still stays at least 15%.

I tried gemma3:1b first. It parsed the matcha note correctly, then invented a purchase when I asked for a mood. gemma3:4b stayed on the entries that were actually there. That is the bar. The smaller tag is still a switch, OLLAMA_MODEL=gemma3:1b, for a laptop that cannot hold the 4B weights. The harness stays put.

Around the model, the app is Next.js 16, TypeScript, and Tailwind. Amounts are integer cents. Onboarding asks for a name, a currency (USD, INR, EUR, or GBP), take-home, how often it lands, how much movement you can stand, and one to three dreams. The note box will finish the word under the cursor from a local list, so spe can become spent. That completion is the word list.

Run it yourself and Node 22's built-in node:sqlite stores the profile, the dreams, and the notes in data/finz.db. The hosted demo cannot keep that file, so its copy of the ledger lives in the browser, and a note that the server cannot read falls back to a direct call from the page to local Ollama. The Mastra path, the one with the repair step, is the app and Ollama on the same computer. A 4B model on a laptop is allowed to be slow: each call can take up to 150 seconds a step.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

This desk is pointless if the note leaves the laptop. The dream in the screenshot is a sister turning 30, and the wish is to be in the room rather than the group chat. That sentence, next to a paycheck, is a bad thing to drop into a request log someone else owns. A closed API can publish a retention policy. Ollama on localhost is a stronger promise: the weights are already on the machine, and the call is to 127.0.0.1.

A side hustle this small also dies if every note has a meter on it. Reading a line, writing two sentences, and sketching three numbers will not support a token bill. One ollama pull and the marginal cost of a mood is electricity. I can charge for the desk, or wait until someone asks to pay, and a vendor's price change does not decide whether the project still runs.

I needed to be able to throw the model out. gemma3:1b lied about a purchase. I pointed the same Mastra agent at gemma3:4b and kept the checks. A closed default model would have left me waiting on someone else's changelog, or paying up a SKU, to fix a failure I could already see. The check that rejects an invented dollar amount is there because an open model will wander, and I get to decide what counts as a finished answer.

Nothing in that loop needs an account, a key, or a network I trust. Pull the weights once. On a plane, on cafe wifi, or on a laptop that has never held an API key, FinZ still reads the note.

Prize Categories
  • Best Use of Gemma. Parsing, the money mood, and the starter split are calls to gemma3:4b through Ollama. The 4B tag replaced 1B because the smaller one invented a purchase.
  • Best Use of Mastra. One Mastra agent, id: "finz", is the harness over that local model. It asks for JSON, and it gets one repair step when a reflection or a split fails the check.

items.title: NOCTURNE: Open-Source AI for Smarter Security Assessments
items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle . What I Built What if small cybersecurity teams could spend less time coordinating tools and more time understanding security risks? Penetration testing often involves switching between terminals, scanners, browsers, notes, and reporting tools. For independent security professionals and small teams, managing this workflow can be time-consuming. We built NOCTURNE , an open-source, AI-assisted penetration testing orchestration platform that brings the different stages of an authorized security assessment into one operator-controlled workspace. NOCTURNE uses an LLM-based multi-agent architecture to coordinate assessment tasks. Instead of manually managing every tool and collecting results separately, an operator can define the scope of an engagement, supervise AI-assisted workflows, review findings, and prepare structured reports. Its main capabilities include: Multi-agent orchestration: A LangGraph-based orchestrator plans tasks and coordinates executor agents. Security tool integration: Support for tools such as Nmap, Nuclei, and other security testing utilities. Interactive operator console: A React dashboard with an agent graph, activity feed, chat, and terminal interfaces. Browser-assisted workflows: Integration with a browser environment for testing web applications. Findings management: Review, verify, dismiss, and organize discovered issues. Structured reporting: Export findings and assessment reports in formats including PDF, JSON, and SARIF. Flexible model configuration: Support for open-weight models, including Gemma, through hosted providers or compatible self-hosted endpoints. Who would pay for it? Our target users are freelance penetration testers, small cybersecurity consultancies, and internal security teams . These users may benefit from a tool that helps organize repetitive assessment steps, reduces context-switching, and consolidates reporting. We see potential for a commercial offering through managed deployments, hosted subscriptions, or per-engagement pricing. Rather than replacing experienced security professionals, the goal is to help them work more efficiently while retaining human oversight. This is an early commercial direction, not a claim that we already have paying customers. Demo 🚀 Explore NOCTURNE — Interactive Demo The public demo allows visitors to explore NOCTURNE's operator interface directly in their browsers without installing dependencies or configuring API keys. It includes sample sessions, agent activity, findings, and interactive dashboard components. Important: The public deployment runs in simulation mode using mock data. It does not perform real penetration tests, invoke live AI models, or connect to an operational security backend. The live-execution architecture is available in the source repository for authorized environments. Operator Dashboard The operator dashboard brings assessment activity, navigation, and monitoring into a unified interface. Findings Management Security findings can be organized and reviewed before being incorporated into reports. Agent Browser The system also provides an interface for supervising browser-assisted assessment workflows. Code GitHub Repository: https://github.com/NullClassifier/nocturne NOCTURNE is publicly available under the MIT License. The repository includes the application source code, development infrastructure, configuration examples, technical documentation, and instructions for local deployment. Developers can inspect its architecture, experiment with supported model configurations, and contribute improvements. How I Built It NOCTURNE combines open-source AI orchestration frameworks, a modular application architecture, and security testing infrastructure. 1. Multi-Agent AI Architecture At the center of the platform is LangGraph , which coordinates the agent workflow. An orchestrator interprets the assessment objectives and delegates work to executor agents. Those agents can interact with available security tools, collect results, and update the engagement state. The architecture is designed to keep the operator involved throughout the workflow, including the ability to steer or stop a run. 2. Open-Weight AI with Gemma One of our main goals was to avoid locking the platform into a single proprietary AI provider. We integrated LiteLLM to provide a configurable abstraction over different language-model endpoints. NOCTURNE supports Gemma through compatible providers, including Google AI Studio, OpenRouter, and custom model-serving endpoints. Our repository documents the use of a self-hosted Gemma model during development. This configuration allows model inference to run on infrastructure controlled by the operator rather than requiring a single external API. Supporting different deployment options also gives users more flexibility over model costs, infrastructure, and data handling. 3. Backend and Execution Infrastructure The backend is built with Python and FastAPI . We separated the API from the agent execution process: FastAPI handles application requests and communication with the operator console. Redis and arq coordinate background jobs and event delivery. PostgreSQL stores structured application information. SeaweedFS provides S3-compatible object storage. Docker supports reproducible environments and isolated security-tool execution. The engine also includes checkpointing capabilities so interrupted workflows can resume. 4. Frontend and Operator Experience The interface is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite . We wanted the experience to feel like a security operations workspace rather than a simple chatbot. The interface combines live activity displays, agent visualization, findings management, terminal components, and report access. For the public demonstration, we use the application's mock API implementation. This provides an interactive frontend without exposing real security testing infrastructure to the Internet. 5. Improvements During Hacktoberfest Week 2 NOCTURNE builds upon an earlier prototype, so not every component of the repository was developed during October 12–18. During the challenge period, our documented improvements included: Expanding model configuration with Google AI Studio, OpenRouter, and custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Adding usage and cost metering for supported hosted Gemma models. Improving reproducibility through SeaweedFS-backed local object storage. Refining model-related interface elements and project documentation. These changes build on the earlier architecture and move NOCTURNE toward a more flexible and accessible developer experience. The public Git history documents both the original foundation and the subsequent improvements. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? For NOCTURNE, open innovation is not simply about publishing source code. It directly influences how the platform can be deployed, adapted, and maintained. 1. Freedom to choose models Different teams have different requirements for model quality, privacy, deployment, and cost. Using open-weight models and an open-source model-integration layer makes it possible to experiment with alternatives instead of depending entirely on one proprietary provider. 2. Greater control over sensitive information Security assessments can involve confidential technical information. A self-hosted model deployment can provide greater control over where inference happens and how assessment information is processed, although secure deployment still depends on the surrounding infrastructure and configuration. 3. A more flexible cost structure Usage-based API pricing can make recurring AI workloads harder to predict. Running an open-weight model on infrastructure a team controls creates another option. It avoids per-token API fees, although hardware, hosting, and maintenance still have real costs. NOCTURNE's model usage tracking also helps operators understand the cost of supported hosted inference. 4. Transparency and customization Security workflows vary between organizations. With an open-source architecture, developers can inspect agent orchestration, modify workflows, integrate additional tools, and improve the project's behavior. This flexibility is especially valuable for specialized professional workflows where a generic AI assistant may not be sufficient. Challenges and Lessons Learned Building an AI-assisted security platform involves more than connecting an LLM to tools. We had to consider the boundaries between agent planning, execution, application state, and operator interaction. Model compatibility is another challenge. Different providers may handle tool calls and structured responses differently, so reliable operation requires careful testing. We also learned that a compelling interface is not a substitute for verified functionality. This is why our public demo is explicitly labeled as simulated, while the repository documents the separate live-execution architecture. Before any commercial deployment, additional work on reliability, security hardening, access controls, and real-world validation would be essential. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma We are entering the Best Use of Gemma category. Gemma is an open-weight model supported by NOCTURNE's agent architecture. The project documents self-hosted Gemma usage and includes provider integrations designed to make compatible Gemma deployments easier to configure. The motivation behind this integration is to make AI-assisted security workflows less dependent on proprietary models and fixed cloud providers. Our interactive public demo is simulated; Gemma integration and model execution are documented in the source repository. Team NOCTURNE was developed collaboratively by the Netrunners team . Ismayil Yusifli DEV: @ismail06 GitHub: @ismayilysfli Huseyn Pashayev DEV: @s8int GitHub: @NullClassifier We collaborated on project development, integration, and documentation, with some code contributions shared outside GitHub before being committed to the repository. What's Next? Our next steps are to improve compatibility across supported models, strengthen reliability, expand testing in authorized lab environments, and gather feedback from cybersecurity professionals. We also want to explore whether a managed version could become a practical service for smaller security teams. Our goal is to make AI-assisted security assessment workflows more accessible, adaptable, and transparent through open-source technology. NOCTURNE is intended exclusively for educational research and authorized security assessments. Security testing must only be performed on systems owned by the operator or covered by explicit permission and an agreed testing scope.

items.title: Building a Memory System for AI Agents: What Works Today and What Comes Next
items.summary: I started this project with a question: how could an AI agent keep useful information between conversations without treating its entire chat history as one big search result? A memory system needs more than a place to save text. It needs a way to decide what to keep, retain where a memory came from, retrieve it later, and avoid silently overwriting newer information. I built Cognitive Memory for AI Agents to explore those pieces in a small, modular Python project. The current implementation covers memory formation, evidence storage, canonical persistence, a FastAPI interface, and a background “Dream Engine” that analyzes memories and proposes decisions. Some parts of the larger design—especially Qdrant semantic search and FalkorDB graph retrieval—are still future work. I’ll separate what is implemented from what I want to build next. The code is in the project repository on GitHub . From an experience to a memory The API’s orchestration layer connects the main steps. An incoming experience goes through an ingestor, which validates and normalizes it while keeping details such as its source and scope. A candidate builder turns that event into a possible memory. JEV, the project’s decision layer, then evaluates what should happen. The current deterministic path is intentionally narrow. It can store a candidate, ignore an exact normalized duplicate in the same scope, or mark a low-confidence candidate as uncertain and requiring review. JEV also defines other actions, such as merging or superseding memories, but defining an action in the decision model does not mean the API automatically carries it out. That distinction matters to me. Similar wording can be a useful clue, but it is not proof that two statements mean the same thing. SQLite as the canonical record When a memory is accepted, SQLite stores the canonical memory record and its domain events. The repository writes these transactionally and tracks a version for each memory. Updates include an expected version, so a stale request can be rejected instead of overwriting a newer change. The way I think about the storage boundary is simple: the canonical record owns the memory’s identity and current state. Search indexes, when added, should help find memories; they should not become competing sources of truth. Keeping evidence attached A memory is more useful when I can trace it back to the information that supported it. The evidence registry stores metadata and connects an evidence identifier to the original content. The object store keeps that content by its SHA-256 hash, which also lets the store verify the bytes when they are retrieved. The orchestrator registers evidence for experiences that proceed to storage, then attaches the resulting evidence identifier to the canonical memory. This gives the system a provenance path to inspect later. There is a boundary here: evidence and canonical memory use separate storage mechanisms. Their writes are not one distributed transaction, so the current implementation does not guarantee that both stores will always succeed or recover together. FastAPI as the interface FastAPI exposes the memory operations under a versioned API. The current service supports creating, listing, fetching, and updating canonical memories, retrieving memory history, and processing incoming experiences through the orchestrator. The health endpoint confirms that the API process responds; it does not prove that every dependency is healthy. This API is the part an agent or application can call without handling SQLite or the evidence files directly. The repository also documents a local development workflow and test suite. Its README reports 158 passing tests for the recorded Phase 5 run; I have not rerun that suite while preparing this post. Where Qdrant and FalkorDB fit I chose Qdrant and FalkorDB for the design because they address different retrieval questions. Qdrant is intended to provide semantic vector search: finding memories that are relevant to a query even when they use different wording. FalkorDB is intended to represent connections between memories and entities, so a later retrieval step could follow relationships between related facts. In the architecture I want to build, those stores would be derived indexes. A retrieval request could use semantic search to find starting memories, then use graph relationships to discover connected context, and finally load the canonical records and their evidence references. The canonical store would remain authoritative. That is the planned direction, not a description of a working end-to-end Qdrant and FalkorDB flow in the current repository. The current source tree does not contain those integrations, so I can’t claim that graph traversal or vector search is already available. The Dream Engine and its limits The project also includes a Dream Engine workflow for selecting memories, finding possible duplicates or conflicts, and producing structured consolidation decisions. Its queue and execution reports are persisted. The current discovery logic uses deterministic similarity, shared-entity checks, and heuristics; it is not a complete semantic conflict detector. Most importantly, the current orchestrator proposes decisions but does not apply them to canonical memories. It reports zero applied mutations. I see this as a useful safety boundary while the decision and review workflow is still evolving. What I learned The main lesson so far is that a memory system is not just retrieval. The hard parts include preserving evidence, keeping one canonical record, handling versions safely, and being clear about which decisions the software can actually execute. I also learned to keep the architecture’s direction separate from the implementation status. Qdrant and FalkorDB are part of the plan, but they need to be integrated and verified before I describe them as working features. There is still a lot to build: vector indexing, graph relationships and traversal, stronger cross-store recovery, authentication and authorization, and measured retrieval evaluation. For now, this project is a working foundation for exploring how those pieces could fit together. AI assistance disclosure: I used an AI coding assistant during development and to help organize this write-up. I checked the implementation claims against the repository and have marked unimplemented components as future work.

items.title: Adding dispute resolution to your billing flow with a REST API
items.summary: Disclosure: I'm Greg, COO at Arbitration.Inc. This is about our API, so I'm biased. I'd like feedback from people who build billing and collections features. Many vertical SaaS products (HOA, gym, field service, subscription billing) have customers whose contracts already include arbitration clauses. Those clauses almost never get used. The unpaid balances are too small for collections or small claims to be worth the effort, so the money gets written off. We built the arbitration process as a REST API so a platform can put "File a dispute" next to an overdue invoice. Here's the flow. 1. Create a case curl -X POST https://api.arb.inc/cases/create \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" The response returns a case ID you use for everything else. 2. File the claim curl -X POST https://api.arb.inc/filings/documents/create \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "caseID": "2026-10-00001", "documentID": "statementOfClaim", "fields": { "claimantName": "Example Fitness LLC", "respondentName": "Jane Doe", "respondentAddress": "123 Main St", "basisForArbitration": "Membership agreement, Section 12", "statementOfFacts": "Dues unpaid for 60 days", "reliefRequested": "Payment of $180.00" } }' (The values above are made up for illustration.) 3. Evidence, notice, and webhooks POST /evidence/uploads/create attaches documents or photos to the case. POST /service-of-notice/mailings/create sends the notice by mail, alongside email. Webhooks fire when a case changes phase (for example, from filing to response), so your UI can show status without polling. There's an OpenAPI 3.0 spec for generating clients. Docs are at docs.arb.inc . Pricing and the platform model Pricing is public: $99 for a single case, $50 per case in a 50-case pack, and $10 per case in a 1,000-case pack. An arbitration award can be confirmed by a court, which turns it into a judgment, but that depends on a valid agreement to arbitrate. items.summary_html:
Disclosure: I'm Greg, COO at Arbitration.Inc. This is about our API, so I'm biased. I'd like feedback from people who build billing and collections features.

Many vertical SaaS products (HOA, gym, field service, subscription billing) have customers whose contracts already include arbitration clauses. Those clauses almost never get used. The unpaid balances are too small for collections or small claims to be worth the effort, so the money gets written off.

We built the arbitration process as a REST API so a platform can put "File a dispute" next to an overdue invoice. Here's the flow.

1. Create a case 
curl -X POST https://api.arb.inc/cases/create \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json"

The response returns a case ID you use for everything else.

2. File the claim 
curl -X POST https://api.arb.inc/filings/documents/create \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "caseID": "2026-10-00001",
    "documentID": "statementOfClaim",
    "fields": {
      "claimantName": "Example Fitness LLC",
      "respondentName": "Jane Doe",
      "respondentAddress": "123 Main St",
      "basisForArbitration": "Membership agreement, Section 12",
      "statementOfFacts": "Dues unpaid for 60 days",
      "reliefRequested": "Payment of $180.00"
    }
  }'

(The values above are made up for illustration.)

3. Evidence, notice, and webhooks
  • POST /evidence/uploads/create attaches documents or photos to the case.
  • POST /service-of-notice/mailings/create sends the notice by mail, alongside email.
  • Webhooks fire when a case changes phase (for example, from filing to response), so your UI can show status without polling.

There's an OpenAPI 3.0 spec for generating clients. Docs are at docs.arb.inc.

Pricing and the platform model

Pricing is public: $99 for a single case, $50 per case in a 50-case pack, and $10 per case in a 1,000-case pack. A platform can buy in bulk, set what its own customers pay, and keep the margin.

Caveats
  • The process is AI-assisted, and under California law these arbitrations may not be binding for California residents.
  • An arbitration award can be confirmed by a court, which turns it into a judgment, but that depends on a valid agreement to arbitrate. If a customer's contract has no arbitration clause, this doesn't apply.
What I'd like to know

If you've built billing or collections features:

  1. Would your customers use something like this, or is unpaid-balance recovery already well handled?
  2. What would stop you from integrating it?
  3. Would you sell it as an add-on or fold it into your plans?

items.title: TinyFish Makes Search Free: What It Really Costs an AI Agent to Read the Web
items.summary: An AI agent that reads the web pays 2 kinds of cost. The first is the retrieval charge: what a search or fetch API bills per request. The second is model processing: content passed from retrieved pages into an AI model consumes tokens, while reasoning and generated responses add further costs. TinyFish , a web infrastructure company for AI agents, argues that teams budget for the model and underestimate how much retrieved content drives it. This article walks through the token math, the context-window impact, and what the Artificial Analysis Search API leaderboard does and does not show. TL;DR What it runs on: TinyFish uses a web-native AI model designed for search, retrieval, and interaction with live websites. The model runs on TinyFish-managed infrastructure, while its cloud browser fleet renders pages and handles website interactions. No local GPU is needed. Access is via REST, Python and TypeScript SDKs, CLI or MCP. Performance: On the Sep 28, 2026 Artificial Analysis snapshot, TinyFish Search (web) scores 71 at $9.30 per 1,000 benchmark tasks, with 59.0 seconds per task (model plus search time). Best: $0 retrieval charge within rate limits (Search: 30 requests/min, 500/hour; Fetch: 150 URLs/min, 1,000/day), and the lowest total cost among the 12 configurations displayed on the leaderboard. Trade-offs: The second longest time per task among displayed configurations, and an Agent product whose built-in model cannot be swapped. Scores: Highest displayed is Perplexity Search (medium) at 80. Lowest displayed is TinyFish Search (web) at 71. The no-search baseline is 33. Retrieval charges vs model processing costs Search and fetch APIs usually bill per request or per page. Whatever they return then enters the model’s context and is billed as input tokens. Reasoning and output tokens come on top. Enterprises now route each task to the cheapest capable model, a trend underlined when Stripe agreed to acquire OpenRouter , a gateway spanning 400+ models from 80+ providers. Routing lowers the price per token. It does not change how many tokens a retrieved page contains. Free Search and Fetch remove TinyFish’s retrieval charge within its limits. The downstream model still incurs inference costs. That is why the size of each returned page matters. How big is one page in tokens? TinyFish ran a fetch quality evaluation on June 2, 2026, across 45 URLs and 5 providers on default settings. For one Daily Mail article with a body of roughly 4,300 characters, the providers returned: Provider Characters returned Est. tokens* Input cost at $1 / 1M tokens* TinyFish Fetch 4,737 ~1,184 ~$0.00118 Exa Contents 65,793 ~16,448 ~$0.01645 Firecrawl Scrape 171,095 ~42,774 ~$0.04277 Tavily Extract 46,433 ~11,608 ~$0.01161 Parallel Extract 600 (excerpt, not the article) ~150 ~$0.00015 *Marktechpost calculation: ~4 characters per token and an illustrative input price of $1 per 1M tokens. Input processing only; excludes retrieval charges, reasoning and output. Real counts vary by tokenizer. Character counts from TinyFish’s evaluation. In this example, Firecrawl returned approximately 36 times as many characters as TinyFish. Parallel also returned only an excerpt rather than the complete article, so its smaller output is not directly comparable to the full-page extractions. While this illustrates how extraction output size can affect token consumption, the difference comes from a single webpage and should not be generalized across all websites. Those percentages are not used for this individual page comparison because outputs above 30,000 characters were truncated before judging. Context limits and repeated calls Assume every extracted character goes into the same context, with no filtering, truncation or summarization. A page containing approximately 42,774 tokens would consume about one-third of a 128K-token context window. Three such pages would require approximately 128,322 tokens, leaving little or no room for system instructions, conversation history, or the agent’s response. Agent loops also resend context. Artificial Analysis notes that each turn resends the full conversation, with earlier input billed at the model’s cached-input price. Caching lowers the cost of rereading a noisy page. It does not remove it, and the page still occupies the window. In that TinyFish internal evaluation, a result counted as covered only with at least 1,000 characters and a judged signal ratio above 30%. Coverage was TinyFish 93%, Tavily 80%, Exa 73%, Firecrawl 62% and Parallel 58%. Among usable results only, median signal was 90.5% for TinyFish and 89.7% for Exa. TinyFish ran the test on itself, the sample is 45 URLs, and news pages drove most of the gap. Why TinyFish makes retrieval free TinyFish frames search as one operation inside execution, like DNS or storage for ordinary software. An agent booking, comparing or filling out a form should care whether the job got done, not which search system found the page. TinyFish attributes its free retrieval pricing to three aspects of its infrastructure: Shared infrastructure: TinyFish built its browser fleet, stealth systems, session hydration and elastic scaling before Search was a product. TinyFish says this changes the marginal economics of search. It does not make the infrastructure free to run. Specialized models: TinyFish says its web-native AI model is designed for search, fetch, and live-site interaction. Its development draws on agent operational trajectories and large volumes of search activity, helping reduce reliance on general-purpose models for intermediate web tasks. No giant index: TinyFish says it would rather learn how work gets done than become an indexing company. TinyFish charges separately for Agent and Browser usage, while Search and Fetch remain free within their published limits. Per the pricing page , Search is free at 30 requests per minute and 500 per hour. Fetch is free at 150 URLs per minute and 1,000 per day. Both keep working at a $0 Wallet balance. Agent costs $0.016 per step with 2 concurrent runs, and Browser costs $0.002 per minute with 5 sessions. New accounts get $8 in Wallet funds. What the benchmark shows, and what it does not Artificial Analysis holds the answer model fixed (GPT-5.6 Luna, medium) and changes only the search provider. Model cost covers input, cached, reasoning and output tokens. Differences between providers reflect returned payloads, how many searches the model runs and how much it reasons. On the Sep 28, 2026 snapshot, model cost ranges from $8.04 to $21.65 per 1,000 tasks across the 12 displayed configurations. These come from 26 products across 13 providers. TinyFish posts $0 for search plus $9.30 for the model, the lowest displayed total. The trade-offs: TinyFish recorded a Search Index score of 71, the lowest among the displayed configurations, and a DeepSearchQA F1 of 67. Its benchmark time was approximately 59 seconds per task, combining estimated model processing time and measured search time rather than representing API latency alone. Because Artificial Analysis uses its own shared extraction layer, the results do not directly measure TinyFish Fetch. Similarly, benchmark costs per 1,000 tasks should not be confused with API prices per 1,000 requests, since a single task may involve multiple searches. How TinyFish compares with closest competitors The table covers 3 selected competitors that appear in both the Artificial Analysis leaderboard and TinyFish’s fetch test. Feature TinyFish Exa Firecrawl Parallel Search price Free (30/min, 500/hr) From $4 per 1k requests (Instant, up to 10 results); $7 Fast/Auto; extra results billed 2 credits per 10 results $1 to $5 per 1k requests (10 results) Page fetch / extract Free (150/min, 1,000/day) $1 per 1k pages, per content type 1 credit per page $1 per 1k Free allowance Search and Fetch at $0 balance, plus $8 Wallet $10 credits/mo 1,000 credits/mo $5 credits/mo (up to 5,000 requests, depending on endpoint) Paid automation or research product** Agent $0.016/step; Browser $0.002/min Agent (research) from $0.012/run Interact (browser) 2 credits/min Task API (research) $0.005 to $2.40/request AA Search Index 71 74 (auto) 73 75 (advanced) AA search + model $ per 1k benchmark tasks $0 + $9.30 $65.57 + $17.73 $30.48 + $12.09 $47.93 + $11.29 AA time per task (model + search) 59.0s 32.3s 62.0s 41.9s Fetch coverage (TinyFish internal evaluation, June 2026) 93% 73% 62% 58% **Browser operation and research tasks are different capabilities, so these prices are not directly comparable. Pricing checked Oct 7, 2026: TinyFish , Exa , Firecrawl , Parallel . Benchmark data: Artificial Analysis (Sep 28, 2026) and its methodology . Coverage: TinyFish internal evaluation (June 2026) , a single-vendor test separate from the third-party benchmark. Key Takeaways Agents pay retrieval charges plus model processing on everything retrieved. The same article ranged from ~1,184 to ~42,774 estimated tokens by provider. 3 large unfiltered pages can exceed a 128K-token window. Free Search and Fetch remove TinyFish’s retrieval charge, not model costs. TinyFish had the lowest displayed total cost on Artificial Analysis, but the lowest displayed score. Thanks to the Tinyfish team for the thought leadership / resources for this article. This article is sponsored by TinyFish.
items.summary_html:
An AI agent that reads the web pays 2 kinds of cost. The first is the retrieval charge: what a search or fetch API bills per request. The second is model processing: content passed from retrieved pages into an AI model consumes tokens, while reasoning and generated responses add further costs. TinyFish, a web infrastructure company for AI agents, argues that teams budget for the model and underestimate how much retrieved content drives it.

This article walks through the token math, the context-window impact, and what the Artificial Analysis Search API leaderboard does and does not show.

TL;DR
  • What it runs on: TinyFish uses a web-native AI model designed for search, retrieval, and interaction with live websites. The model runs on TinyFish-managed infrastructure, while its cloud browser fleet renders pages and handles website interactions. No local GPU is needed. Access is via REST, Python and TypeScript SDKs, CLI or MCP.
  • Performance: On the Sep 28, 2026 Artificial Analysis snapshot, TinyFish Search (web) scores 71 at $9.30 per 1,000 benchmark tasks, with 59.0 seconds per task (model plus search time).
  • Best: $0 retrieval charge within rate limits (Search: 30 requests/min, 500/hour; Fetch: 150 URLs/min, 1,000/day), and the lowest total cost among the 12 configurations displayed on the leaderboard.
  • Trade-offs: The second longest time per task among displayed configurations, and an Agent product whose built-in model cannot be swapped.
  • Scores: Highest displayed is Perplexity Search (medium) at 80. Lowest displayed is TinyFish Search (web) at 71. The no-search baseline is 33.
Retrieval charges vs model processing costs

Search and fetch APIs usually bill per request or per page. Whatever they return then enters the model’s context and is billed as input tokens. Reasoning and output tokens come on top.

Enterprises now route each task to the cheapest capable model, a trend underlined when Stripe agreed to acquire OpenRouter, a gateway spanning 400+ models from 80+ providers. Routing lowers the price per token. It does not change how many tokens a retrieved page contains.

Free Search and Fetch remove TinyFish’s retrieval charge within its limits. The downstream model still incurs inference costs. That is why the size of each returned page matters.

How big is one page in tokens?

TinyFish ran a fetch quality evaluation on June 2, 2026, across 45 URLs and 5 providers on default settings. For one Daily Mail article with a body of roughly 4,300 characters, the providers returned:

ProviderCharacters returnedEst. tokens*Input cost at $1 / 1M tokens*TinyFish Fetch4,737~1,184~$0.00118Exa Contents65,793~16,448~$0.01645Firecrawl Scrape171,095~42,774~$0.04277Tavily Extract46,433~11,608~$0.01161Parallel Extract600 (excerpt, not the article)~150~$0.00015

*Marktechpost calculation: ~4 characters per token and an illustrative input price of $1 per 1M tokens. Input processing only; excludes retrieval charges, reasoning and output. Real counts vary by tokenizer. Character counts from TinyFish’s evaluation.

In this example, Firecrawl returned approximately 36 times as many characters as TinyFish.  Parallel also returned only an excerpt rather than the complete article, so its smaller output is not directly comparable to the full-page extractions.

While this illustrates how extraction output size can affect token consumption, the difference comes from a single webpage and should not be generalized across all websites. Those percentages are not used for this individual page comparison because outputs above 30,000 characters were truncated before judging.

Context limits and repeated calls

Assume every extracted character goes into the same context, with no filtering, truncation or summarization. A page containing approximately 42,774 tokens would consume about one-third of a 128K-token context window. Three such pages would require approximately 128,322 tokens, leaving little or no room for system instructions, conversation history, or the agent’s response.

Agent loops also resend context. Artificial Analysis notes that each turn resends the full conversation, with earlier input billed at the model’s cached-input price. Caching lowers the cost of rereading a noisy page. It does not remove it, and the page still occupies the window.

In that TinyFish internal evaluation, a result counted as covered only with at least 1,000 characters and a judged signal ratio above 30%. Coverage was TinyFish 93%, Tavily 80%, Exa 73%, Firecrawl 62% and Parallel 58%. Among usable results only, median signal was 90.5% for TinyFish and 89.7% for Exa. TinyFish ran the test on itself, the sample is 45 URLs, and news pages drove most of the gap.

Why TinyFish makes retrieval free

TinyFish frames search as one operation inside execution, like DNS or storage for ordinary software. An agent booking, comparing or filling out a form should care whether the job got done, not which search system found the page. 

TinyFish attributes its free retrieval pricing to three aspects of its infrastructure:

  • Shared infrastructure: TinyFish built its browser fleet, stealth systems, session hydration and elastic scaling before Search was a product. TinyFish says this changes the marginal economics of search. It does not make the infrastructure free to run.
  • Specialized models: TinyFish says its web-native AI model is designed for search, fetch, and live-site interaction. Its development draws on agent operational trajectories and large volumes of search activity, helping reduce reliance on general-purpose models for intermediate web tasks.
  • No giant index: TinyFish says it would rather learn how work gets done than become an indexing company.

TinyFish charges separately for Agent and Browser usage, while Search and Fetch remain free within their published limits. Per the pricing page, Search is free at 30 requests per minute and 500 per hour. Fetch is free at 150 URLs per minute and 1,000 per day. Both keep working at a $0 Wallet balance. Agent costs $0.016 per step with 2 concurrent runs, and Browser costs $0.002 per minute with 5 sessions. New accounts get $8 in Wallet funds.

What the benchmark shows, and what it does not

Artificial Analysis holds the answer model fixed (GPT-5.6 Luna, medium) and changes only the search provider. Model cost covers input, cached, reasoning and output tokens. Differences between providers reflect returned payloads, how many searches the model runs and how much it reasons.

On the Sep 28, 2026 snapshot, model cost ranges from $8.04 to $21.65 per 1,000 tasks across the 12 displayed configurations. These come from 26 products across 13 providers. TinyFish posts $0 for search plus $9.30 for the model, the lowest displayed total.

The trade-offs: TinyFish recorded a Search Index score of 71, the lowest among the displayed configurations, and a DeepSearchQA F1 of 67. Its benchmark time was approximately 59 seconds per task, combining estimated model processing time and measured search time rather than representing API latency alone. Because Artificial Analysis uses its own shared extraction layer, the results do not directly measure TinyFish Fetch. Similarly, benchmark costs per 1,000 tasks should not be confused with API prices per 1,000 requests, since a single task may involve multiple searches.

How TinyFish compares with closest competitors

The table covers 3 selected competitors that appear in both the Artificial Analysis leaderboard and TinyFish’s fetch test.

FeatureTinyFishExaFirecrawlParallelSearch priceFree (30/min, 500/hr)From $4 per 1k requests (Instant, up to 10 results); $7 Fast/Auto; extra results billed2 credits per 10 results$1 to $5 per 1k requests (10 results)Page fetch / extractFree (150/min, 1,000/day)$1 per 1k pages, per content type1 credit per page$1 per 1kFree allowanceSearch and Fetch at $0 balance, plus $8 Wallet$10 credits/mo1,000 credits/mo$5 credits/mo (up to 5,000 requests, depending on endpoint)Paid automation or research product**Agent $0.016/step; Browser $0.002/minAgent (research) from $0.012/runInteract (browser) 2 credits/minTask API (research) $0.005 to $2.40/requestAA Search Index7174 (auto)7375 (advanced)AA search + model $ per 1k benchmark tasks$0 + $9.30$65.57 + $17.73$30.48 + $12.09$47.93 + $11.29AA time per task (model + search)59.0s32.3s62.0s41.9sFetch coverage (TinyFish internal evaluation, June 2026)93%73%62%58%

**Browser operation and research tasks are different capabilities, so these prices are not directly comparable. Pricing checked Oct 7, 2026: TinyFish, Exa, Firecrawl, Parallel. Benchmark data: Artificial Analysis (Sep 28, 2026) and its methodology. Coverage: TinyFish internal evaluation (June 2026), a single-vendor test separate from the third-party benchmark.

Key Takeaways
  • Agents pay retrieval charges plus model processing on everything retrieved.
  • The same article ranged from ~1,184 to ~42,774 estimated tokens by provider.
  • 3 large unfiltered pages can exceed a 128K-token window.
  • Free Search and Fetch remove TinyFish’s retrieval charge, not model costs.
  • TinyFish had the lowest displayed total cost on Artificial Analysis, but the lowest displayed score.

Thanks to the Tinyfish team for the thought leadership / resources for this article. This article is sponsored by TinyFish.

items.title: Director Blows $1.5 Million Generating Horrendous AI Slop Movie, Says AI Actually Saved Him Tens of Millions
items.summary: Just when you thought the holiday season couldn’t arrive any earlier this year, here comes an AI-generated Christmas movie. Titled “Merry the Christmas Witch,” it’s based on a children’s book and will inspire awe in its young audience about the magic of the holidays — through ghoulish and uncanny AI imagery (you can see footage here ). The film — which currently has no distributor — cost $1.5 million to make, but its director brags that using AI actually saved him tens of millions of dollars. “We would never have gotten a movie like ‘Merry’ made if we didn’t take that chance,” Tom Walsh, CEO of the indeopendent production company TW3 Entertainment, and who directed and co-wrote the film, told Variety . According to Walsh, when he was inspired to make a movie out of author Bobbi Hess’s original book, he realized that it would cost $80 million to make. An “unknown property” like this one would be a hard sell to studios, he explained. “We were kind of stuck,” Walsh told Varietey . “The doors are not very open to new kind[s] of ideas and new kind[s] of stories and everything, and that makes it a little tough for independent filmmakers, so that’s where AI came in.” You can sympathize with his position. A movie industry obsessed with intellectual property and averse to risk-taking has made it harder than ever for independent creatives to fund their projects and reach an audience. Still, many filmmakers dedicated to the art form figure out a way to do it, and by and large, they’re not relying on AI to generate their movies wholesale . This year’s breakout hit “Obsession,” for example, made half a billion dollars on a budget of less than a million with an original story, becoming even more profitable than the 1999 found-footage sensation “The Blair Witch Project.” I need someone to tell me with a straight face that they'd sit in a theater to watch this pic.twitter.com/BbpJfHXSe6 — Nuñez (@guycen) October 13, 2026 In all, roughly 50 people worked on “Merry the Christmas Witch” for 10 months in what Walsh described as a “hybrid AI production.” But really, it sounds like it was mostly AI. Walsh hired human actors to record the script and help guide how the characters moved and sounded. In the end, though, he decided to replace their performances with AI-generated voices using ElevenLab’s AI voice synthesizer, alongside video generators like Seedance and Nanobanana for the imagery. The human element, he insists, was still important. “The quality of your AI production depends on the quality of your traditional production staff,” he told Variety . “If you have inexperienced people who don’t know production…and timing and how shots should look, it’s going to look like garbage.” Of course, relying on AI probably did save him millions of dollars. But the end result is that the million and a half he did put in was to churn out obvious slop. More on AI: AI Agent Blamed for Deleting Entire Upcoming Season of TV Show

Still, many filmmakers dedicated to the art form figure out a way to do it, and by and large, they’re not relying on AI to generate their movies wholesale. This year’s breakout hit “Obsession,” for example, made half a billion dollars on a budget of less than a million with an original story, becoming even more profitable than the 1999 found-footage sensation “The Blair Witch Project.”

I need someone to tell me with a straight face that they'd sit in a theater to watch this pic.twitter.com/BbpJfHXSe6

— Nuñez (@guycen) October 13, 2026

In all, roughly 50 people worked on “Merry the Christmas Witch” for 10 months in what Walsh described as a “hybrid AI production.” But really, it sounds like it was mostly AI. Walsh hired human actors to record the script and help guide how the characters moved and sounded. In the end, though, he decided to replace their performances with AI-generated voices using ElevenLab’s AI voice synthesizer, alongside video generators like Seedance and Nanobanana for the imagery.

The human element, he insists, was still important.

“The quality of your AI production depends on the quality of your traditional production staff,” he told Variety. “If you have inexperienced people who don’t know production…and timing and how shots should look, it’s going to look like garbage.”

Of course, relying on AI probably did save him millions of dollars. But the end result is that the million and a half he did put in was to churn out obvious slop.

items.title: Anthropic gives outside AI watchdog “employee-like” access
items.summary: Anthropic has granted external evaluators “employee-like access” to assess the risks of its models, following through on a commitment to increase safeguards over concerns the technology could run catastrophically out of control. METR, a nonprofit that has worked with leading labs including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, now has a team embedded in the Claude maker’s office with access to its hardware and internal systems. A greater role for third-party evaluators is among the main concrete steps the labs have proposed in response to rising concern about the dangers more capable AI systems could pose to the economy, cyber security and humanity at large. items.title: Neocloud Shakeout Looms, and Nvidia Has a Lot to Lose
items.summary: How many young AI cloud providers can the market, and Nvidia, support? That’s one of the big questions after a week in which investors worried about the data center buildout and the risks that its unproven participants, known as neoclouds, are taking. Those risks include loading up on debt (CoreWeave) or trying to go public without much of a track record (Firmus and Nscale). Firmus abruptly pulled its public offering last week while shares of CoreWeave and its smaller rivals fell around 20%. The concerns even hit bigger AI cloud providers like Oracle. Data center and neocloud executives told me there’s a limit to the number of AI cloud providers that can exist, even if Nvidia provides many of them with investment or backstops.

items.title: Gemini 4 Argon vs. Claude Opus 5.5: Half the price and about half as accurate
items.summary: When Google announced Gemini 4 Argon to a small group of testers on September 30, it came with a benchmark table that put Argon ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 on 14 of 18 tests. Those include DeepSWE (77.9% vs. 74.2%) and GraphWalks at 256K to 1 million tokens (84.2% vs. 66.8%). Two weeks later, on October 13, Google opened Argon to paid Gemini API developers. To its credit, Google also showed where Opus 5.5 wins. Opus leads on the other four benchmarks, including Terminal-bench 4.0 (66.4% vs. 57.4%), which tests agentic work in a command line. Google is also undercutting Anthropic on price, at least for now. Through November 30, Argon costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, half the price of Opus 5.5. On December 1, it rises to $4 and $20, matching Opus. That gives developers about six weeks to decide whether Argon is better or just cheaper. That gives developers about six weeks to decide whether Argon is better or just cheaper. Benchmarks don’t always match real work, and a half-price window only matters if the model matches the competitor on quality. To see whether Argon is better or just cheaper (for now), I tested both models head-to-head on three hard tasks from categories where Google claims a lead. The tests I ran each test once per model through OpenRouter, on Google’s and Anthropic’s own servers, at default reasoning settings. A script graded every answer against keys I built and verified before testing either model. The answer key adds more scoring areas to help ensure the quality and thoroughness of each test. Bug hunt – A 3,500-line Python library with 14 planted logic bugs and five decoys. Each model reviewed the code, then fixed what it found. Billing spec – A spec for a subscription billing engine, graded by 80 hidden tests on daylight saving, month-end dates, and rounding. A follow-up added two currencies and 20 more tests. Long context – A fake wiki of 400 services with scattered dependencies, at three sizes. Each model answered three graph questions with planted traps. Bug hunt This one was a tie. Both models found all 14 bugs, including four that only show up when you follow a value across three or more files. Neither flagged a decoy. In the follow-up, both fixed all 14 bugs without breaking any of the 93 existing tests. Argon was cheaper. Its review cost averaged 1 cent per bug found, compared to Opus’s 2.4 cents, an average I calculated from the per-call total rather than measured per bug. Argon would still come out cheaper at its full Dec. 1 price, because it used fewer tokens. The numbers: Review Argon 53,031 in, 3,964 out, $0.15, 43.0 s. Opus 64,572 in, 4,053 out, $0.34, 38.9 s. Fix Argon 54,923 in, 24,292 out, $0.35, 186.6 s. Opus 66,465 in, 34,263 out, $0.95, 219.8 s. Billing specs Here’s where accuracy began to differ between the two models. Opus passed all 80 hidden tests, then all 100 after the currency follow-up. Argon passed 11 of 80, then 20 of 100. Argon didn’t fail the majority of the tests because its logic was bad. It failed because it made a small mistake early on. Its code passed an extra argument to Python’s `datetime.combine()`, which raises an error, and most of the module depends on that helper. When I corrected that one line myself, Argon scored 80/80 and 100/100. I kept the official scores as graded but wanted to explain what happened, not just list the scores, on this one. Overall, Argon was cheaper, but the difference between Opus and Argon pricing will disappear once the lower-cost period ends, though Argon’s lower token use would still make it cheaper on this test. The numbers: Build Argon 3,907 in, 3,727 out, $0.05, 54.1 s. Opus 5,236 in, 7,763 out, $0.18, 63.0 s. Follow-up Argon 8,881 in, 4,673 out, $0.06, 41.5 s. Opus 11,807 in, 7,267 out, $0.19, 51.9 s. Long context Each vendor counts tokens differently. My 500K document came to 549,483 tokens on Argon and 784,087 on Opus. My 900K document came to 1.4 million tokens on Claude’s tokenizer, so Anthropic’s API rejected it. I added a third document of about 600K tokens, the largest that both models could fit. Both models answered two of the three questions perfectly at every size they ran. The split came on the blast radius question, which asks for every service that goes down when one fails. The answer is 33 services. Opus got all 33 at 500K and 32 at 600K, with no wrong entries. At 500K, Argon got 20 right and 8 wrong; at 600K, 19 right and 16 wrong; and at 900K, 23 right and 2 wrong. At 600K and 900K, it treated a dependency as removed after the wiki reinstated it. Unlike the billing bug, this wasn’t a small slip. Argon got the reasoning wrong at every size. This is a big red flag. Unlike the billing bug, this wasn’t a small slip. Argon got the reasoning wrong across the entire answer. This is a big red flag. Another thing I noticed is that Argon raced through this long-context test. Argon answered quickly without showing any step-by-step work, and Opus took longer because it reasoned first. This shows up in token usage. Opus used over 5,000 tokens, most for reasoning, vs. Argon’s 243-425. That likely connects to Argon’s wrong answers, though I can’t prove the cause from one run. Argon was cheaper here, but it’s not worth using it on a similar task, as it was largely inaccurate and sloppy. The numbers: 500k Argon 549,483 in, 264 out, $1.10, 24.2 s. Opus 784,087 in, 5,532 out, $3.25, 68.3 s. 600k Argon 652,492 in, 425 out, $1.31, 32.4 s. Opus 935,332 in, 5,158 out, $3.84, 69.1 s. 900K Argon 982,367 in, 243 out, $1.97, 41.5 s. Opus not run. Argon tied Opus on code review and fixing at under half the cost. It lost the spec test over one bad line of code, and it missed or invented services on every long-context blast-radius question. What do I think? Based on these tests, I wouldn’t use Argon. Yes, it was cheaper and as accurate as Opus on the bug hunt, but after working with it on the other tests, I wouldn’t unquestioningly trust Argon on any task. I wouldn’t unquestioningly trust Argon on any task. Opus 5.5 is one of Anthropic’s leading models, and Artificial Analysis’s independent index ranks it at 58, ahead of Argon’s 53. While Google is working hard to catch up, it hasn’t yet.

To its credit, Google also showed where Opus 5.5 wins. Opus leads on the other four benchmarks, including Terminal-bench 4.0 (66.4% vs. 57.4%), which tests agentic work in a command line.

Google is also undercutting Anthropic on price, at least for now. Through November 30, Argon costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, half the price of Opus 5.5. On December 1, it rises to $4 and $20, matching Opus. That gives developers about six weeks to decide whether Argon is better or just cheaper.

That gives developers about six weeks to decide whether Argon is better or just cheaper.

Benchmarks don’t always match real work, and a half-price window only matters if the model matches the competitor on quality. To see whether Argon is better or just cheaper (for now), I tested both models head-to-head on three hard tasks from categories where Google claims a lead.

The tests

A script graded every answer against keys I built and verified before testing either model. The answer key adds more scoring areas to help ensure the quality and thoroughness of each test.

  • Bug hunt – A 3,500-line Python library with 14 planted logic bugs and five decoys. Each model reviewed the code, then fixed what it found.
  • Billing spec – A spec for a subscription billing engine, graded by 80 hidden tests on daylight saving, month-end dates, and rounding. A follow-up added two currencies and 20 more tests.
  • Long context – A fake wiki of 400 services with scattered dependencies, at three sizes. Each model answered three graph questions with planted traps.
Bug hunt

This one was a tie. Both models found all 14 bugs, including four that only show up when you follow a value across three or more files. Neither flagged a decoy. In the follow-up, both fixed all 14 bugs without breaking any of the 93 existing tests.

Argon was cheaper. Its review cost averaged 1 cent per bug found, compared to Opus’s 2.4 cents, an average I calculated from the per-call total rather than measured per bug. Argon would still come out cheaper at its full Dec. 1 price, because it used fewer tokens.

  • The numbers:
    • Review
      • Argon 53,031 in, 3,964 out, $0.15, 43.0 s. 
      • Opus 64,572 in, 4,053 out, $0.34, 38.9 s.
    • Fix
      • Argon 54,923 in, 24,292 out, $0.35, 186.6 s.
      • Opus 66,465 in, 34,263 out, $0.95, 219.8 s.
Billing specs

Here’s where accuracy began to differ between the two models. Opus passed all 80 hidden tests, then all 100 after the currency follow-up. Argon passed 11 of 80, then 20 of 100.

Argon didn’t fail the majority of the tests because its logic was bad. It failed because it made a small mistake early on. Its code passed an extra argument to Python’s `datetime.combine()`, which raises an error, and most of the module depends on that helper. When I corrected that one line myself, Argon scored 80/80 and 100/100. I kept the official scores as graded but wanted to explain what happened, not just list the scores, on this one.

Overall, Argon was cheaper, but the difference between Opus and Argon pricing will disappear once the lower-cost period ends, though Argon’s lower token use would still make it cheaper on this test.

  • The numbers:
    • Build
      • Argon 3,907 in, 3,727 out, $0.05, 54.1 s.
      • Opus 5,236 in, 7,763 out, $0.18, 63.0 s.
    • Follow-up
      • Argon 8,881 in, 4,673 out, $0.06, 41.5 s. 
      • Opus 11,807 in, 7,267 out, $0.19, 51.9 s.

Each vendor counts tokens differently. My 500K document came to 549,483 tokens on Argon and 784,087 on Opus. My 900K document came to 1.4 million tokens on Claude’s tokenizer, so Anthropic’s API rejected it. I added a third document of about 600K tokens, the largest that both models could fit.

Both models answered two of the three questions perfectly at every size they ran. The split came on the blast radius question, which asks for every service that goes down when one fails. The answer is 33 services.

Opus got all 33 at 500K and 32 at 600K, with no wrong entries. At 500K, Argon got 20 right and 8 wrong; at 600K, 19 right and 16 wrong; and at 900K, 23 right and 2 wrong. At 600K and 900K, it treated a dependency as removed after the wiki reinstated it. Unlike the billing bug, this wasn’t a small slip. Argon got the reasoning wrong at every size. This is a big red flag.

Unlike the billing bug, this wasn’t a small slip. Argon got the reasoning wrong across the entire answer. This is a big red flag.

Another thing I noticed is that Argon raced through this long-context test. Argon answered quickly without showing any step-by-step work, and Opus took longer because it reasoned first. This shows up in token usage. Opus used over 5,000 tokens, most for reasoning, vs. Argon’s 243-425. That likely connects to Argon’s wrong answers, though I can’t prove the cause from one run.
