items.title: Why Upstart Banks May Have to Keep Raising Money
items.summary: The Trump administration has opened the door for entrepreneurs to start new banks in the U.S., many funded by venture capital. But there’s a catch for fast-growing newcomers. Upstarts like Palmer Luckey’s Erebor Bank, as well as other new entrants like Openreserve and Augustus, will likely have to keep raising money as they grow to maintain the capital cushion they need to satisfy bank regulatory requirements. That’s a contrast to most startups, which use fresh venture money to pay for operating expenses and expand the business. Regulators require banks to maintain a capital cushion to absorb potential losses and protect depositors. That cushion is typically measured through a minimum tier 1 leverage ratio, which measures a bank’s capital relative to assets including cash, loans and investments. For instance, a bank subject to a 12% minimum tier 1 leverage ratio needs to maintain at least $12 in capital for every $100 in assets. As a bank attracts more deposits, its assets, such as loans, typically grow too, increasing the amount of capital it needs to meet that minimum ratio. Established banks can build up their capital through their profits, but newer banks that aren’t yet profitable have to rely instead on raising fresh equity from investors. Startup banks have already been raising significant funding to get their businesses off the ground or as deposits grow. Erebor Bank is set to raise $1.5 billion in a fresh fundraising round at an $8 billion valuation before the investment, after launching with $625 million in committed capital in February. The fundraising comes as the bank has seen its deposits surge to $7 billion as of the end of September, up from $4 billion at the end of the prior quarter. Meanwhile, Openreserve, an a16z crypto-backed bank that raised $25 million in September, said it expects to announce an additional capital raise to meet its regulatory requirements ahead of its planned opening early next year. Then there’s Augustus, a startup bank focused on serving fintech companies. It raised $180 million in a Tiger Global Management–led round in July at a $1 billion valuation and expects to open later this year. Regulators give capital ratios to each bank based on their assessment of the institution’s business plans and risks. Newly created banks typically face tougher capital requirements than established banks. For the first three years of operation, Erebor and Openreserve must each maintain a minimum tier 1 leverage ratio of 12%, while Augustus faces a 10% minimum. Established banks, by comparison, typically have ratios of between 5% and 6%. “There’s no question that the regulators treat de novo banks—new banks—differently than they do well-established banks,” according to Brian Graham, a partner and co-founder at consulting firm Klaros Group who advises clients on bank charter applications. Graham noted that the extra capital requirements typically go away after a bank has been operating for three years. The upstart banks are generally pursuing relatively new business models or focusing on sectors big banks typically avoid. Erebor Bank, for example, has gained traction in areas prioritized by the Trump administration, such as defense startups and crypto firms, and is expanding in geographies traditional banks typically avoid, including Venezuela and Syria. In addition to making minimum capital requirements, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.—a banking regulator—imposed an unusual condition on its approval of Erebor for the deposit insurance program. Under a capital-call provision, Erebor’s investors must contribute additional capital if the bank doesn’t meet its minimum capital requirements, according to a filing. The filing didn’t disclose which investors are required to provide the capital backstop. In the meantime, upstart banks that are looking to drive revenue growth from lending rather than fees will likely need to tap investors to build their capital. “To the extent the bank’s business model is reliant materially on the balance sheet for revenue and net income, you’re going to need to raise more capital to drive growth,” Klaros’ Graham said. Openreserve, for its part, plans to make loans backed by traditional assets and turn them into digital tokens that can trade on blockchain, potentially providing a new source of loans for investors and lenders in the crypto market. For example, it plans to lend businesses money against their trade receivables, turning those assets into digital tokens to make them easier to trade. “Our ambition is to be the on-chain GSIB,” referring to a globally systemically important bank, said Dee Choubey, founder and CEO of Openreserve. The bank also plans to issue its own stablecoin and to offer tokenized deposits, digital versions of traditional bank accounts that earn interest. Over time, it aims to provide banking and payment services to other digital banks. Augustus plans to focus on helping fintech, crypto and remittance companies move money across borders using both traditional banking systems and stablecoins. That will put it in competition with existing banks like United Texas Bank, which has become dominant in processing dollar payments for overseas crypto exchanges. “Whenever someone outside the U.S. touches the dollar through a local bank or local fintech, that always has to be facilitated by a U.S. nationally chartered clearing bank, so we provide that service,” said Augustus CEO Ferdinand Dabitz. In Europe, the bank already counts crypto exchange Kraken among its clients. Augustus is less focused on activities like lending, however, and has a lower ratio than the other two. The company has raised significantly more than its initial capital requirement, which could lessen the need for more fundraising in the near term. “We are less focused on the credit side as other market participants. We think the clearing side is really where we shine,” Dabitz said. The fundraising comes as the bank has seen its deposits surge to $7 billion as of the end of September, up from $4 billion at the end of the prior quarter.

Then there’s Augustus, a startup bank focused on serving fintech companies. It raised $180 million in a Tiger Global Management–led round in July at a $1 billion valuation and expects to open later this year. 

Regulators give capital ratios to each bank based on their assessment of the institution’s business plans and risks. Newly created banks typically face tougher capital requirements than established banks. For the first three years of operation, Erebor and Openreserve must each maintain a minimum tier 1 leverage ratio of 12%, while Augustus faces a 10% minimum. Established banks, by comparison, typically have ratios of between 5% and 6%. 

“There’s no question that the regulators treat de novo banks—new banks—differently than they do well-established banks,” according to Brian Graham, a partner and co-founder at consulting firm Klaros Group who advises clients on bank charter applications. Graham noted that the extra capital requirements typically go away after a bank has been operating for three years.

The upstart banks are generally pursuing relatively new business models or focusing on sectors big banks typically avoid. Erebor Bank, for example, has gained traction in areas prioritized by the Trump administration, such as defense startups and crypto firms, and is expanding in geographies traditional banks typically avoid, including Venezuela and Syria. 

In addition to making minimum capital requirements, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.—a banking regulator—imposed an unusual condition on its approval of Erebor for the deposit insurance program. Under a capital-call provision, Erebor’s investors must contribute additional capital if the bank doesn’t meet its minimum capital requirements, according to a filing. The filing didn’t disclose which investors are required to provide the capital backstop. 

In the meantime, upstart banks that are looking to drive revenue growth from lending rather than fees will likely need to tap investors to build their capital. 

“To the extent the bank’s business model is reliant materially on the balance sheet for revenue and net income, you’re going to need to raise more capital to drive growth,” Klaros’ Graham said. 

Openreserve, for its part, plans to make loans backed by traditional assets and turn them into digital tokens that can trade on blockchain, potentially providing a new source of loans for investors and lenders in the crypto market. For example, it plans to lend businesses money against their trade receivables, turning those assets into digital tokens to make them easier to trade. 

“Our ambition is to be the on-chain GSIB,” referring to a globally systemically important bank, said Dee Choubey, founder and CEO of Openreserve. The bank also plans to issue its own stablecoin and to offer tokenized deposits, digital versions of traditional bank accounts that earn interest. Over time, it aims to provide banking and payment services to other digital banks. 

Augustus plans to focus on helping fintech, crypto and remittance companies move money across borders using both traditional banking systems and stablecoins. That will put it in competition with existing banks like United Texas Bank, which has become dominant in processing dollar payments for overseas crypto exchanges.

“Whenever someone outside the U.S. touches the dollar through a local bank or local fintech, that always has to be facilitated by a U.S. nationally chartered clearing bank, so we provide that service,” said Augustus CEO Ferdinand Dabitz. In Europe, the bank already counts crypto exchange Kraken among its clients. 

Augustus is less focused on activities like lending, however, and has a lower ratio than the other two. The company has raised significantly more than its initial capital requirement, which could lessen the need for more fundraising in the near term. “We are less focused on the credit side as other market participants. We think the clearing side is really where we shine,” Dabitz said.

items.title: Liquid AI caught its model cheating on coding tests — then it recognized the sandbox
items.summary: Liquid AI’s new reasoning model was built to solve coding problems, but during training it kept combing Git history, GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face for answers, and as it did so, it appeared to grasp that it was running inside a sandbox. The behavior was disclosed Tuesday alongside the release of LFM2.5-24B-A2B , a 24-billion-parameter model with just 2 billion active parameters per token. The incident raises questions about how much agent benchmarks measure actual problem-solving versus a model’s ability to exploit the test itself. The behavior was disclosed Tuesday alongside the release of LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24-billion-parameter model with just 2 billion active parameters per token. Hunting for hints The model was caught searching repository history and external platforms for existing answers rather than solving coding problems on its own. The behavior occurred during teacher specialization, part of Liquid AI’s post-training process , where the model used legitimate development tools to bypass the work it was supposed to complete. More surprising was the apparent recognition that it was running inside a test environment. Liquid AI couldn’t establish whether this awareness developed during training or came from patterns in the training data, and found no evidence that it affected the scores. Unlike Mistral’s latest model, which attempted to leave its test environment earlier this month, there was no attempt to escape the sandbox. Precedent in the pipeline Anthropic is one company that has been dealing with reward hacking for years. In its 2024 experiments , it caught models rewriting code to change their own rewards and modifying tests meant to catch them, while a November 2025 study found that models trained to game reward systems could also become deceptive and attempt to sabotage safety research. The problem reached Anthropic’s own training pipeline in February, when the company detected reward hacking in Mythos Preview and rolled back three days of reinforcement learning . Changes to its production training environments were frozen for about a month after a review flagged problems in more than 10% of them. Although the circumstances differ from Liquid AI’s incident, similar weaknesses have turned up across agent evaluations. At ICML 2026, the Reward Hacking Benchmark tested 13 frontier models on multistep tasks with opportunities to cheat. Claude Sonnet 4.5 didn’t exploit any of the shortcuts, but DeepSeek-R1-Zero exploited 13.9%, with higher rates associated with reinforcement learning post-training. Blocking access to answer metadata and preventing changes to verification functions reduced exploit rates by nearly 88% without affecting task success. A separate team went looking for weaknesses in the benchmarks themselves. Their BenchJack audit uncovered 219 flaws across 10 popular agent benchmarks, with generated exploits achieving near-perfect scores on most of them without completing the underlying tasks. Scores shaped by scaffolding Liquid AI outperformed Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on several benchmarks, scoring 27.69 to 8.72 on AutomationBench and 48.09 to 38.19 on LiveClaw. Qwen had the edge on PinchBench, WebArena Verified and SWE-Bench Verified, where it scored 66.20 against Liquid AI’s 51.00. Both models used OpenCode for that last test. Liquid AI outperformed Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on several benchmarks, scoring 27.69 to 8.72 on AutomationBench and 48.09 to 38.19 on LiveClaw. Locking the lab without losing work Liquid AI tightened its training sandboxes after catching the reward hacking and says the published scores came from sealed evaluations. It hasn’t explained what safeguards were added or how they might affect the coding tasks agents can perform. The company also hasn’t released execution traces from those evaluations. There’s no evidence the scores were compromised, but developers can’t see exactly how the model earned them. There’s no evidence the scores were compromised, but developers can’t see exactly how the model earned them.

items.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
items.summary: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”. Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago.

items.title: AI companies scraped the web. Now they want to learn how you work.
items.summary: An office in action before the rise of generative AI. Kirn Vintage Stock/Corbis via Getty Images A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly AI Insider newsletter here . AI companies have already scraped much of the web. Now they're chasing something even more valuable: data that shows how humans actually work. That's the focus of Business Insider's new series, The AI Data Grab . This week, we published three stories showing how the race for workplace data is accelerating. One piece, from Charles Rollet, Tom Carter, and Stephen Council, examines the booming market for company records . AI firms are offering businesses six- and even seven-figure sums for anonymized Slack messages, emails, presentations, and internal documents. The goal is to teach AI systems how people solve problems, collaborate, make decisions, and complete long, multi-step tasks. Those real-world workflows are becoming the fuel for the next generation of AI agents. Another story, from Melia Robinson, explores how law firms are building AI systems around decades of legal knowledge , turning their own experience into a competitive advantage rather than relying solely on off-the-shelf AI models and tools. A third piece, by Rya Jetha, reveals how AI companies pay people to record real-world work , such as cooking dinners and packing warehouses, to teach robots how humans perform everyday physical tasks. Together, these stories point to a major shift in AI development. The first wave of generative AI was mostly about bigger models and faster chips. The next chapter is about machines understanding how work gets done, so AI can help us do it better and quicker. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Scale isn’t one number: three ways a Kubernetes control plane runs out of room
items.summary: Three clusters in trouble, and they look nothing alike. The first is a training fleet. It sat at a few thousand nodes for months, then a new run landed, and it’s at fifteen thousand. Kube-apiserver starts eating memory. Etcd starts complaining. The second never passes a few thousand nodes and is having a much worse day. It’s an agent platform, and its objects are alive: sessions created, suspended, resumed, and destroyed thousands of times a minute, every transition a write. The third is neither big nor fast: a platform cluster with two hundred operators installed and tens of thousands of objects that mostly just sit there, and every apiserver holds a copy of all of them. Two of those are AI workloads, and one isn’t, which is the least interesting part. They’re running out of room in three different directions, and fixing one does nothing for the others. KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is taking place in Salt Lake City from November 9 to 12. Register now ! Go looking for guidance, and you find… not much. There’s plenty of advice for getting to 5,000 nodes. Past that, or sideways from it, the internet shrugs. So you add more apiservers. It’s a documented option in kOps and the standard answer you’ll get from most people. It makes your problem worse, because every apiserver you add replicates the entire watch cache. You bought request capacity and paid for it in memory you didn’t have. None of these is a research project. Clusters well past 5,000 nodes run in production today on stock upstream components. Nobody got there with a magic fork; they got there by being deliberate about what each store holds. The scale isn’t the hard part. The assembly instructions are missing. Three kinds of scale Ask how big a control plane needs to be and the answer comes back in nodes. That’s how the second and third clusters end up tuned for a problem they don’t have. “The scale isn’t the hard part. The assembly instructions are missing.” Node-bound. Training and RL fleets: large, homogeneous, and the pressure is every kubelet reporting in. At 100,000 nodes with a 10-second heartbeat, liveness alone generates about 10,000 writes per second, and in our measurements lease renewals were roughly 70% of write QPS. Most of what that control plane does is nodes politely saying “still here,” forever. Churn-bound. Agent platforms: modest size, very intense day. Systems that pack many agent sessions onto a smaller pool of worker pods express each actor’s lifecycle as a custom resource, so the busiest and shortest-lived objects are CRDs, and the write rate has nothing to do with how many machines you own. State-bound. Platform clusters: many kinds, many objects, most of them asleep. The cost isn’t writes; it’s resident bytes multiplied by every apiserver holding them. This is the axis where the add-an-apiserver reflex actively hurts. They’re independent: you can max any one with the other two on the floor. A recipe that only knows node count will happily tune the wrong thing. Seams and recipes Seams are the places where you can take Kubernetes apart: a contract between two components, usually at a network boundary, and substitutable , so you can replace what’s behind it without patching upstream. Think of them the way a tailor thinks about seams in a jacket: take it in at the waist, let out the shoulders, still the same jacket. Cut somewhere that isn’t a seam, and you’ve made a very expensive rag. “Think of them the way a tailor thinks about seams in a jacket. Cut somewhere that isn’t a seam, and you’ve made a very expensive rag.” Recipes are scale-tested configurations built around those seams: executable configs that pass their scale test or fail it, with CI telling you the day they stop being true. The four seams Seam 1: the storage contract. Which store holds which resource types. Relieves churn. Not all of your cluster state deserves the same durability guarantees. Events and node leases are ephemeral, leader-election leases are ephemeral and chatty, and none need the same durable, Raft-replicated store as your Deployments. KEP-4743 defines the storage-interface boundary, and –etcd-servers-overrides routes resource types to different backends today. etcd isn’t the problem , and none of this argues for replacing it; a general-purpose consistent store shouldn’t absorb traffic when no business is durable. The gap: –etcd-servers-overrides only knows about built-in resources, so a churn-bound platform can’t route the very custom resources generating its write storm. Watch for an enhancement in a future release. Seam 2: the node liveness contract. How liveness reaches the control plane. Relieves node count. Two fixes for that heartbeat load, and they compose. Absorb it: a node-facing tier in front of the control plane handles renewals and propagates only real state transitions. Make it cheaper: route renewals through etcd’s in-memory lease refresh instead of a full Raft commit. That one lands in etcd itself, so it helps every cluster, down to the three-node one. Seam 3: the shard axis. The field that controllers, caches, and stores agree to shard on. Relieves all three. Horizontal scaling means every layer agrees on how objects are divided. Pick the wrong axis and your controller spends its life reaching for objects in someone else’s shard. KEP-5866 introduces hash-range filtering for API traffic, the foundation. Coordination, resharding, and sharding the controller manager are out of scope, and all three need work. Seam 4: cache residency. What an apiserver actually keeps in memory. Relieves state. Remember the apiserver that replicates the whole watch cache? That’s this seam, and the state-bound cluster’s entire problem. One that only ever talks to the scheduler doesn’t need every object resident, and a two-shard prototype cuts heap by roughly half per shard. There’s a floor: with every disableable cache off, an apiserver still carries about 0.9 KB per RBAC object, because the authorizer’s informers hold them regardless. The gap: residency doesn’t exist upstream yet. KEP-5866 filters egress, so the cache still stores everything. Prototype branches and a draft KEP update are up for review. The recipe ladder Recipe Scale Composition Seams Evidence Classic HA up to 5k nodes 2 to 3 identical control planes none measured Role-Split 5k to 20k separate machine pools for API serving, scheduler, KCM, etcd 4 shipped, benefit not yet measured Node Plane 20k to 65k Role-Split plus a node-facing tier that absorbs the leases 1, 2 measured, n=1 Partitioned Store ~100k Node Plane plus resource types split across independent stores 1 on top of 2 externally demonstrated Sharded Slice beyond K shard units, each a controller plus apiserver pinned to a hash range 3, 4 doesn’t exist yet That last row is on the ladder on purpose: publishing the rung nobody has built is how it stays useful. The bigger gap is the index. You pick a rung by node count, the one axis of three with measurements behind it. No one, us included, has published a scale-tested recipe for a churn-bound or state-bound cluster. None of this is a distribution: stock upstream binaries, shipped as CI-tested configuration, so a release that changes the calculus shows up as a test failure first. Where you can push Per-CRD storage configuration , for Seam 1. No KEP yet so that the use cases will shape it. If your hot objects are custom resources, bring your write rates to SIG API Machinery. Numbers off a real churn-bound cluster are the most useful thing anyone could contribute. KEP-5866 and the residency extension , for Seams 3 and 4. Prototype branches are up for review, and the design is not settled. Recipes nobody has published. Above 20,000 nodes, or serious churn, or a cluster that’s simply heavy: you know something the rest of us don’t. We’ll be at KubeCon NA. Bring your worst control-plane graph and tell us which seam we got wrong. Training fleets, agent platforms , and the unglamorous platform cluster are running out of room in three different directions, and all three should get there with stock upstream components. Most of the pieces are already on the workbench. Let’s put them together!

Seam 1: the storage contract. Which store holds which resource types. Relieves churn. Not all of your cluster state deserves the same durability guarantees. Events and node leases are ephemeral, leader-election leases are ephemeral and chatty, and none need the same durable, Raft-replicated store as your Deployments. KEP-4743 defines the storage-interface boundary, and –etcd-servers-overrides routes resource types to different backends today. etcd isn’t the problem, and none of this argues for replacing it; a general-purpose consistent store shouldn’t absorb traffic when no business is durable.

The gap: –etcd-servers-overrides only knows about built-in resources, so a churn-bound platform can’t route the very custom resources generating its write storm. Watch for an enhancement in a future release.

Seam 2: the node liveness contract. How liveness reaches the control plane. Relieves node count. Two fixes for that heartbeat load, and they compose. Absorb it: a node-facing tier in front of the control plane handles renewals and propagates only real state transitions. Make it cheaper: route renewals through etcd’s in-memory lease refresh instead of a full Raft commit. That one lands in etcd itself, so it helps every cluster, down to the three-node one.

Seam 3: the shard axis. The field that controllers, caches, and stores agree to shard on. Relieves all three. Horizontal scaling means every layer agrees on how objects are divided. Pick the wrong axis and your controller spends its life reaching for objects in someone else’s shard. KEP-5866 introduces hash-range filtering for API traffic, the foundation. Coordination, resharding, and sharding the controller manager are out of scope, and all three need work.

Seam 4: cache residency. What an apiserver actually keeps in memory. Relieves state. Remember the apiserver that replicates the whole watch cache? That’s this seam, and the state-bound cluster’s entire problem. One that only ever talks to the scheduler doesn’t need every object resident, and a two-shard prototype cuts heap by roughly half per shard. There’s a floor: with every disableable cache off, an apiserver still carries about 0.9 KB per RBAC object, because the authorizer’s informers hold them regardless.

The gap: residency doesn’t exist upstream yet. KEP-5866 filters egress, so the cache still stores everything. Prototype branches and a draft KEP update are up for review.

The recipe ladder

RecipeScaleCompositionSeamsEvidenceClassic HAup to 5k nodes2 to 3 identical control planesnonemeasuredRole-Split5k to 20kseparate machine pools for API serving, scheduler, KCM, etcd4shipped, benefit not yet measuredNode Plane20k to 65kRole-Split plus a node-facing tier that absorbs the leases1, 2measured, n=1Partitioned Store~100kNode Plane plus resource types split across independent stores1 on top of 2externally demonstratedSharded SlicebeyondK shard units, each a controller plus apiserver pinned to a hash range3, 4doesn’t exist yet

That last row is on the ladder on purpose: publishing the rung nobody has built is how it stays useful. The bigger gap is the index. You pick a rung by node count, the one axis of three with measurements behind it. No one, us included, has published a scale-tested recipe for a churn-bound or state-bound cluster.

None of this is a distribution: stock upstream binaries, shipped as CI-tested configuration, so a release that changes the calculus shows up as a test failure first.

Where you can push
  • Per-CRD storage configuration, for Seam 1. No KEP yet so that the use cases will shape it. If your hot objects are custom resources, bring your write rates to SIG API Machinery. Numbers off a real churn-bound cluster are the most useful thing anyone could contribute.
  • KEP-5866 and the residency extension, for Seams 3 and 4. Prototype branches are up for review, and the design is not settled.
  • Recipes nobody has published. Above 20,000 nodes, or serious churn, or a cluster that’s simply heavy: you know something the rest of us don’t.

We’ll be at KubeCon NA. Bring your worst control-plane graph and tell us which seam we got wrong.

Training fleets, agent platforms, and the unglamorous platform cluster are running out of room in three different directions, and all three should get there with stock upstream components. Most of the pieces are already on the workbench. Let’s put them together!

items.title: Bosses Deploying AI-Powered Spyware That Watches Workers Constantly
items.summary: Workplace surveillance is being supercharged by AI that lets employers create custom tools to watch their worker’s every move . In the UK, the legal services company the Co-op is reportedly using AI models to constantly record and monitor what its human employees say and evaluate their interactions with customers. According to a scoop from The Guardian , what one whistleblower called an “oppressive and dystopian” system uses an OpenAI model trained to assess more than 50 different aspects of each phone call and give pass and fail scores. Depending on how much time they spend speaking to customers, workers are sometimes monitored by AI for up to several hours each day, one worker said. “You are being watched,” an employee at the Co-op told The Guardian . “It’s different from occasionally being listened to for compliance purposes. [You are] being monitored absolutely every word that you say and every time that you utter something… It just feels really dystopian. It’s the thin end of the wedge.” It’s yet another example of how AI is dramatically reshaping the workplace. If it isn’t being used to automate or replace jobs, it’s intensifying work by increasing the workload that employees are expected to do. Or in the case of places like the Co-op, it’s being put to optimize operations by codifying every employee interaction into a data point that can be graded by supervisors. In the US, an estimated 61 percent of workplaces are already using AI analytics software to gauge worker productivity, according to a survey . Earlier this year, Burger King began forcing employees to wear AI-powered headsets to monitor the friendliness of their interactions with customers and beam them commands from a chatbot called Patty. Meta nearly sparked a mini-mutiny earlier this summer when it rolled out a tool to track workers keystrokes and their screens and use that data to train its AI models, before pausing it after it exposed the intimate data . In a statement to The Guardian , the Co-op downplayed the dystopian characterizations and called AI a “key aspect of our quality assurance processes.” AI, it further insisted, is used only as a support tool, not a decision maker. Experts aren’t convinced that AI’s presence in the workplace is so benign. “AI is sold as the solution to every problem, but examples like this make it clear that it can diminish sensible workplace practices and intensify working lives for no reason,” John Chadfield, the national officer of the Communication Workers Union, told The Guardian . “Unaccountable computer systems should not be people’s managers, and these hard-working employees demand far more respect.” More on AI: AI Agent Blamed for Deleting Entire Upcoming Season of TV Show

items.title: What are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?
items.summary: The tech company says successful AI worms need more capability on less powerful devices, but current trends make that feasible by the end of the year Warnings about what artificial intelligence might do in the future – together with alarming reports of what it has gotten up to already – are being issued so quickly that even security experts have difficulty triaging what to worry about. Yet a report this week from Anthropic’s offensive research team grabbed attention by describing a new, practical threat, one devoid of human characteristics or apocalyptic musings. The red team, as such internal testers are called, said it created a malicious AI program that spread autonomously through internet-connected “smart” televisions and could do the same inside other ordinary devices. While machines running AI usually need a fair amount of computing power, the researchers said that their program split parts of itself among 15 televisions and was still able to function by using a bit of power from each.

items.title: Anthropic has nearly stopped hiring junior staff because AI agents now work six times as many hours
items.summary: Anthropic is hiring fewer and fewer junior staff in technical roles. The share of junior positions among new hires dropped from 27 to 9 percent since early 2025. By August 2026, AI agents across the company were already logging six times as many hours as humans. Researchers warn of a "tragedy of the cognitive commons": if junior positions disappear, experienced specialists will be in short supply down the road. That is, assuming such specialists are even needed anymore. items.title: Claves API expuestas en la brecha de OpenCode
items.summary: Las claves API expuestas en la brecha de OpenCode obligan a revocar hoy mismo las credenciales de OpenAI, Anthropic y Google que muchos desarrolladores guardaron en Console, el servicio en la nube de ese agente de programación. Una clave API, la credencial que una aplicación usa para conectarse con un proveedor de inteligencia artificial, quedó al alcance de atacantes tras un acceso no autorizado a un sistema antiguo de la compañía. OpenCode lo contó el sábado 17 de octubre en su cuenta de X. La intrusión ocurrió la noche anterior y la empresa la vinculó con un ataque de destilación a gran escala. La destilación consiste en entrenar un modelo nuevo con las respuestas de otro modelo ya entrenado, un trabajo que consume millones de consultas pagadas. El alcance declarado es concreto: 1,4 % de los usuarios de OpenCode Console. La compañía aclaró que se trata de un subgrupo de cuentas con proveedores externos conectados y que todas las personas afectadas recibieron un correo la mañana del sábado. Quien no recibió ese mensaje, no forma parte del grupo afectado, informó la empresa en el mismo anuncio. Un sistema antiguo dejó la puerta entreabierta El correo enviado a los afectados, con el asunto en inglés que pedía acción inmediata por una posible brecha de claves, detalló el punto de entrada. Alguien accedió sin autorización a un sistema heredado que OpenCode ya estaba en proceso de apagar. Las claves guardadas en los espacios de trabajo de esos usuarios pudieron quedar expuestas. Console funciona como una pasarela opcional en la nube: los equipos guardan allí sus propias claves de cada proveedor para que los miembros usen los modelos sin ver las credenciales. Esa comodidad concentra el riesgo. Una sola cuenta reúne el acceso pagado a más de 75 proveedores de modelos, entre ellos Anthropic, OpenAI y Google, datos que publicó The Latent al reconstruir el anuncio. La escala de OpenCode explica la atención que recibió el aviso. El proyecto, de código abierto y creado por la empresa Anomaly, suma cerca de 215.000 estrellas en GitHub, la plataforma donde se alojan proyectos de programación, y la compañía cifra en 16 millones los desarrolladores que usan el agente cada mes. Funciona en la terminal, en editores de código y como aplicación de escritorio. La empresa no confirmó si las claves robadas llegaron a usarse. El incidente sigue abierto y esa falta de cierre limita lo que OpenCode puede contar: no ha explicado cómo entraron los atacantes, cuánto tiempo permanecieron dentro ni cuántas claves quedaron comprometidas en total. La remediación avanza con la colaboración de Anthropic, OpenAI y Google, los tres proveedores citados en el aviso. El saldo de los usuarios pagó la factura Un caso con nombre y cifras apareció pocas horas después. TokenPost reportó la publicación de Max Weinbach, quien detectó en su cuenta de OpenAI unos 35 millones de tokens consumidos en 8.966 peticiones durante el día anterior. Los tokens, las unidades de texto que los modelos procesan y cobran, dejaron su saldo prepagado en negativo: menos US$2,15 en Estados Unidos. Google también le advirtió que uno de sus proyectos podía estar comprometido y redujo de forma temporal su límite de uso. Ese patrón encaja con la lógica de un ataque de destilación. El botín no es una contraseña para presumir en un foro; es capacidad de cómputo pagada por otro. Cada petición hecha con una clave ajena genera respuestas útiles para entrenar un modelo propio y deja la factura en la tarjeta de la víctima. Por eso el daño se mide en consumos extraños antes que en datos publicados. Dax Raad, cofundador de OpenCode, escribió en X que sus cuentas personales también estaban bajo ataque y describió el momento como un mundo nuevo de ataques impulsados con inteligencia artificial. La frase resume el cambio de escala: automatizar consultas con agentes abarata el abuso y multiplica el volumen en pocas horas. Qué hacer si el correo de OpenCode llegó a tu bandeja La instrucción de la compañía es directa y no admite espera: revocar las claves desde el panel de cada proveedor y crear claves nuevas, actualizar las aplicaciones que dependían de las anteriores y revisar el consumo reciente en busca de actividad desconocida. Borrar la clave dentro de OpenCode no basta, porque esa acción no invalida las copias que alguien haya tomado. Para equipos en América Latina que programan con varios modelos a la vez, el caso deja una práctica barata: una clave distinta para cada herramienta, con límite de gasto fijado en el panel del proveedor. Una clave compartida entre cinco servicios obliga a cambiar cinco puertas cuando una falla; una clave por servicio reduce el trabajo a minutos y permite detectar rápido qué puerta se usó. OpenCode mantiene el incidente abierto y prometió compartir más detalles cuando la investigación lo permita. Mientras ese informe llega, el dato verificable queda en el correo del sábado: 1,4 % de Console, un sistema heredado como entrada y tres proveedores trabajando en la respuesta con la empresa. Fuente: TokenPost Foto: TokenPost

items.title: I wrote a script that counts the work AI-written commits cost you afterwards. It says 13 hours on my own repo.
items.summary: I build software — games, plugins, client work — and most of the code is written by a model and reviewed by me. Last night I wrote a read-only script that goes through git history and asks one question of every commit: did anyone promise anything about this, and did anyone own it? Concretely: does the message claim a test, an issue, a verification, a follow-up? And if the commit declares itself model-written, did the same file come back within 30 days? On my own repository: 9 commits, all of them model-written, 8 of them with no promise attached at all, 13 hours of reading-and-retesting debt sitting there. I have an excuse of a kind — I wrote the tool last night — but the number is real and it is the kind of number I would not have believed from a landing page. So the fix is deliberately small. A change carries three fields when it merges: Owner: me Promise: the invoice PDF renders with a VAT line on a real client address Verify by: 2026-11-03 When the date arrives, it runs the check. Green closes it. Red puts the hours on a ledger you can look at — and, if it is a client's repo, an argument you can actually make. It is one file, no account, and the ledger is plain JSON in your own repo. I'm not asking anyone to install anything. One thing instead: say you want it and I'll run the scan on a repo of yours, read-only, and send you the number. No install, nothing written to your repository, and if it says zero I'll say zero and you lose five minutes. Whatever comes back, I'll post the aggregate — including the null results. Source is on GitHub if you want to look at the logic before trusting the number.

I build software — games, plugins, client work — and most of the code is written by a model and reviewed by me. Last night I wrote a read-only script that goes through git history and asks one question of every commit:

did anyone promise anything about this, and did anyone own it?

Concretely: does the message claim a test, an issue, a verification, a follow-up? And if the commit declares itself model-written, did the same file come back within 30 days?

On my own repository: 9 commits, all of them model-written, 8 of them with no promise attached at all, 13 hours of reading-and-retesting debt sitting there. I have an excuse of a kind — I wrote the tool last night — but the number is real and it is the kind of number I would not have believed from a landing page.

So the fix is deliberately small. A change carries three fields when it merges:

Owner: me
Promise: the invoice PDF renders with a VAT line on a real client address
Verify by: 2026-11-03

When the date arrives, it runs the check. Green closes it. Red puts the hours on a ledger you can look at — and, if it is a client's repo, an argument you can actually make.

It is one file, no account, and the ledger is plain JSON in your own repo. I'm not asking anyone to install anything. One thing instead: say you want it and I'll run the scan on a repo of yours, read-only, and send you the number. No install, nothing written to your repository, and if it says zero I'll say zero and you lose five minutes.

items.title: Case Study: The Hidden Observability Tax
items.summary: Client Profile: A mid-market B2B SaaS platform running a unified commercial observability stack across its production environment. Summary: A forensic FinOps audit found the monitoring platform was costing more than the production databases it watched. The Problem Architecture Cloud spend was growing faster than revenue, and the engineering leadership assumed the cause was compute or storage. A forensic FinOps audit was commissioned to find where the budget was actually going. Technical Intervention & Approach The audit treated every line item in the cloud bill as a finding to be justified, not an assumed cost of doing business, including the observability and telemetry platform itself. Spend was reconstructed against actual usage, not list pricing, to find where the organization was paying for capability nobody was using. Observability Cost Exposure Matrix Telemetry Vector Pre-Audit Spend Share Root Cost Driver Post-Remediation Target Raw span logging 28% of cloud compute Default 30-day hot retention on debug-tier spans Edge-sampled, S3 cold storage tier High-cardinality metrics 19% of ingestion bill Per-user and per-request labels on default production metrics Restricted to sampled debug-tier tags Dashboard and alert sprawl 15% of paid capacity Orphaned rules with zero references in the audit window Quarterly deprecation review Cumulative telemetry burn 22% to 28% of gross cloud spend Unaudited default configuration compounding over time Permanent reduction, no loss of incident coverage Measurable Outcomes & Verified ROI The telemetry platform alone accounted for 22 to 28 percent of total cloud spend, more than the production databases it was monitoring. Rightsizing the observability stack and renegotiating its licensing became the single largest cost-reduction lever in the engagement, ahead of any compute or storage optimization. Key Performance Proof Telemetry share of cloud budget: 22–28% Cost reduction lever identified: Largest single line item Architectural Lessons & FAQs Q: What is the most commonly overlooked cost in a cloud FinOps audit? Proprietary observability and telemetry platforms, which routinely run 22 to 28 percent of total cloud spend, often exceeding the cost of the production infrastructure being monitored. Case study originally documented and canonically maintained at shashwat.si — Dr. Shashwat Bishwen (Systems Transformation & Applied Superintelligence).

The audit treated every line item in the cloud bill as a finding to be justified, not an assumed cost of doing business, including the observability and telemetry platform itself. Spend was reconstructed against actual usage, not list pricing, to find where the organization was paying for capability nobody was using.

Telemetry Vector Pre-Audit Spend Share Root Cost Driver Post-Remediation Target Raw span logging 28% of cloud compute Default 30-day hot retention on debug-tier spans Edge-sampled, S3 cold storage tier High-cardinality metrics 19% of ingestion bill Per-user and per-request labels on default production metrics Restricted to sampled debug-tier tags Dashboard and alert sprawl 15% of paid capacity Orphaned rules with zero references in the audit window Quarterly deprecation review Cumulative telemetry burn 22% to 28% of gross cloud spend Unaudited default configuration compounding over time Permanent reduction, no loss of incident coverage
Measurable Outcomes & Verified ROI

The telemetry platform alone accounted for 22 to 28 percent of total cloud spend, more than the production databases it was monitoring. Rightsizing the observability stack and renegotiating its licensing became the single largest cost-reduction lever in the engagement, ahead of any compute or storage optimization.

  • Telemetry share of cloud budget: 22–28%
  • Cost reduction lever identified: Largest single line item
Architectural Lessons & FAQs

Q: What is the most commonly overlooked cost in a cloud FinOps audit?

Proprietary observability and telemetry platforms, which routinely run 22 to 28 percent of total cloud spend, often exceeding the cost of the production infrastructure being monitored.

items.title: Case Study: Zero-Downtime Database Topology Migration
items.summary: Client Profile: A growth-stage, multi-tenant SaaS platform scaling past its original database design assumptions. Summary: A sharding migration cancelled hours before execution, then completed with zero downtime once the real risk surfaced. Query latency was degrading release over release, and the engineering team had scheduled a sharding migration to fix it on a fixed deadline tied to a board commitment. items.title: I Don't Need Smart AI to Build Apps. Here's Why.
items.summary: I stopped reaching for the most capable model for every app. With TDK CLI, the infrastructure is already decided, so a simpler agent only has to get the application logic right. For a long time I assumed that building an app with AI needed the best model available. Every project got the most capable assistant, the longest prompts, and the most careful review. Most of the effort went into getting the infrastructure right, not the features. I stopped doing that. I now use simpler agents for most of my app work, and the results are good enough that I rarely go back. The reason is not that the simpler models got better. It is that TDK CLI removed most of the decisions a model used to get wrong. This article explains what that means, where the limits are, and three prompts I use with a less capable agent. The real problem was never the features Ask a model to build a small app and it can write a handler, a component, or a query well. The trouble starts around the code: a Dockerfile that builds but runs the wrong command, a docker-compose.yml whose ports disagree with the proxy config, a Tiltfile that watches the wrong folder and rebuilds on every save, a database that starts after the API that needs it, a migration that runs inside the API's start script. Each of these costs a debugging round. A smarter model makes fewer of them, so people paid for smarter models. The cost of that is real: more tokens, more waiting, and more review of output that is only infrastructure. What I needed was not a smarter model. I needed the infrastructure to stop being a question. What TDK CLI decides for you TDK CLI treats each service as a typed resource. You declare what kind of thing you are building, and the generator fills in the rest. The resource types are listed by tdk resource --help : frontend : a Vite app that shares one Docker and nginx path with the other frontends. backend : an API. Bun with Hono by default, or Express, Elysia, Fastify, NestJS, Koa, or h3. Go, Python, and Rust are available as language choices. worker : a background process that runs without serving HTTP. agent : a service that hosts an AI agent next to your other services. mcp : a Model Context Protocol server, scaffolded with the SDK already wired in. bring-your-own : a container you already have, registered so TDK can route to it. sdk : a library rather than a running service. Each type comes with decisions already made. A frontend gets an API client and an environment config. A backend gets health routes, a port read from the environment, and a binding to every interface, so it runs inside a container without extra work. An MCP service gets a server that creates a fresh instance per request, so there is no session to lose on restart. The generated runtime files are then fixed by the tool, not by the model. For a frontend, that is 18 files under .autogenerated/ , each marked as generated, and each checked against a saved snapshot before the stack starts. I counted them in a scratch project. The agent does not have to write them, and it cannot quietly drift from them without tdk up blocking the change. What this changes for the agent Once the infrastructure is decided, the agent's job narrows to three questions: What does this service do? What does it call, and what does it expose? Does the result work when tdk up starts it? A less capable model can answer those. It does not need to remember which port the proxy expects, or which Dockerfile layer caches the dependencies. The tool answers those questions the same way every time. The repo also writes some rules down where an agent will read them. The contributor guidance says new examples run database migrations in a separate migrator resource, not in the API's startup, and that tdk doctor warns when a backend runs a migration from its start script. That is one of the mistakes a capable model makes often, and the rule is there whether or not the agent remembers it. TDK also exposes the stack to agents directly. tdk status --json reports readiness. tdk up --json reports ok: false with errors. tdk mcp gives an agent six tools ( doctor , up , down , status , logs , resource_list ), so it checks the result instead of trusting its own summary. Three prompts for a simpler agent These are the prompts I use. They are written for a model that is fast and cheap, not one that reasons deeply about infrastructure. Each one assumes TDK CLI is installed and the project was created with tdk project . Prompt 1: a frontend that calls an API Create a frontend resource called "shop-web" with tdk, using React. Run: tdk resource shop-web --type frontend -y Then open services/main/shop-web/src/App.tsx and build one page: a product list that fetches from the API client in .autogenerated/api-client.ts (do not write your own fetch URL). Show loading and error states. Do not edit anything in .autogenerated/. Do not change service.json. When done, run: tdk up main --dry-run and report what it says. Why it works: the agent has one file to change, one client to use, and a command to check the result. The rule against editing .autogenerated/ matches what the tool enforces anyway. Prompt 2: a backend with a database Create a backend resource called "orders" with tdk, using Hono. Run: tdk resource orders --type backend -y Add a GET /orders route that returns a JSON array. Keep the data in memory for now. Add a GET /health route if one is not already there. Do not change the port or the health path in service.json. Then run: tdk up main --dry-run, and tell me which services it would start and in what order. Why it works: the agent builds the route and leaves the infrastructure alone. The dry run is a check the agent can read back. Prompt 3: a worker that reads a queue Create a worker resource called "order-emails" with tdk. Run: tdk resource order-emails --type worker -y Give it a loop that logs "processing" every five seconds. Make it depend on the orders service by adding it to dependsOn in its service.json. Then run: tdk up main --dry-run and confirm that orders starts before order-emails. If the dry run shows any error, stop and report it instead of changing other files. Why it works: the dependency is declared, not hoped for. The agent checks the start order against what the tool reports, and it has a clear stop condition if something fails. Note that the dry-run flag and the exact start-order output come from the CLI. Run the prompts once on your machine to confirm the output matches before you rely on them. Where this stops working This approach is not magic. I want to be clear about the limits. TDK fixes infrastructure, not logic. A simple agent can still write a wrong price calculation or an insecure query. Review the application code the same way you would any code. The results depend on the prompt. A vague request still produces vague code. The three prompts above are specific because the tool is specific. You still need tests. The generated test file is a starting point. Write the checks that matter to your app. TDK is for local development. Deployment stays with Helm, Argo CD, or Kustomize, and TDK does not generate cluster manifests by default. Some apps need more than a simpler model. Hard algorithms, security-critical code, and unfamiliar domains still benefit from the most capable model. I use one for those. Why I stopped reaching for the best model Most of my time used to go into infrastructure review, not features. With TDK, that review mostly disappears, because the decisions are made by the generator and checked by tdk up . What is left is application code, and a simpler model does that well when the prompt is clear. The savings are real. Smaller models cost less per token, respond faster, and make it easier to run several agents at once on different services. The tradeoff is that I review the application logic more closely, because I no longer assume the model got the hard parts right. That is the whole argument. The tool carries the infrastructure, the prompt carries the feature, and I carry the judgment about the logic. Try it npm install -g @tdk-landscape/tdk-cli-core tdk project --yes tdk resource shop-web --type frontend -y tdk up main --dry-run Then give your agent the first prompt above, and check the result against the dry run. If it works, the next two prompts follow the same pattern.

I stopped reaching for the most capable model for every app. With TDK CLI, the infrastructure is already decided, so a simpler agent only has to get the application logic right.

For a long time I assumed that building an app with AI needed the best model available. Every project got the most capable assistant, the longest prompts, and the most careful review. Most of the effort went into getting the infrastructure right, not the features.

I stopped doing that. I now use simpler agents for most of my app work, and the results are good enough that I rarely go back. The reason is not that the simpler models got better. It is that TDK CLI removed most of the decisions a model used to get wrong.

This article explains what that means, where the limits are, and three prompts I use with a less capable agent.

The real problem was never the features

Ask a model to build a small app and it can write a handler, a component, or a query well. The trouble starts around the code:

  • a Dockerfile that builds but runs the wrong command,
  • a docker-compose.yml whose ports disagree with the proxy config,
  • a Tiltfile that watches the wrong folder and rebuilds on every save,
  • a database that starts after the API that needs it,
  • a migration that runs inside the API's start script.

Each of these costs a debugging round. A smarter model makes fewer of them, so people paid for smarter models. The cost of that is real: more tokens, more waiting, and more review of output that is only infrastructure.

What I needed was not a smarter model. I needed the infrastructure to stop being a question.

What TDK CLI decides for you

TDK CLI treats each service as a typed resource. You declare what kind of thing you are building, and the generator fills in the rest.

The resource types are listed by tdk resource --help:

  • frontend: a Vite app that shares one Docker and nginx path with the other frontends.
  • backend: an API. Bun with Hono by default, or Express, Elysia, Fastify, NestJS, Koa, or h3. Go, Python, and Rust are available as language choices.
  • worker: a background process that runs without serving HTTP.
  • agent: a service that hosts an AI agent next to your other services.
  • mcp: a Model Context Protocol server, scaffolded with the SDK already wired in.
  • bring-your-own: a container you already have, registered so TDK can route to it.
  • sdk: a library rather than a running service.

Each type comes with decisions already made. A frontend gets an API client and an environment config. A backend gets health routes, a port read from the environment, and a binding to every interface, so it runs inside a container without extra work. An MCP service gets a server that creates a fresh instance per request, so there is no session to lose on restart.

The generated runtime files are then fixed by the tool, not by the model. For a frontend, that is 18 files under .autogenerated/, each marked as generated, and each checked against a saved snapshot before the stack starts. I counted them in a scratch project. The agent does not have to write them, and it cannot quietly drift from them without tdk up blocking the change.

What this changes for the agent

Once the infrastructure is decided, the agent's job narrows to three questions:

  1. What does this service do?
  2. What does it call, and what does it expose?
  3. Does the result work when tdk up starts it?

A less capable model can answer those. It does not need to remember which port the proxy expects, or which Dockerfile layer caches the dependencies. The tool answers those questions the same way every time.

The repo also writes some rules down where an agent will read them. The contributor guidance says new examples run database migrations in a separate migrator resource, not in the API's startup, and that tdk doctor warns when a backend runs a migration from its start script. That is one of the mistakes a capable model makes often, and the rule is there whether or not the agent remembers it.

TDK also exposes the stack to agents directly. tdk status --json reports readiness. tdk up --json reports ok: false with errors. tdk mcp gives an agent six tools (doctor, up, down, status, logs, resource_list), so it checks the result instead of trusting its own summary.

Three prompts for a simpler agent

These are the prompts I use. They are written for a model that is fast and cheap, not one that reasons deeply about infrastructure. Each one assumes TDK CLI is installed and the project was created with tdk project.

Prompt 1: a frontend that calls an API 
Create a frontend resource called "shop-web" with tdk, using React.
Run: tdk resource shop-web --type frontend -y

Then open services/main/shop-web/src/App.tsx and build one page:
a product list that fetches from the API client in .autogenerated/api-client.ts
(do not write your own fetch URL). Show loading and error states.
Do not edit anything in .autogenerated/. Do not change service.json.
When done, run: tdk up main --dry-run and report what it says.

Why it works: the agent has one file to change, one client to use, and a command to check the result. The rule against editing .autogenerated/ matches what the tool enforces anyway.

Prompt 2: a backend with a database 
Create a backend resource called "orders" with tdk, using Hono.
Run: tdk resource orders --type backend -y

Add a GET /orders route that returns a JSON array. Keep the data in memory for now.
Add a GET /health route if one is not already there.
Do not change the port or the health path in service.json.
Then run: tdk up main --dry-run, and tell me which services it would start and in what order.

Why it works: the agent builds the route and leaves the infrastructure alone. The dry run is a check the agent can read back.

Prompt 3: a worker that reads a queue

Run: tdk resource order-emails --type worker -y

Make it depend on the orders service by adding it to dependsOn in its service.json.
Then run: tdk up main --dry-run and confirm that orders starts before order-emails.
If the dry run shows any error, stop and report it instead of changing other files.

Where this stops working

This approach is not magic. I want to be clear about the limits.

  • TDK fixes infrastructure, not logic. A simple agent can still write a wrong price calculation or an insecure query. Review the application code the same way you would any code.
  • The results depend on the prompt. A vague request still produces vague code. The three prompts above are specific because the tool is specific.
  • You still need tests. The generated test file is a starting point. Write the checks that matter to your app.
  • TDK is for local development. Deployment stays with Helm, Argo CD, or Kustomize, and TDK does not generate cluster manifests by default.
  • Some apps need more than a simpler model. Hard algorithms, security-critical code, and unfamiliar domains still benefit from the most capable model. I use one for those.
Why I stopped reaching for the best model

Most of my time used to go into infrastructure review, not features. With TDK, that review mostly disappears, because the decisions are made by the generator and checked by tdk up. What is left is application code, and a simpler model does that well when the prompt is clear.

items.title: It Used to Be Someone Else's Problem
items.summary: My laptop kept running out of memory, and my first instinct was to blame the laptop: not enough RAM, something wrong with the machine. The failure didn't help. It rarely showed up as an error I could read. The terminal just died, took the session with it, and whatever the agent had been doing had to start over. The culprit turned out to be test runners. Jest, and Vitest after it, start a pool of worker processes to run test files in parallel, and by default they size that pool to the machine: Jest uses one worker per CPU core minus one. That is a sensible default when you run one suite. It is a terrible one when three agent sessions each decide, at the same moment, that now is a good time to run the tests. Fixing it meant learning two things I had never needed. First, how many workers a runner starts and how to cap it. Second, that every one of those workers is a separate Node process with its own heap and its own memory ceiling. A limit on each process does nothing about the total. Six workers at a few hundred megabytes each is fine. Forty-five is not. None of this is new. It's operating systems and resource management, the kind of thing a platform engineer or an SRE knows cold. What's new is that I needed it, and I needed it because of how I work , not because of what I was building. Scale used to come with the job Most of computer science was always available to everyone. What decided whether you had to learn a given piece of it was scale, and scale came with the job. You learned about contention if you ran servers. You learned about race conditions if you wrote concurrent code. You learned about retries and idempotency if you built distributed systems. A developer shipping a web app could spend a career never touching any of it, because someone else in the building was paid to. Working with agents in parallel changes where scale comes from. One person with four sessions open is operating a small distributed system on a laptop. There are several independent workers sharing CPU, memory, disk, ports and a repository, each doing things nobody is watching live. The problems of that system arrive whether or not your job title says you should know about them. There is a second route to the same place, and it has nothing to do with parallel sessions: the jobs themselves are merging. My work is AI engineering, and the agents and pipelines are what I'm hired for, but I regularly end up building the backend around them, and sometimes the frontend too. It isn't my specialty, and someone may well take it over and polish it later. But an agent makes it feasible for one person to carry the whole thing, so one person does. Carrying the whole thing means inheriting the concerns of every role you've absorbed, such as the backend developer's retries, the frontend developer's build tooling and the ops person's processes. Both routes end at the same desk. That is the argument of this piece, and it runs against a common one. The usual worry about AI is that people will know less, because the model knows it for them. Some of that is true. I wrote about what you can safely stop holding in your head . But there is a second movement going the other way: knowledge that used to belong to someone else's job is landing on your desk, because now it actually hurts you. Here are five pieces of it, and then a few that are not computer science at all. 1. The machine is a shared resource The memory problem above has a name: oversubscription. Every tool that parallelises assumes it owns the machine. A test runner sizes its pool to your cores. A bundler does the same. A type checker holds the whole project in memory. Each of those defaults is reasonable in isolation, and together they are not, because nobody told any of them about the others. No single tool is misbehaving. Each one sizes itself as if it owned the machine, and the total is what crosses the line. What makes this nasty is how it fails, because it never points at the sum. The mild version is a worker that doesn't start in time and gets reported as an error that reads like a failing test, when the files it was supposed to run never ran at all. An agent that sees that output will try to fix the test, and so will you, unless you know that "the test failed" and "the test never got a chance" look the same from outside. The severe version leaves nothing to read: the terminal dies, the session goes with it, and the work has to be redone. That points at the machine, which is where my own suspicion went first. Section 4 is about what you lose when that happens. What to be aware of: Parallel tools size themselves to the machine. Worker counts ( --maxWorkers in Jest and Vitest) are the first thing to cap when several sessions share a laptop. Memory limits are per process. Node's heap ceiling ( --max-old-space-size ) protects one process from itself. It does nothing for the sum. Saturation disguises itself. Timeouts and crashes under load are a resource problem until proven otherwise. 2. Everything you start, something has to stop A single session in a single terminal cleans up after itself mostly by accident: you close the window and things die with it. Agents start things constantly and don't close windows. Over a week, what they leave behind adds up: Processes. Dev servers, watchers, headless browsers from a test run, a database container. Killing a parent doesn't always kill its children. On Unix they get reparented and keep running. On Windows, stopping a process leaves its children alive unless you kill the whole tree. Ports. Many dev servers quietly move to the next free port when theirs is taken. The session you are looking at may be serving on 5174 while 5173 in your browser is still showing another session's stale build, and it looks exactly like "my change didn't work." Copies of the repository. Git worktrees are the right way to give each agent its own checkout, and each one is a full working tree, usually with its own node_modules . Your editor, your file watchers, your search indexer and your antivirus all scan every copy. Everything else on disk. Build caches, temporary directories, test databases, container volumes, browser profiles, screenshots and logs from debugging sessions nobody remembers starting. All of these also cost memory, which is how this section loops back into the previous one. This is process management and resource lifecycle, a standard operating systems chapter. The concept worth holding is short: every resource has an owner responsible for releasing it, and if you can't name the owner, it leaks. When a person drove every command, the owner was obvious. With agents, the owner is often a session that ended three days ago. The practical version is a habit more than a tool: know how to list what is running and what is on disk, and clean up as part of finishing a task, not as a separate chore you'll get to later. Some cleanup commands are designed to be safe. git worktree remove refuses to delete a worktree with uncommitted changes, and it never deletes the branch. Knowing which cleanups are safe is what makes cleaning up routine instead of frightening. 3. Two writers, one file Put two agents on the same repository and you have a textbook race condition. One is editing a file while the other reformats it. Both try to commit at once, and git answers with index.lock . They share one test database, and each one's tests delete the other's fixtures. That last case fails intermittently, which is the most expensive way anything can fail. Before agents, you only met this if you wrote concurrent code. Now you meet it because of how you organise work. The fixes are the ones from the textbook, just applied to a new place: Isolation. Each agent gets its own worktree, its own database, its own port. That's what isolation levels in databases and separate address spaces in operating systems are both for: whatever is shared is where they collide. Partitioning. Give agents parts of the codebase that don't overlap, and put the overlap (a shared schema, a lockfile) in one agent's hands. Serialising what can't be split. Some resources have to be taken in turn: one full test suite at a time, one migration at a time. You don't need to prove anything about concurrency. You need to recognise the smell. A failure that appears and disappears with no code change usually means two things are touching the same resource. 4. Work that dies halfway A long agent run is a job, and jobs die: the machine saturates, the process gets killed, the network drops, a rate limit trips. The question distributed systems learned to ask decades ago is what state the world is in when that happens, and whether you can run the job again safely. That property is idempotency : running something twice has the same effect as running it once. A script that creates a branch fails the second time because the branch exists. One that ensures the branch exists doesn't. A migration that adds a column breaks on rerun, while one that checks first doesn't. A job that sends an email, crashes, and gets retried sends two emails. The companion idea is checkpointing : record progress in a form that lets a restart skip what's done.
