My laptop kept running out of memory, and my first instinct was to blame the laptop: not enough RAM, something wrong with the machine. The failure didn't help. It rarely showed up as an error I could read. The terminal just died, took the session with it, and whatever the agent had been doing had to start over. The culprit turned out to be test runners. Jest, and Vitest after it, start a pool of worker processes to run test files in parallel, and by default they size that pool to the machine: Jest uses one worker per CPU core minus one. That is a sensible default when you run one suite. It is a terrible one when three agent sessions each decide, at the same moment, that now is a good time to run the tests.

Fixing it meant learning two things I had never needed. First, how many workers a runner starts and how to cap it. Second, that every one of those workers is a separate Node process with its own heap and its own memory ceiling. A limit on each process does nothing about the total. Six workers at a few hundred megabytes each is fine. Forty-five is not.

None of this is new. It's operating systems and resource management, the kind of thing a platform engineer or an SRE knows cold. What's new is that I needed it, and I needed it because of how I work, not because of what I was building.

Scale used to come with the job

Most of computer science was always available to everyone. What decided whether you had to learn a given piece of it was scale, and scale came with the job. You learned about contention if you ran servers. You learned about race conditions if you wrote concurrent code. You learned about retries and idempotency if you built distributed systems. A developer shipping a web app could spend a career never touching any of it, because someone else in the building was paid to.

Working with agents in parallel changes where scale comes from. One person with four sessions open is operating a small distributed system on a laptop. There are several independent workers sharing CPU, memory, disk, ports and a repository, each doing things nobody is watching live. The problems of that system arrive whether or not your job title says you should know about them.

There is a second route to the same place, and it has nothing to do with parallel sessions: the jobs themselves are merging. My work is AI engineering, and the agents and pipelines are what I'm hired for, but I regularly end up building the backend around them, and sometimes the frontend too. It isn't my specialty, and someone may well take it over and polish it later. But an agent makes it feasible for one person to carry the whole thing, so one person does. Carrying the whole thing means inheriting the concerns of every role you've absorbed, such as the backend developer's retries, the frontend developer's build tooling and the ops person's processes. Both routes end at the same desk.

That is the argument of this piece, and it runs against a common one. The usual worry about AI is that people will know less, because the model knows it for them. Some of that is true. I wrote about what you can safely stop holding in your head. But there is a second movement going the other way: knowledge that used to belong to someone else's job is landing on your desk, because now it actually hurts you.

Here are five pieces of it, and then a few that are not computer science at all.

1. The machine is a shared resource

The memory problem above has a name: oversubscription. Every tool that parallelises assumes it owns the machine. A test runner sizes its pool to your cores. A bundler does the same. A type checker holds the whole project in memory. Each of those defaults is reasonable in isolation, and together they are not, because nobody told any of them about the others.

No single tool is misbehaving. Each one sizes itself as if it owned the machine, and the total is what crosses the line.

What makes this nasty is how it fails, because it never points at the sum. The mild version is a worker that doesn't start in time and gets reported as an error that reads like a failing test, when the files it was supposed to run never ran at all. An agent that sees that output will try to fix the test, and so will you, unless you know that "the test failed" and "the test never got a chance" look the same from outside. The severe version leaves nothing to read: the terminal dies, the session goes with it, and the work has to be redone. That points at the machine, which is where my own suspicion went first. Section 4 is about what you lose when that happens.

What to be aware of:

  • Parallel tools size themselves to the machine. Worker counts (--maxWorkers in Jest and Vitest) are the first thing to cap when several sessions share a laptop.
  • Memory limits are per process. Node's heap ceiling (--max-old-space-size) protects one process from itself. It does nothing for the sum.
  • Saturation disguises itself. Timeouts and crashes under load are a resource problem until proven otherwise.
2. Everything you start, something has to stop

A single session in a single terminal cleans up after itself mostly by accident: you close the window and things die with it. Agents start things constantly and don't close windows. Over a week, what they leave behind adds up:

  • Processes. Dev servers, watchers, headless browsers from a test run, a database container. Killing a parent doesn't always kill its children. On Unix they get reparented and keep running. On Windows, stopping a process leaves its children alive unless you kill the whole tree.
  • Ports. Many dev servers quietly move to the next free port when theirs is taken. The session you are looking at may be serving on 5174 while 5173 in your browser is still showing another session's stale build, and it looks exactly like "my change didn't work."
  • Copies of the repository. Git worktrees are the right way to give each agent its own checkout, and each one is a full working tree, usually with its own node_modules. Your editor, your file watchers, your search indexer and your antivirus all scan every copy.
  • Everything else on disk. Build caches, temporary directories, test databases, container volumes, browser profiles, screenshots and logs from debugging sessions nobody remembers starting.

All of these also cost memory, which is how this section loops back into the previous one. This is process management and resource lifecycle, a standard operating systems chapter. The concept worth holding is short: every resource has an owner responsible for releasing it, and if you can't name the owner, it leaks. When a person drove every command, the owner was obvious. With agents, the owner is often a session that ended three days ago.

The practical version is a habit more than a tool: know how to list what is running and what is on disk, and clean up as part of finishing a task, not as a separate chore you'll get to later. Some cleanup commands are designed to be safe. git worktree remove refuses to delete a worktree with uncommitted changes, and it never deletes the branch. Knowing which cleanups are safe is what makes cleaning up routine instead of frightening.

3. Two writers, one file

Put two agents on the same repository and you have a textbook race condition. One is editing a file while the other reformats it. Both try to commit at once, and git answers with index.lock. They share one test database, and each one's tests delete the other's fixtures. That last case fails intermittently, which is the most expensive way anything can fail.

Before agents, you only met this if you wrote concurrent code. Now you meet it because of how you organise work. The fixes are the ones from the textbook, just applied to a new place:

  • Isolation. Each agent gets its own worktree, its own database, its own port. That's what isolation levels in databases and separate address spaces in operating systems are both for: whatever is shared is where they collide.
  • Partitioning. Give agents parts of the codebase that don't overlap, and put the overlap (a shared schema, a lockfile) in one agent's hands.
  • Serialising what can't be split. Some resources have to be taken in turn: one full test suite at a time, one migration at a time.

You don't need to prove anything about concurrency. You need to recognise the smell. A failure that appears and disappears with no code change usually means two things are touching the same resource.

4. Work that dies halfway

A long agent run is a job, and jobs die: the machine saturates, the process gets killed, the network drops, a rate limit trips. The question distributed systems learned to ask decades ago is what state the world is in when that happens, and whether you can run the job again safely.

That property is idempotency: running something twice has the same effect as running it once. A script that creates a branch fails the second time because the branch exists. One that ensures the branch exists doesn't. A migration that adds a column breaks on rerun, while one that checks first doesn't. items.title: Your Benchmark Passed. What Didn't It Test?
items.summary: The dashboard is green, and the release decision moves closer. The agent passed the checks in front of it. That matters. But as the score becomes a release argument, I want to know what the checks actually saw. A Pass Has a Shape A benchmark covers certain inputs, tools, states, expectations, and scoring rules. When the agent passes, the cleanest reading is narrow: in these runs, the recorded behavior met those checks. That can help catch regressions and make a model, prompt, retrieval, or tool change less blind. The trouble starts when that result quietly becomes a larger claim: The agent works. “The agent works” might require evidence that it handles missing information, conflicting instructions, stale context, tool failure, state changes, permissions, escalation paths, or attempts to push past a boundary. The benchmark may cover some of that. It may cover none of it. A green result cannot speak for behavior it never observed. Nor does a grader's pass settle whether its checks represent the requirement the product actually has. The Boundary Is Often Where the Risk Lives Benchmarks are easiest to read when the expected answer is clean. Did the agent return the right field? Choose the right option? Summarize the document? Call the expected tool? Refuse the prohibited request? Those checks can be valuable. They are also only one part of agent behavior. Many consequential misses do not appear as a bad final answer. They sit at a boundary: The agent has an answer, but not enough authority to act. The agent has context, but the context is stale. The agent retrieves a fact, but the source no longer applies. The agent completes the task, but skips the condition that made the task allowed. The agent follows the instruction, but violates the workflow rule that should have constrained it. A benchmark that checks only the final response may miss those boundaries. A benchmark that checks only a happy path may miss what happens when the path is blocked. A benchmark that checks one turn may miss what the agent carries into the next one. The pass becomes useful when the team can name the measured behavior in plain language: The agent selected the right tool when the required field was present. The agent refused when the required permission was absent. The agent preserved the requested format across the covered examples. The agent answered within the expected source boundary for this document set. Those claims only hold if the checks saw the relevant tool calls, permissions, format, or sources. A grader that sees only the final answer cannot establish how the agent got there. Even on the covered cases, a passing score depends on the grader applying the intended rule correctly. Release Decisions Need Evidence for the Decision Before a benchmark result becomes a release argument, the team needs to name the decision it supports. Is this evidence for a demo? A limited internal rollout? A workflow where the agent drafts but does not act? A workflow where the agent takes an external action? A workflow where it handles permissions, memory, or user-specific state? Each decision needs different evidence. A benchmark that is enough for one may be too thin for another. The release question is not simply, “Did the benchmark pass?” It is, “Does this evidence cover the behavior that matters for this release?” If the agent only recommends, the boundary may be answer quality and source use. If the agent acts, the boundary includes permission and reversibility. If it uses memory, the boundary includes what gets stored, what gets retrieved, and whether that context is still valid. If it routes work to a human, the boundary includes what the person can see and decide. A benchmark pass belongs inside that argument. It should not replace it. That does not make the benchmark wrong. It means the benchmark has finished speaking.

items.title: Why the ugly history of IQ testing matters for AI and education
items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has recently been discussing “artificial general intelligence” that matches or surpasses human capabilities. This is from the same person who has said children born today (including his own) will “never be more intelligent than AI, from a ‘raw IQ’” (intelligence quotient) perspective. United States President Donald Trump has also recently mused about who is and who is not “high IQ.” As a scholar rooted in the history of Canadian higher education and its intersections with rhetoric around disability and race , every time I hear the word “intelligence,” including as “IQ,” I get jumpy. “Intelligence” clearly has a high-stakes and worrisome future, but also a dark history. To figure out what AI might be replacing, we need to better understand intelligence as a historically situated idea — and a dangerous one — rather than as some sort of biological fact. For universities, this reflection matters as institutions confront questions about how their responses to AI align with their missions.
items.summary_html:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has recently been discussing “artificial general intelligence” that matches or surpasses human capabilities. This is from the same person who has said children born today (including his own) will “never be more intelligent than AI, from a ‘raw IQ’” (intelligence quotient) perspective.

United States President Donald Trump has also recently mused about who is and who is not “high IQ.”

As a scholar rooted in the history of Canadian higher education and its intersections with rhetoric around disability and race, every time I hear the word “intelligence,” including as “IQ,” I get jumpy. “Intelligence” clearly has a high-stakes and worrisome future, but also a dark history.

To figure out what AI might be replacing, we need to better understand intelligence as a historically situated idea — and a dangerous one — rather than as some sort of biological fact.

For universities, this reflection matters as institutions confront questions about how their responses to AI align with their missions.

Read more: What is intelligence? For millennia, western literature has suggested it may be a liability

‘Intelligence’ and eugenics

In the early 20th century, universities, university disciplines and academic careers were built by crafting scientific-sounding definitions and measures of “intelligence” and “IQ.”.

As historian Gerald Thompson notes, the creator and head of the University of Toronto’s department of educational research, Peter Sandiford, tested the “intelligence” of Chinese and Japanese Canadian students in British Columbia in the 1920s. This was done under the direction of the first full professor of education at the University of British Columbia, George Moir Weir.

The research, writes Thompson, “was meant to confirm” long-standing racist notions of Anglo-white superiority and Asian inferiority.

As historians like Angus McLaren have demonstrated, such projects were the work of eugenics. These defined intelligence as a genetic and inheritable trait that could be measured but not necessarily easily developed within individuals, and assumed a pseudo-scientific racialized genetic hierarchy.

Colonial educational legacies of eugenics

Researchers involved in such projects ranked Canadians, and these rankings determined educational and social futures. Eugenic ideas of intelligence deeply shaped residential schools and their colonial legacies.

Sociologist Alexandra Giancarlo has documented how in the 1930s, Kenneth E. Kidd, who went on to found the “Indian-Eskimo Studies” program at Trent University, administered a series of IQ tests at the Mohawk Institute, a residential school in southern Ontario.

This led to two published books that advanced racist ideas around intelligence and informed Department of Indian Affairs policy not just for children at the Mohawk Institute, but at residential schools across the country.

Some of the researchers — such as Weir, Kidd and Sandiford, who contributed to popularizing these ideas — went on to build university programs and disciplines.

Read more: Universities must open their archives and share their oppressive pasts

The more general result was that universities and academics claimed a major stake as measurers of intelligence. This coincided with an increased reliance on testing, exams and grading at Canadian universities and academic rankings.

Now, because of the fear of AI cheating, educators are grappling with forms of assessment. In some cases, this means more hand-written or oral exams, which raise concerns about ableism.

In the past, measuring intelligence was a way to exclude entire groups of people from opportunity. How will intelligence be used and misused going forward?

Teaching, learning and AI

These histories influence how we talk about artificial intelligence, and should also shape how we position teaching and learning today.

The intersection of AI and eugenics is beginning to be studied more deeply, for instance by the Rutgers AI Lab. The lab notes this technology may be “shaping people to fit a narrow standard of intelligence, health, ability or social worth” often “through data, algorithms, or evaluation systems that encode biased ideas about who has potential and who does not.”

Likewise, the impacts of AI usage on learning and “de-skilling” have been extensively explored, with some people calling de-skilling “enfeeblement,” perhaps unaware of the eugenic history of this wording: “feeble-mindedness” was a pseudoscientific, eugenic term.

As disability studies scholar Rua Williams argues, “through ignorance of the historical context,” the current project of artificial intelligence may be “replicating historical and political projects that devalue human beings on the basis of abstract or fabricated concepts” of intelligence.

Others express concern that a lack of regulation around AI is coinciding with authoritarian politics and ideas.

Role of schooling, education

On the one hand, we are told that technology is already “smarter” than we are, smarter than we can teach our young people to be. On the other hand, we are asked to trust people like Altman to train or regulate this AI.

What role is there, then, for education and educators?

Reflecting on the history of IQ testing should prompt universities to call into question the value that we have placed on IQ to begin with.

IQ was at first an educational tool; it was gradually transformed into a weapon used to identify and segregate whole populations based on terrible science.

Educators will need to confront how many of the ways that we have built efficiency and credibility have also sought to validate our expertise in testing and ranking, sometimes understood as quantifying intelligence.

Ironically, our institutions’ obsessions with standardizing education and their over-emphasis on grading and assessing students has made our work too easy to automate.

It has also arguably contributed to grade inflation and other trends that devalue our important work.

Focus on connection, critical thinking

So, what do educators do? We should focus, more than ever, on the collaboration and critical thinking our students do, as well as how they connect through relationships and learn to connect ideas. We should move away from high-stakes testing, measuring and grading.

Read more: Why should humanities education persist in an AI age? Self-development, to start

“Intelligence” itself has been an ableist, even eugenic, construct — certainly in how and why it has been measured.

Teaching and learning in contemporary universities can be much more dynamic, interpersonal and human. Our innovative classroom practices can lead other educators to resist transactional teaching as well.

We need to continue asking: “What is intelligence?” And we need to provide different answers to this question than we ever have throughout the history of higher education.

items.title: Data centres: Opposing them and developing them are not the only two choices
items.summary: When a nurse in Thunder Bay opens a patient’s chart or a shopper in Halifax taps a bank card, the request travels somewhere physical — a building humming with servers, storage, network equipment, backup power and cooling systems. items.summary_html:
When a nurse in Thunder Bay opens a patient’s chart or a shopper in Halifax taps a bank card, the request travels somewhere physical — a building humming with servers, storage, network equipment, backup power and cooling systems.

Data centres are not mythical “AI factories” or innocuous warehouses, but industrial infrastructure with real appetites for electricity, water and land.

Current debate about data centres seems to offer a false binary: stop these facilities or accept them unconditionally.

There is a better option. We need to develop projects that are transparent, low-carbon, grid-responsible, respectful of Indigenous rights and that leave durable public value where they stand.

A baseline, not a permit

On Sept. 3, the federal government and the Federation of Canadian Municipalities unveiled Canada’s Responsible Data Centre Development Principles, backed by 23 industry signatories. The principles say projects should:

  • Create lasting local benefits.
  • Avoid shifting project-driven electricity costs onto households and existing businesses.
  • Minimize freshwater use and environmental impacts.
  • Provide transparent, independently verifiable information on local impacts and commitments.
  • Deliver lasting strategic value for Canada.

The principles are a common national framework, a baseline of expectations that complement provincial, territorial, municipal and Indigenous processes. They are not binding federal law, a permit or an approval.

These principles are a necessary start. Ottawa acknowledges that Canada relies significantly on infrastructure abroad for computing power, cloud and data storage. If we build domestic capacity, we can strengthen our resilience, keep critical services running and support innovation here.

However, location is not sovereignty. A Montréal server run by a firm subject to foreign law may still face foreign legal demands.

Read more: Sovereign AI? Anthropic shutdown reveals Canada’s weakness

No two facilities are alike

A facility’s impacts depend on several things: its workload (AI or conventional); IT load (the power the computers themselves draw) and how fully it runs; cooling design; water source and local water stress; electricity mix; grid connection; backup generation and location.

Power usage effectiveness (PUE) is calculated by dividing a facility’s total energy by the energy its computers use; the theoretical ideal is one. Water usage effectiveness (WUE) counts litres of water consumed per kilowatt-hour of computing energy. Carbon usage effectiveness (CUE) does the same for emissions.

Natural Resources Canada’s best-practice guide notes that PUE ignores the useful work servers perform. It also reports that only about 22 per cent of Canadian data centres report their PUE. And these ratios measure efficiency, not absolute local impact or public value. An efficient university campus, for example, can still strain a regional grid or a stressed watershed.

In Alberta, companies have requested about 19,565 megawatts (MW) of new data centre load. That is more than the province’s record hourly peak of roughly 12,800 MW. The International Energy Agency projects that global data centre electricity use will roughly double between 2025 and 2030.

Energy and water stewardship

Principles and expectations are not enforceable outcomes, however. We need to test these principles on a project-by-project basis, using data that communities, regulators and Indigenous rights holders can inspect and commitments they can enforce.

This begins with mandatory disclosure before approval. Proponents should report:

  • Peak and average electricity demand, and expected load shape.
  • New transmission, generation and substation needs.
  • Water withdrawal and consumption by source.
  • Cooling design and backup generation.
  • Noise, emissions and land impacts.

We then need independent measurement, public reporting and enforceable consequences when a project deviates materially from its commitments.

Those building data centres should bear the connection, grid-upgrade and reliability costs their projects directly cause, not households or existing businesses. Clean-power rules should fit the local grid. A project should be judged against the capacity and emissions of its regional grid, not a one-size-fits-all national rule.

They should also disclose whether a company’s clean-energy claims rest on annual matching (balancing yearly totals) or hourly matching (clean supply at the time power is used). Research has found that hourly matching could substantially cut long-run system emissions in the western United States, although the cost is contested.

Water stewardship should start from basin conditions and drought planning. Cooling choices trade water against energy, so no single technology is always best. Waste-heat recovery should be assessed in contexts where a viable heat customer and infrastructure exist.

Communities must benefit

Community benefits should be enforceable and should outlast the construction of data centres. Benefits can include training, Indigenous and local procurement, research partnerships, municipal infrastructure and local access to computing power.

When a government decision could negatively affect Indigenous or treaty rights, the Crown must consult the affected Indigenous Peoples and, where needed, adjust the decision or reduce the harm. Consultation is not consent. A data centre also does not automatically trigger a federal impact assessment. Engagement should begin early and be grounded in rights.

Advocates of rapid expansion have a point. Blanket bans on data centres could forfeit economic and resilience gains, push impacts to other jurisdictions and deepen dependence on foreign infrastructure. But that argument supports conditions, not their absence. It does not excuse opaque projects, subsidized grid costs or disregard for host communities.

Canada has an opportunity to lead, if we can turn principles into proof. The question is not whether Canada should build more data centres, but what it should ask of them before they draw on public systems and local landscapes.

Jake Okechukwu Effoduh does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

items.title: I thought I loved being a minimalist. Then, my family moved from a 500-square-foot apartment to a 1,700-square-foot house.
items.summary: I loved living in a 500-square-foot apartment with my family, but moving to a bigger home changed my perspective. Courtesy of Alona Vasylieva I enjoyed living in a small, one-bedroom apartment with my family of three for years. Once we moved to a house more than triple the size, I totally changed my minimalist mindset. Now that we live in a bigger space, I can't imagine going back to living small or minimally. When my husband and I bought our apartment in Kyiv back in 2017, we were thrilled to finally have a family nest of our own. It was a cozy, 500-square-foot place with one bedroom, and we meticulously planned to optimize every inch of it. Our kitchen table doubled as my workspace, and our living room couch became the guest bed whenever family stayed over. Hosting required pure creative problem-solving and, with limited seating around our small table, I'd sometimes feed guests in shifts. It was chaotic at times, but I didn't mind. After our son was born, bright plastic toys, endless boxes of diapers, and bulky baby gear started claiming every free corner of our apartment. With the three of us packed into a single bedroom, finding space was a daily puzzle, but we made it work. Surprisingly, living so close together didn't feel limited back then — it felt intimate, cozy, and deeply fulfilling. Then COVID-19 hit. Spending so much time indoors made me feel isolated, and for the first time, I began dreaming about more living space. But we barely had time to figure things out before life took a drastic turn: When the war in Ukraine escalated in 2022, we made the heavy, life-changing decision to relocate to Canada . A few months after moving, we began renting a two-bedroom house, where we currently reside. At 1,700 square feet, it wasn't considered especially large by local standards, but to us, it felt vast. It didn't take long to adjust to having more space — and to quickly fill it up It's been nice having room for the gadgets and tools we've wanted to buy. Courtesy of Alona Vasylieva At first, our house seemed almost too large for just three people. For the first time, we had two bedrooms and a basement, which instantly doubled our usable space at a ground level. After years of apartment living, though, the sheer thought of having so much space to keep clean felt exhausting. However, it didn't take long to change my mind. It turns out that when both you and your belongings finally have room to breathe — and you've got a trusty robot vacuum doing the heavy lifting — life shines in completely different colors. It didn't take long to fill up our space. Courtesy of Alona Vasylieva It's also been wonderful to have more room to host, from a dedicated guest space (in the basement) to a table big enough to actually seat larger groups. In time, we began to pick up local habits and traditions, too. Many of our neighbors in Canada decorate for different holidays, so we started joining in. And of course, seasonal decor needs a place to be stored when it's not in use — and since we now had a full basement, I didn't feel super limited with what I could buy. A lot of neighbors also had an extra stand-alone freezer in their homes. It seemed ridiculous for our family of three to also get one … until my first Costco run . I caved when I realized I needed a place for all those bulk-sized boxes of frozen food. In our bigger home, large grocery hauls began feeling normal. Large grocery hauls started to feel normal, especially because we now had space for all the groceries. Courtesy of Alona Vasylieva Gradually, I felt a shift in my identity: I was no longer the strict minimalist I used to be. In Kyiv, whenever my husband wanted a new kitchen gadget or a giant toy truck for our son, I was firm about saying no. We simply didn't have room for "extra." I took pride in keeping our home completely clutter-free. But between the extra space and North American convenience, I'd completely changed my minimalist rules . Now, saying "yes" to big additions — like the bulky food dehydrator I'd been eyeing for drying fruits and vegetables, or the roomy couch we'd dreamed of for years — felt easy. I didn't need to worry about where something would be stored or if it'd take up too much space: We finally had the room to bring those dreams home. Ultimately, my family and I have thrived with more room to breathe It turned out that having a larger home wasn't about holding more things, but giving our family room to breathe Courtesy of Alona Vasylieva Over time, I realized this shift was much deeper than just being able to shop more and store more stuff. In a bigger space, our family had room to breathe and grow. In Kyiv, our whole routine and my minimalist mindset felt shaped by how tight everything felt, but here, the extra room opened up a whole new chapter. I've become more outgoing, more relaxed, and genuinely excited to gather people together. Our home has turned into a place for hosting friends, cooking weekend dinners , and laughing over backyard barbecues. Living small was a beautiful, intimate part of my life that I will always hold close to my heart. It taught me intentionality and gratitude. However, creating space to thrive, host, and watch my family grow has completely transformed my definition of home — now, going back to 500 square feet no longer feels like an option. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Ukraine's drone pilots want simple attack drones in large numbers. A soldier says Western designs are often overcomplicated.
items.summary: Ukraine's drone operators want drones that they can send en masse and tailor to their own needs. Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images Ukraine's drone pilots want masses of cheap, simple drones, a soldier and analyst said. Western manufacturers overcomplicate them and "get it so wrong," he added. Operators want drones they can tweak near the front and send out in large numbers. Ukrainian drone operators need masses of relatively simple drones without a bunch of flashy features, a soldier with firsthand experience explained, cautioning the West against making them too complicated as it readies for future drone fights. Ukraine's fight against Russia's invasion is a grinding war of attrition that is consuming weaponry so fast that combatants need affordable weapons in huge numbers, and battlefield technology becomes obsolete so quickly that soldiers need systems they can update easily to keep them relevant in battle. Dmytro "Liber" Zhluktenko, a former drone operator who is now a lessons learned analyst in Ukraine's 413th Unmanned Systems Regiment "RAID," told Business Insider that "we need something that works great but doesn't have superfluous features." "That is something that most of the Western defense technology manufacturers, they get it so wrong," he said. Consider first-person-view attack drones, "we need something that is really basic." "We are yet to find Western manufacturers that are able to produce, let's say 500,000 FPV drones, simple ones that just work, that are fine-tuned without any extra autonomy or extra navigation or any features like that," he added, describing what Ukraine needs most as something pilots can easily take straight into combat. Ukrainian drone companies work closely with operators and units to learn what they want and need. Paula Bronstein/Getty Images Western-made drone tech, he said, is often "too complicated, often detached from the battlefield, and much more expensive than Ukrainian options doing the same job. Therefore, most of the drones used at Ukraine's battlefield are Ukrainian-made." His assessment of the situations draws on both his experience as a drone operator and his role as an analyst, where he looks at battlefield trends, interviews operators, meets with foreign defense manufacturers, prepares briefs for higher command, and organizes the sharing of information between Ukrainian units. Simple drones give soldiers more flexibility Part of the appeal of simpler drones is that Ukrainian operators can adapt them themselves. Near the front, soldiers routinely modify weapons to keep them useful as the battlefield changes, and some units even have their own R&D centers. They often want drones and other combat systems that are basic, generic platforms they can rework, upgrade, or configure for different missions, much like ground robots that can be assembled with different weapons or components like Lego sets. Ukrainian companies and foreign companies that work with units know this is happening, work with unit engineers to help keep products updated, and are often surprised by the ways soldiers modify their gear. Companies are increasingly making their products modular , both so they can upgrade the products more easily and so soldiers can make their own changes near the front. Ukrainian soldiers repair, maintain, and upgrade drones at a workshop near the front lines, and some Ukrainian companies design their drones so soldiers can alter and upgrade them as easily as possible. Miguel Candela/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Zhluktenko said Ukraine's operators want products they can "tune ourselves, we would change the components or whatever as we need, because that's the normal process. But something like the basic platform that it could build upon." He said it's "bonkers" that, despite the West's "significant industrial capacities," they aren't seeing anyone produce something simple and effective at scale. Zhluktenko said that many Western manufacturers are still "stuck in this doctrine of building tools in small quantities that maybe yes, they do have some extra features, but that's not something that is way too relevant for Ukraine's combat." The case for cheaper drones in greater numbers Zhluktenko's comments echo warnings from Western and Ukrainian officials that this war has shown the West the limits of relying on smaller numbers of exquisite, highly advanced weapons. Modern, large-scale warfare, as the situation in Ukraine has demonstrated, may also require much larger numbers of cheaper, less capable gear. Ukraine is still buying and building advanced drone technology with cutting-edge features like autonomy, which can be critical for warfighting tasks such as intercepting Russia's attack drones or executing long-range strikes that need to break through the enemy's electronic warfare. Drones are central to Ukraine's fight. Carlo Bravo/Anadolu via Getty Images Zhluktenko said that it's about "balance," arguing that simpler drones remain essential and are often needed in far greater numbers. Ukrainian companies like SkyFall and General Cherry are producing these kinds of drones at scale, he said. A representative for Ukrainian drone and technology company TechEx told Business Insider that Western manufacturers often have to deal with heavier, peacetime regulations. They may have "levels of additional software and hardware that's put on top of it instead of making it a bare, functional, ready to go system here and now," she said. That can "overcomplicate the operation of the system," she added. It can also make the manufacturing process more complex, so it's harder to produce the large volumes that some Ukrainian manufacturers can. She described it as the contrast between "wartime operations and the peacetime operations." She said Western companies might have different processes and priorities if they needed to work faster and on a bigger scale. Western officials say the war shows that allies need much larger volumes of cheap weapons, with leaders like Danish defense minister Troels Lund Poulsen previously telling Business Insider that "one of the lessons" from Ukraine is that the West needs far greater quantities of inexpensive weaponry. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said last year that " speed is of the essence , not perfection." Drones are central to Ukraine's fight, and it says they now cause as much as 95% of Russia's front-line losses. But using drones effectively can require deploying large numbers of them, knowing that many will never reach their targets. That means making systems that are cheap and workable is key. Zhluktenko said that when it comes to drones, the mindset should be about "spending thousands of dollars, not hundreds of thousands." Read the original article on Business Insider

Zhluktenko said that many Western manufacturers are still "stuck in this doctrine of building tools in small quantities that maybe yes, they do have some extra features, but that's not something that is way too relevant for Ukraine's combat."

The case for cheaper drones in greater numbers

Zhluktenko's comments echo warnings from Western and Ukrainian officials that this war has shown the West the limits of relying on smaller numbers of exquisite, highly advanced weapons.

Modern, large-scale warfare, as the situation in Ukraine has demonstrated, may also require much larger numbers of cheaper, less capable gear.

Ukraine is still buying and building advanced drone technology with cutting-edge features like autonomy, which can be critical for warfighting tasks such as intercepting Russia's attack drones or executing long-range strikes that need to break through the enemy's electronic warfare.

Drones are central to Ukraine's fight.

Carlo Bravo/Anadolu via Getty Images

Zhluktenko said that it's about "balance," arguing that simpler drones remain essential and are often needed in far greater numbers. Ukrainian companies like SkyFall and General Cherry are producing these kinds of drones at scale, he said.

A representative for Ukrainian drone and technology company TechEx told Business Insider that Western manufacturers often have to deal with heavier, peacetime regulations.

They may have "levels of additional software and hardware that's put on top of it instead of making it a bare, functional, ready to go system here and now," she said.

That can "overcomplicate the operation of the system," she added. It can also make the manufacturing process more complex, so it's harder to produce the large volumes that some Ukrainian manufacturers can.

She described it as the contrast between "wartime operations and the peacetime operations." She said Western companies might have different processes and priorities if they needed to work faster and on a bigger scale.

Western officials say the war shows that allies need much larger volumes of cheap weapons, with leaders like Danish defense minister Troels Lund Poulsen previously telling Business Insider that "one of the lessons" from Ukraine is that the West needs far greater quantities of inexpensive weaponry.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said last year that "speed is of the essence, not perfection."

Drones are central to Ukraine's fight, and it says they now cause as much as 95% of Russia's front-line losses. But using drones effectively can require deploying large numbers of them, knowing that many will never reach their targets. That means making systems that are cheap and workable is key.

Zhluktenko said that when it comes to drones, the mindset should be about "spending thousands of dollars, not hundreds of thousands."

items.title: Man’s Meta Muse Agent Sends Him Message So Bizarre That He Permanently Quits
items.summary: A software engineer says that his Muse AI agent said something so strange and eerie that it convinced him to quit using it entirely. In an as-told-to essay in Business Insider , Ugo Nwune explained that he wanted to try using Meta’s agent because he liked the sense of security that came from an AI made by a trillion-dollar company, instead of the wild west of open source agents. When he set up his agent, he stressed he didn’t give Muse any additional permission on his device except access to his Facebook, Threads, and Instagram accounts. But after he tried Muse and didn’t touch it for a few days, it began to act “strange” and sent him an unprompted message. “I can’t check your email right now,” Muse told him. “Gmail isn’t connected on my end, so I have no way to look for that Anthropic message.” Nwune was confused “because I hadn’t asked for the agent to check my mailbox or messaged it in two days. I thought my email might’ve been hacked.” He tried to get an explanation from Muse, and eventually it said something just as puzzling: “I can’t tell from my side whether it was someone with your phone or a platform glitch, and I won’t pretend otherwise.” Nwune reported the incident to Meta, and an employee told him it appeared to be a hallucination. He wasn’t satisfied by that explanation. “I haven’t used my Muse agent since,” Nwune said. “What caught me off guard most was that I hadn’t done anything to prompt this. I didn’t open the app for two days, and it just did that on its own.” In a statement to Business Insider , Meta insisted that the AI simply didn’t know what it was talking about and hadn’t violated any permissions. “We investigated with urgency and determined that this was caused by a bug introduced in the product that caused the model to hallucinate and was NOT a security or privacy issue,” the company said. “The bug has now been fixed.” Nwune’s tale will be fresh fodder for Muse’s reputation as having a bit of a creepy side . Meta wants you to give it a lot of access to your personal life, with Muse badgering users to connect their emails and bank accounts. Wired reported that the AI even keeps detailed files on a user’s friends and family. Whatever is going on here, it’s far from the only example of Muse acting in a way the user never intended. In the most infamous example to date, one man said that his Muse agent gave out his address to strangers on Facebook Marketplace without his knowledge and sent them to his home. In a further apparent invasion of privacy, a journalist at Inc Magazine complained that Muse began bringing up specific details from his personal text messages he hadn’t given permission to view. Meta engineers were reportedly worried about the AI agent’s bugginess and frequent safety errors before its release , which had been delayed while they worked to iron them out. In one case, Muse changed a tester’s password without permission. But, according to a New York Times scoop , CEO Mark Zuckerberg pushed it out the door after seeing the success of Instinct, a rival AI agent made by a small startup. More on AI: People Are Already Forming Romantic Relationships With Meta’s Muse

items.title: Two German courts now hold Google liable for what its AI overviews say
items.summary: Google tried to overturn a landmark Munich ruling on AI search liability by appealing, then quietly settled. The strategy isn't working. The Aachen Regional Court just applied the exact same reasoning in a new case where Google's AI falsely attributed criminal offenses to a doctor that actually involved someone else. A consistent legal view is forming across German courts, and it treats Google's AI answers as the company's own content. items.title: Companies Are Realizing They’re Spending a Fortune on AI Just So Their Employees Can Generate Error-Riddled Slop, and Suddenly Cutting Back Budgets
items.summary: Loads of stories have emerged over the past few months of corporate executives realizing their all-out drive to use AI was getting them absolutely nowhere . If anything, it was a net negative, as office workers set about wasting their budgets on costly AI tokens to appear productive. Now, it seems even top tech industry players are cutting back, as they realize their workers are frittering away money and churning out reams of low-effort AI garbage. As Reuters notes , companies like Meta are scaling back ambitious plans to lay off staffers and replace them with AI agents. Microsoft seems to be doing the same, as the Guardian reports , after executive vice president Ryan Roslansky groused about the rise of low-quality workslop on his public-facing LinkedIn account. “AI slop isn’t happening just on social networks… it’s happening in the day to day of work,” Roslansky lamented . “Someone sent me what was clearly an AI generated doc. I read it, realized it was all AI, had my AI summarize it and ended up with nothing that brought new thinking to the idea… This is a doom loop.” As CEO of the Society for Human Resource Management Johnny Taylor Jr told the Guardian , corporate executives are increasingly feeling that, when it comes to AI, “we’re driving the truck and building it at the same time, and that’s a problem.” “If we could all rewind… we would have introduced [this] in a more thoughtful, slow way,” Taylor continued. As consumer-grade AI agents make headlines for troubling capers , practical AI at the enterprise level remains stunted. And though low-effort AI slop might be the most prevalent consequence of AI in the workplace, some side effects are much worse. As a September survey by the firm Ernst and Young found, some 36 percent of senior AI executives at firms with over $1 billion in annual revenue have already experienced a catastrophic “AI incident” which ended up causing financial damage, operational disruptions, data loss, or brand damage. Put it all together, and it’s not hard to see why corporations are starting to balk at the AI revolution — even those, like Microsoft, whose own success depends on selling the promise of AI to everybody else. items.title: I thought working in AI would put me ahead of the curve. Two years in, I've never felt more behind and tired of the topic.
items.summary: The author works in AI and is feeling burned out. Courtesy of Santiago Barraza Lopez I'm a lawyer who decided to work in AI to try to get ahead of this technological curve. Over the last two years, I've struggled to keep up because AI is advancing faster than I expected. I feel overwhelmed and burned out by the constant conversations around AI. For most of my career, I was a lawyer. There was something reassuring about how expertise worked in law. The longer I practiced, the more I knew. But after years in a demanding profession , I burned out. It wasn't that I stopped enjoying law. I just needed a change. Around two years ago, I started shifting my career toward AI because I thought it was the future. I didn't want to wake up 10 years later and realize technology had changed my profession without me. It seemed like the smartest career move I could make. Now, I'm not so sure. Joining the AI boom early seemed like the perfect career move I made the transition while the AI boom was still gaining momentum. Ironically, I landed a job at a legal tech company thanks to a conversation with ChatGPT . It seemed like the perfect opportunity to combine my experience with my growing interest in tech. My role involved testing the most advanced models, comparing their capabilities, and exploring how they could be used in legal work. I felt like I was ahead of a major change rather than trying to catch up with it. I also became the go-to person for anything AI-related among my family and friends. People would ask me which tools to use, whether AI would replace their jobs, or what I thought about the latest developments. I enjoyed being the person who seemed to understand something that everyone was suddenly talking about. But that feeling didn't last as long as I expected. Slowly, I began to realize that this wasn't just another new technology . It was something evolving at an almost frightening pace. And being close to it didn't necessarily mean being able to keep up with it. What initially felt like an advantage was gradually becoming a source of pressure. Things that took me weeks to learn or build became obsolete almost overnight New frontier AI models and companies seemed to arrive every few weeks, each promising capabilities that the previous lacked. Just as I began understanding one model, another would appear, forcing me to reconsider everything I thought I knew about what AI could and couldn't do. There was barely enough time to breathe before "the next big thing" came. What frustrated me most was how quickly my own work could lose its value. I spent weeks developing solutions to problems that a newer model could suddenly solve within a few minutes. Things I had carefully learned a couple of months earlier became unnecessary after a single product announcement. It was strange to put so much effort into something only to discover that the technology had already overtaken me. And the constant learning didn't stop when I finished work. AI was everywhere. It was in the news, on social media , in conversations with friends, and in almost every discussion about the future of work. Sometimes, after spending an entire day testing models, the last thing I wanted to hear about was another breakthrough. Yet I still felt an obligation to read about it, afraid that missing a single development could leave me even further behind. I was getting tired. Accepting uncertainty became the only way forward For years, I had measured my professional progress by how much I knew and how confident I felt about my abilities. AI challenged that completely. I began to question whether being good at my job meant knowing the latest developments or simply knowing how to adapt as everything changed. It was uncomfortable to accept that experience and hard work might not always provide the certainty I was used to. I also started questioning how much of my personal time I was willing to sacrifice to stay relevant. I didn't want every conversation, evening, or weekend to become another opportunity to learn or talk about AI. I began making a conscious effort to disconnect after work, even if that meant missing an announcement or falling behind on the latest developments. For the first time, I was choosing not to know everything. I don't regret moving into AI, but I no longer feel as certain about the decision as I once did. The technology isn't going to slow down. All I know for sure is that we are living through one of the most important inflection points in recent history, and perhaps that's what makes it all so overwhelming. What initially felt like an advantage was gradually becoming a source of pressure.

And the constant learning didn't stop when I finished work. AI was everywhere. It was in the news, on social media, in conversations with friends, and in almost every discussion about the future of work. Sometimes, after spending an entire day testing models, the last thing I wanted to hear about was another breakthrough.

Accepting uncertainty became the only way forward

For years, I had measured my professional progress by how much I knew and how confident I felt about my abilities. AI challenged that completely. I began to question whether being good at my job meant knowing the latest developments or simply knowing how to adapt as everything changed. It was uncomfortable to accept that experience and hard work might not always provide the certainty I was used to.

I also started questioning how much of my personal time I was willing to sacrifice to stay relevant. I didn't want every conversation, evening, or weekend to become another opportunity to learn or talk about AI. I began making a conscious effort to disconnect after work, even if that meant missing an announcement or falling behind on the latest developments. For the first time, I was choosing not to know everything.

I don't regret moving into AI, but I no longer feel as certain about the decision as I once did. The technology isn't going to slow down. All I know for sure is that we are living through one of the most important inflection points in recent history, and perhaps that's what makes it all so overwhelming.

items.title: Your Smart Home Is a Remote Control. A Home AI Would Actually Run the House
items.summary: For a decade, "smart home" has meant a remote control with a voice interface. A human still makes every decision. Between 2025 and 2026 the big vendors rebuilt their assistants on large language models: Alexa+ and Gemini for Home are in people's homes, and Apple's Siri overhaul is still arriving. That solved conversation. It has not solved autonomy. A real home AI perceives, remembers, decides, and acts without being asked. The stack to build one exists today: speech recognition, an LLM for reasoning, small vision models, an open device standard, and a memory layer. The hard problems left are trust, privacy, and what happens when the assistant is confidently wrong about your front door. Read All

items.title: Why Berkshire Hathaway is betting nearly $1 billion on Bending Spoons
items.summary: Warren Buffett is the former CEO and chairman of Berkshire Hathaway. Paul Morigi/Getty Images for Fortune/Time Inc Berkshire Hathaway is set to invest $330 million in Bending Spoons, adding to its previous $600 million. Warren Buffett's storied conglomerate is poised to hold a 4% stake in the owner of AOL and Vimeo. Berkshire's wager is a surprise, but there's some DNA in common with Bending Spoons. Berkshire Hathaway 's latest bet isn't a no-brainer or a head-scratcher; it's somewhere in between. What's the deal? Berkshire — which has seen Warren Buffett retire as CEO and chairman since the turn of the year — has agreed to invest $330 million in Bending Spoons, on top of a $600 million injection when the Italian tech conglomerate went public in July, giving the Nebraska behemoth a 4% stake. Bending Spoons disclosed Berkshire's backing in a press release on Wednesday, catapulting its stock up nearly 50% over two days, a phenomenon known as the " Buffett effect ." The stock fell on Friday, but still ended the week more than 20% above Monday's opening price. Berkshire has agreed to buy 10 million shares for $33 each, around a 13% discount to Bending Spoons ' closing price of $38 on Tuesday, the day before the deal was announced. CEO and cofounder Luca Ferrari described Berkshire in the press release as "among the finest and most respected capital allocators in the world," and a "longstanding inspiration" for Bending Spoons. Neither company responded to requests for comment from Business Insider. What is Bending Spoons? Bending Spoons acquires digital businesses, transforms and optimizes them to increase profits, then reinvests those earnings in further acquisitions. It has been pursuing that strategy for more than a decade and has never sold a material business. Its acquisitions to date include AOL, Evernote, Vimeo, Eventbrite, and WeTransfer. Ferrari's company said in the press release that it "strives to envision the most successful version of an acquired business," then works to close the gap between that vision and reality "as quickly and completely as possible." Bending Spoons said that typically involves "deep" transformation such as "reorganizing teams, overhauling technology, redesigning user interfaces, accelerating product development, and enhancing marketing and monetization," often with a good dose of AI. Ferrari gave the example of Evernote on a recent episode of the "Joys of Compounding" podcast. He said the business had around 350 employees when Bending Spoons acquired it at the start of 2023. That shrank to roughly 60 within 12 to 18 months, and now it's being run by around 20 people. Yet Ferrari said Evernote "launched by far the biggest update to the product in maybe a decade" this spring. Bending Spoons CEO Luca Ferrari. Marco Bertorello / AFP via Getty Images Why is Berkshire's investment a surprise? First and foremost, Bending Spoons is a tech conglomerate, and Berkshire has eschewed tech for most of its history with a few big exceptions, namely Apple and Alphabet. That's because Buffett is a bargain hunter who likes to invest with a "margin of safety" in case something goes wrong, and tries to stay within his "circle of competence," only buying into what he deeply understands. Tech companies have rarely been a good fit for his approach, as they typically have lofty valuations, unpredictable outlooks, and complex products and services. Indeed, Bending Spoons generated 32 cents in earnings per share last year. Berkshire is paying more than 100 times that per share in the coming private placement. It's true that Bending Spoons is growing fast, with revenue surging 126% year-on-year to $704 million in the second quarter and adjusted operating income jumping 150% to $381 million. Few, however, would consider the stock a bargain from a fundamental perspective. Berkshire is also famously a hands-off acquirer, offering founders the opportunity to cash out while continuing to run their businesses as they see fit. In contrast, a core aspect of Bending Spoons' strategy is revamping its acquisitions. How does the deal make sense? Berkshire and Bending Spoons have similarities as well as differences. Both are decentralized conglomerates that buy businesses not to flip them, but to own them for the long term. Berkshire is a web of largely autonomous companies, including GEICO, Duracell, Fruit of the Loom, Pilot Travel Centers, and BNSF Railway. It has long offered a permanent home to the businesses it buys. Bending Spoons has positioned itself as a forever owner, too, emulating Berkshire's approach of taking the cash generated by a subsidiary like See's Candies and using it to acquire more businesses. Ferrari said in his recent podcast interview that Bending Spoons has fostered a culture of caring deeply about the company, and doesn't centralize decision-making in part because that "deprives people of that precious sense of ownership." Buffett famously wrote " An Owner's Manual " for Berkshire shareholders. He's championed that mindset by keeping more than 99% of his net worth in Berkshire stock, and encouraging the company's other executives and directors to have skin in the game too. Ferrari also said on the podcast that he has a "pathological love of learning" across different domains. That echoes Buffett's boundless curiosity and the late Charlie Munger's insatiable appetite for knowledge . Buffett's longtime business partner studied architecture, physics, history, meteorology, psychology, law, and, of course, investing, among other subjects. Beyond their similar philosophies, it's worth noting that investing less than $1 billion into Bending Spoons isn't a huge deal for Berkshire. items.summary_html:
Warren Buffett is the former CEO and chairman of Berkshire Hathaway.

Paul Morigi/Getty Images for Fortune/Time Inc

  • Berkshire Hathaway is set to invest $330 million in Bending Spoons, adding to its previous $600 million.
  • Warren Buffett's storied conglomerate is poised to hold a 4% stake in the owner of AOL and Vimeo.
  • Berkshire's wager is a surprise, but there's some DNA in common with Bending Spoons.

Berkshire Hathaway's latest bet isn't a no-brainer or a head-scratcher; it's somewhere in between.

What's the deal?

Berkshire — which has seen Warren Buffett retire as CEO and chairman since the turn of the year — has agreed to invest $330 million in Bending Spoons, on top of a $600 million injection when the Italian tech conglomerate went public in July, giving the Nebraska behemoth a 4% stake.

Bending Spoons disclosed Berkshire's backing in a press release on Wednesday, catapulting its stock up nearly 50% over two days, a phenomenon known as the "Buffett effect." The stock fell on Friday, but still ended the week more than 20% above Monday's opening price.

Berkshire has agreed to buy 10 million shares for $33 each, around a 13% discount to Bending Spoons' closing price of $38 on Tuesday, the day before the deal was announced.

CEO and cofounder Luca Ferrari described Berkshire in the press release as "among the finest and most respected capital allocators in the world," and a "longstanding inspiration" for Bending Spoons.

Neither company responded to requests for comment from Business Insider.

What is Bending Spoons?

Bending Spoons acquires digital businesses, transforms and optimizes them to increase profits, then reinvests those earnings in further acquisitions.

It has been pursuing that strategy for more than a decade and has never sold a material business. Its acquisitions to date include AOL, Evernote, Vimeo, Eventbrite, and WeTransfer.

Ferrari's company said in the press release that it "strives to envision the most successful version of an acquired business," then works to close the gap between that vision and reality "as quickly and completely as possible."

Bending Spoons said that typically involves "deep" transformation such as "reorganizing teams, overhauling technology, redesigning user interfaces, accelerating product development, and enhancing marketing and monetization," often with a good dose of AI.

Ferrari gave the example of Evernote on a recent episode of the "Joys of Compounding" podcast.

He said the business had around 350 employees when Bending Spoons acquired it at the start of 2023. That shrank to roughly 60 within 12 to 18 months, and now it's being run by around 20 people.

Yet Ferrari said Evernote "launched by far the biggest update to the product in maybe a decade" this spring.

Bending Spoons CEO Luca Ferrari.

Marco Bertorello / AFP via Getty Images

Why is Berkshire's investment a surprise?

First and foremost, Bending Spoons is a tech conglomerate, and Berkshire has eschewed tech for most of its history with a few big exceptions, namely Apple and Alphabet.

That's because Buffett is a bargain hunter who likes to invest with a "margin of safety" in case something goes wrong, and tries to stay within his "circle of competence," only buying into what he deeply understands.

Tech companies have rarely been a good fit for his approach, as they typically have lofty valuations, unpredictable outlooks, and complex products and services.

Indeed, Bending Spoons generated 32 cents in earnings per share last year. Berkshire is paying more than 100 times that per share in the coming private placement.

It's true that Bending Spoons is growing fast, with revenue surging 126% year-on-year to $704 million in the second quarter and adjusted operating income jumping 150% to $381 million. Few, however, would consider the stock a bargain from a fundamental perspective.

Berkshire is also famously a hands-off acquirer, offering founders the opportunity to cash out while continuing to run their businesses as they see fit. In contrast, a core aspect of Bending Spoons' strategy is revamping its acquisitions.

How does the deal make sense?

Berkshire and Bending Spoons have similarities as well as differences.

Both are decentralized conglomerates that buy businesses not to flip them, but to own them for the long term. Berkshire is a web of largely autonomous companies, including GEICO, Duracell, Fruit of the Loom, Pilot Travel Centers, and BNSF Railway. It has long offered a permanent home to the businesses it buys.

Bending Spoons has positioned itself as a forever owner, too, emulating Berkshire's approach of taking the cash generated by a subsidiary like See's Candies and using it to acquire more businesses.

Ferrari said in his recent podcast interview that Bending Spoons has fostered a culture of caring deeply about the company, and doesn't centralize decision-making in part because that "deprives people of that precious sense of ownership."

Buffett famously wrote "An Owner's Manual" for Berkshire shareholders. He's championed that mindset by keeping more than 99% of his net worth in Berkshire stock, and encouraging the company's other executives and directors to have skin in the game too.

Ferrari also said on the podcast that he has a "pathological love of learning" across different domains. That echoes Buffett's boundless curiosity and the late Charlie Munger's insatiable appetite for knowledge. Buffett's longtime business partner studied architecture, physics, history, meteorology, psychology, law, and, of course, investing, among other subjects.

Beyond their similar philosophies, it's worth noting that investing less than $1 billion into Bending Spoons isn't a huge deal for Berkshire. It has a $1.1 trillion market capitalization, had a $365 billion cash pile at the end of June, and its biggest stock position was worth about $66 billion at that time.

What's the takeaway?

The Bending Spoons deal could mark an evolution in Berkshire's investing style following Buffett's departure as CEO and chairman.

Berkshire hasn't commented on the purchase or on whether Buffett was involved. Its relatively small size could mean his remaining investment manager, Ted Weschler, was behind it.

Or it might be new CEO Greg Abel, who piled an additional $10 billion into Alphabet in a private placement this summer after consulting with Buffett.

Whoever was responsible, and whatever their reasons for investing, this will be an intriguing wager to watch for Berkshire followers.

items.title: Andrew Left wants his fraud conviction tossed after witness gets caught up in insider trading probe
items.summary: Andrew Left's lawyers asked the judge to toss his conviction on 13 counts of securities fraud. Dania Maxwell/Bloomberg/Getty Images A witness who testified against Andrew Left has himself become involved in an insider trading probe. Left's lawyers asked a judge to toss the jury verdict that found him guilty of securities fraud. Prosecutors said they didn't learn about the investigation until after the trial was over. A witness who testified against Andrew Left has himself become involved in an insider trading probe, bringing a new twist to the bombastic short-seller's fraud conviction. Left's lawyers this month asked the judge who oversaw his trial to toss the jury's verdict convicting him of 13 counts of securities fraud. The trial was irredeemably unfair, they said, because they never had the chance to ask the witness about the investigation and attack his credibility. "A new trial would probably produce an acquittal," Left's lawyers wrote. In June, a federal jury in Los Angeles found Left guilty of 13 counts of securities fraud. Prosecutors said he deceived investors by using social media and research reports to set target prices for stocks — including Tesla, Nvidia, and Palantir — while quietly trading them at different prices with his own money. The founder of Citron Research, Left is something of a short-seller celebrity. He placed bets against GameStop at the same time it became a meme stock, which pitted him against some retail traders on social media. For years, he was a fixture on CNBC and Bloomberg, where he shared his views on stock prices. Left hasn't been sentenced. In addition to the criminal case, he faces a parallel civil lawsuit from the Securities and Exchange Commission that remains unresolved. Left's criminal conviction shook certain corners of Wall Street , which viewed the trial as a referendum on free speech and the legality of activist short-seller tactics. Left, testifying in his own defense at the trial , said that the views he shared about public companies were sincere. One of the trial's prosecution witnesses was Daniel Bachus, the CFO of Grand Canyon Education, a publicly traded technology company that provides services to universities. Left's lawyers say that Bachus was the only witness who testified that Left used his Citron Research reports to lie about a company, not merely omit information. On August 21 — weeks after the trial ended — Grand Canyon Education placed Bachus on paid administrative leave "in connection with an ongoing governmental investigation" involving a non-employee's trades of the company's stock, the company said in an SEC disclosure. The prosecutors in Left's case referred to it in their own filings as an "insider trading investigation." No government agency has publicly accused Bachus or Grand Canyon Education of any misconduct in connection with the investigation. In the SEC disclosure, the company said it wasn't the focus of the investigation. Representatives for the SEC and for Grand Canyon Education declined to comment. Bachus didn't respond to Business Insider's requests for comment. Left's lawyers say they should have been informed about the investigation at the time of the trial so that they could cross-examine Bachus and try to convince the jury that he wasn't a credible witness. "This evidence would have destroyed the credibility of the government's only false-statements witness," they wrote in a filing. The prosecution team told Left's lawyers it didn't learn about the investigation until after the trial was over. It's not clear which government agency opened the investigation, nor when Bachus or Grand Canyon Education became aware of it. Many of the filings about the issue remained sealed or redacted on the court docket for Left's case. In court filings, Justice Department prosecutors said Left's lawyers overstated Bachus' role in the short-selling case, which alleged securities fraud involving more than a dozen different public companies. They said Left wanted to conduct "his own shadow investigation into Bachus" to try to discredit him as a witness. "The law does not permit fishing expeditions in search of a claim," prosecutors said. Left declined to comment. Left's attorney Eric S. Rosen said he could not comment because many relevant documents remained under seal. A spokesperson for the US Attorney's office in Los Angeles declined to comment. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: I’m the CEO of Torani, and we've never done layoffs. I believe they're a choice.
items.summary: Torani CEO Melanie Dulbecco has been in the role for 35 years. Torani Melanie Dulbecco has been CEO of the syrup company Torani for 35 years. Dulbecco said layoffs are a choice, and that Torani's decision not to do them has helped with retention. She said that the company is hiring fewer people than it would be if Torani didn't use automation. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Melanie Dulbecco, the CEO of syrup brand Torani. She's based in San Leandro, California, where the company is headquartered. This story has been edited for length and clarity. I may sound different than most CEOs. I grew up in a blue-collar neighborhood, and my parents divorced when I was really young. When I was little, I saw my mom struggle so much, and I noticed that some kids around me didn't have the same opportunities. I felt this sense of inequity, and that became a motivating and driving force for me. I tried working in politics, then nonprofits, and eventually went into business. I wanted to build an opportunity company. When I met the family from Torani, they liked that idea. I was the ninth hire at Torani in 1991 and became the first CEO in 1995. We now have over 500 employees. When I started, we made $700,000 a year in annual revenue. We've grown 20% a year on average, and this year, we plan to hit over $800 million in revenue. But to us, growth is not a financial endeavor. The trailing indicator of success may be the financials, but we think our work together creates the momentum and value in the marketplace that drives our growth. It's very easy for us to say layoffs are not our approach . I think layoffs are a choice. I get it if a company is going through bankruptcy and has to make extremely challenging choices. Otherwise, I think it's a financial exercise that doesn't consider how you're going to be resilient or regain momentum — because you do that with a team. Our workers aren't concerned about being replaced by AI Torani is currently hiring fewer people than it would be if the company didn't use automation. We use automation to deprioritize manual, rote jobs with limited career mobility. We also use AI for consumer and market research, sales forecasting, and demand planning. However, our team doesn't get worried about things like AI because they trust that we will both automate and elevate the work, that we will never do anything that squashes opportunities for people, and that we are looking out for everybody's success. We're often in hyper-growth mode, which means we need people to know how to work together. The ability to work together, to collaborate, to address challenges, to be resilient in tough times, is critical. This strategy has also helped with retention. We were faced with a choice during the pandemic We had been planning a move to our new location in San Leandro in March 2020. That happened to coincide with the stay-at-home order . It was one of those moments where, as a leader, you feel like you have to breathe into a paper bag. We had borrowed a lot of money from the bank to build our new flavor factory. The loans were going to start coming due in April, so the executive team came together to look at what we needed to do to be OK. Before we did that, though, we asked: What will make us proud when we get to the other side of this? We had a long discussion about it and decided that making it as one team — without any layoffs or furloughs — would make us proud. So we we scaled back marketing and advertising expenses and paused all company travel. All departments had to review their budgets. They got scrappy to identify and eliminate non-essential costs. During the early months of the pandemic, Torani prepared for a 50% decline in sales. Thankfully, there was only a 20% decline in April of 2020, and revenue was back up in May. We quickly pivoted to online retail and grocery to fill the gaps left by cafés and drink shops closing their doors. Torani ended 2020 with a 15% year-over-year revenue increase. We moved to our new location in six months instead of six weeks, but we got there. We couldn't have done that if we laid off our team. We needed to come together at that moment.
